description: Sign in as an integration client and make an authenticated request.
reader: integrator
---

Use this sequence for an unattended system. Read [Signing in and tokens](/docs/integrate/signing-in-and-tokens/) for lifetimes and rotation.

1. Ask an administrator to [create a client](/docs/administer/clients/) with only the access your integration needs. Receive the instance address, client ID and one-time secret through your normal secure credential channel. A new client has no access until granted it.
2. Open the [OAuth token operation](/docs/api/?api=management#tag/oauth). Exchange the credentials using the client-credentials grant. Choose management for management operations or consumer for consumer reads. Use one supported credential method; sending both is refused.
3. Keep the returned bearer token in memory or your system's protected token store. Schedule renewal from the returned lifetime. Do not put the secret or token in source files, URLs or diagnostic logs.
4. For management access, call the [caller operation](/docs/api/?api=management#tag/security). For consumer access, read the [API index](/docs/api/?api=management). Check that the intended workspace and API are available. A token can be valid while the necessary grant is absent.
5. Before expiry, exchange the credentials again. Clients do not receive refresh tokens. On an authentication refusal, check the reason before retrying; on a throttled token request, wait for the retry interval.

If the token works but a data call is forbidden, have the administrator review the client's grants for that workspace and API. Reissuing the same token does not add permissions. If the client was deactivated, agree the recovery with its administrator before resuming.

## Make the exchange

This short example is a consumer connection. Set `INSTANCE_URL` to the HTTPS instance address without a trailing slash. Supply `CLIENT_ID` and `CLIENT_SECRET` from your protected credential store; the placeholders are not credentials. The [token operation](/docs/api/?api=management#tag/oauth) describes the complete request contract.

```sh
curl --silent --show-error --fail-with-body \
  --user "$CLIENT_ID:$CLIENT_SECRET" \
  --data-urlencode 'grant_type=client_credentials' \
  --data-urlencode 'scope=consumer' \
  "$INSTANCE_URL/oauth/token"
```

On success, HTTP 200 contains `access_token`, `token_type` equal to `Bearer`, `expires_in` in seconds and `scope` equal to `consumer`. Store the token without printing it in a production log. With `ACCESS_TOKEN` set from that answer, check discovery:

```sh
curl --silent --show-error --fail-with-body \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS_TOKEN" \
  "$INSTANCE_URL/api/consumer?workspace=graubuenden"
```

The workspace in this request is a **reference-data example**. Replace it with the workspace you were granted. The answer lists only APIs this consumer client may read there; an empty `items` list can mean the grant is missing. Follow `nextCursor` when present. For a management connection, exchange with `scope=management` and check the caller operation linked in step 4 instead. Keep separate tokens when one process needs both interfaces.

## Recover or stop

A failed exchange has an OAuth `error` and `error_description`, rather than a data route's `error.code`. For `invalid_client`, check which secret is current, whether its overlap ended and whether the client is active. For `invalid_scope`, check both the requested audience and client kind. A 429 includes `Retry-After`; wait that interval. Do not repeatedly exchange a secret known to have expired.

When retiring an integration, stop scheduled calls and remove its stored token and secret. Ask its administrator to deactivate the client or remove its grants. Deactivation is checked on the next request; deleting a local token alone does not revoke another copy. [Client administration](/docs/administer/clients/) covers rotation and deactivation.
guide/src/content/docs/guide/integrate/l:
---
title: Load, then follow changes
description: Build a complete mirror and continue from the exact position matching its baseline.
reader: integrator
---

Use this sequence to keep another system in step without a gap between its initial load and incremental changes. Read [Following changes](/docs/integrate/following-changes/) for position and retention rules.

1. Give the integration Browse and Feed access in the workspace. Read its [model and capabilities](/docs/api/?api=management#tag/model). Decide the exact scope your mirror holds.
2. Request a live [export](/docs/api/?api=management#tag/exports) of that scope, including required relationships. Wait for the [job](/docs/api/?api=management#tag/jobs) to complete. Save its output metadata, especially the feed position matching its database snapshot. Do not substitute a head read before or after the export.
3. Download the completed output and build the local baseline. Check its size and checksum. Store the baseline and its position together so a restart cannot pair an old dataset with a new checkpoint.
4. Read the [workspace feed](/docs/api/?api=management#tag/workspaces) after that position. Apply creates, updates, deletions and type changes to the mirror, rereading records for values. A deletion removes the local record; a publication marker identifies the snapshot boundary.
5. Commit local effects before saving the returned continuation position. Make replay safe by workspace and position. Follow all pages until the returned continuation equals the head; sparse filtered pages must still advance the checkpoint.
6. After interruption, continue from the stored position. If it expired, reread the publication named in the refusal and continue from its feed position, or repeat the live-export baseline. If it is ahead of the head, check for a wrong workspace or restored database and rebuild the baseline.

A publication is an alternative starting point: page its immutable records and relationships through the [management reads](/docs/api/?api=management#tag/objects), then continue after its feed position. Do not use an unpositioned old publication as a synchronization checkpoint. A filtered feed cannot repair data omitted from an incompatible baseline; keep the scope and recovery policy explicit.

## Use a consumer contract instead

A consumer-only client cannot request management exports or the raw workspace feed. Use the contract's Publications, Lists and Events operations instead. The contract must declare lists covering the objects you need and events covering the changes you need; the reference `stops-changed` event watches code, name and validity, not every stop field.

1. Read the contract's [Publications operation](/docs/api/?api=consumer-stops-v1#consumer-stops-v1/GET/api/consumer/stops/v1/publications). Select a compatible publication with a non-null `eventSequence`. Save its ID and sequence.
2. Page every required list with that explicit publication ID. Keep the same workspace, API name, contract version, filters and publication while traversing. Build a separate local generation and promote it only when all lists finish.
3. Start the contract's [Events operation](/docs/api/?api=consumer-stops-v1#consumer-stops-v1/GET/api/consumer/stops/v1/events) with `after` equal to that publication's sequence. Event reads are live: do not send `publication` on them.
4. After each durable page, save the returned `cursor`, not just the last integer position. Continue with that cursor and without `after`. Several events can share a position. Even a caught-up page's cursor is your next polling checkpoint.
5. Deduplicate by event ID. Full payloads describe the current object, not its state at the event time. For identity payloads, reread the object; it may already have been deleted. Remove local data on deletion and preserve unknown event kinds for reconciliation.

The complete [event example](/docs/integrate/consumer-events-and-webhooks/#a-declaration-and-the-event-it-exposes) shows the envelope, composition position and lasting cursor. A filtered contract can miss a surviving object's departure from a scope; schedule reconciliation of such a mirror. On expired events, rebuild from the baseline identified in the refusal. If no compatible positioned publication exists, arrange one with the people publishing data rather than substituting today's head.

## Restart after a restore or configuration change

Store your baseline and continuation together in your own backups. After either system is restored, verify the instance, workspace and contract before resuming. A checkpoint ahead of the restored server requires a new baseline. Changing scope, model mapping or contract version also needs an explicit reconciliation decision; an old checkpoint does not establish that the new dataset was ever loaded.

To retire a pull mirror, stop polling and archive or remove its local data and checkpoint as required. Pulling creates no server subscription. A webhook mirror additionally needs its [subscription suspended or deleted](/docs/guide/integrate/subscribe-a-webhook-and-verify-it/).
guide/src/content/docs/guide/integrate/m:
---
title: Move records between models
description: Preview a mapped copy or move and publish its target before any source deletion.
reader: integrator
---

Use a model mapping when the destination has a different structure. Counterpart file imports only handle workspaces of the same model. Read [Model and release operations](/docs/integrate/model-and-release-operations/) for the distinction.

1. Read both workspaces' models and release identities. Obtain Browse on the source and Copy and move on the target; a move also needs Work in change sets at the source. Publication requires the relevant publish or approval rights separately.
2. Create or select a [model mapping](/docs/api/?api=management#tag/model%20mappings). Review its type and relationship coverage, parent placements, attribute conversion, defaults and match keys. Resolve its reported problems against the releases the workspaces run.
3. Start a preview through the [move operation](/docs/api/?api=management#tag/moves). Choose copy to leave the source intact, or move to prepare source deletions too. Select the exact records, types or subtree and whether the source is live or a publication. Related records outside the selection are not automatically included.
4. Follow the [job](/docs/api/?api=management#tag/jobs) and page its rows. Review refused and not-moved records, missing parent or relationship mappings, uncarried values and possible duplicates. Correct the mapping and dry-run again when necessary. No data or change set is created by the preview.
5. Confirm the reviewed job. A changed mapping or workspace release refuses confirmation; review another dry run. On success, read the target change-set identity and execution outcomes. Target rules are checked again as the load runs.
6. Review and publish the target change set through the [change-set operations](/docs/api/?api=management#tag/change-sets), following the workspace's approval policy. Until publication, the copied data is absent from consumer reads.
7. For a move, inspect any prepared source-deletion change set. Source records changed since preview or needed by records left behind can be retained with a reason. Publish source deletions only after the target copy is published. If the target copy was discarded, discard the dependent deletion instead of forcing it.

Keep both jobs and change-set identities in your reconciliation record. A completed load prepares changes; it does not mean the full two-workspace transfer has been published.

## Keep the two publication boundaries visible

Save the source selection/context, both releases, mapping key/version, preview job, target change set and any source-deletion change set in one transfer record. Download or retain the row outcomes before job retention removes them. Keep the source-to-target identities, including reused target records, so a retry can be reconciled instead of assumed to be a new copy.

After loading, inspect both change sets and their latest versions before any publication action. A successful target publication makes that side visible. A failed source publication leaves the source records present; it does not undo the target. This intermediate state can be legitimate while conflicts are resolved. Report the transfer as complete only when the intended publication on each side has succeeded, or when the owner deliberately chooses to keep both copies.

If a preview is wrong, cancel it and submit another after correcting the mapping. If loading fails or is cancelled, inspect the job and any linked change sets before starting new work; committed prepared rows are not evidence that the transfer finished. Do not publish a partial target merely to unblock source deletion. If the transfer is abandoned, discard unwanted open change sets through the [change-set operations](/docs/api/?api=management#tag/change-sets), claiming their current versions. A set already published needs a new reviewed correction; job cancellation does not reverse it.

A transfer is not a database restore and creates no ongoing synchronization schedule. Back up the integration's transfer record separately from the instance's [operator backup](/docs/run/backup-and-restore/). Recheck actual publication state after either side is restored.
guide/src/content/docs/guide/integrate/r:
---
title: Read a collection completely and resume
description: Traverse bounded pages and checkpoint a resumable read.
reader: integrator
---

Use cursors to walk an entire collection. Read [Identifiers, paging and errors](/docs/integrate/identifiers-paging-and-errors/) before choosing your checkpoint strategy.

1. Choose the workspace and context. If rows must stay fixed throughout the read, choose a publication. Discover the record type and supported filters through the [model operations](/docs/api/?api=management#tag/model).
2. Request the first page through the [object collection operation](/docs/api/?api=management#tag/objects), with the intended filter and order. Use a bounded page size supported by that operation. Request totals only if the task needs them.
3. Process the page. Make local writes repeatable by public ID. Commit them before storing the continuation cursor; a crash between these steps can replay a page, so make replay harmless.
4. Request the next page with the returned cursor and the same query and context. Continue until there is no next cursor. An individual short page is not your stopping rule.
5. To resume, load the saved query and cursor together. Do not combine it with a newly chosen workspace, sort or filter. On `INVALID_CURSOR`, restart the intended read and reconcile records already stored.

Use a returned anchor to reopen a page, or a position to jump to a row. Neither replaces the continuation checkpoint for reading every row. Live records can change while you traverse them; for ongoing synchronization, use [Load, then follow changes](/docs/guide/integrate/load-then-follow-changes/).

## Keep one durable checkpoint

Store the operation, workspace, context or publication ID, filters, order, business date if present, and continuation cursor as one checkpoint. Keep the consumer API name and contract version too when using a consumer list. This is integration state in your system; include it in that system's backup and restore procedure. A token is renewed separately and is not the checkpoint.

The processing sequence is:

```text
read page using saved query and cursor
upsert each returned record into local storage by public ID
commit local changes
save nextCursor with the unchanged query
repeat while nextCursor is present
```

If your storage can commit rows and the checkpoint in one transaction, do so. Otherwise replay after a crash can repeat the last committed page. An empty first page with no continuation is a complete empty collection. A short page with a continuation still has more to read.

For a fresh full replacement, load into a separate local generation and switch readers to it only after the final page succeeds. Do not delete records missing from an incomplete extract. On a restored local backup, resume its matching checkpoint, not a newer cursor from another machine. If the context is gone or the cursor is rejected, rebuild the generation from a new first page. For live data this is not a consistent snapshot; use a fixed publication when the task needs one.

To stop a read, stop issuing requests and retain or remove the local checkpoint according to whether you plan to resume. A collection read creates no server-side job to cancel.

---
title: Read as of a date
description: Find records effective on one day and keep the date fixed while paging.
reader: integrator
---

Use this when a downstream system needs data valid on a business day. [Business dates](/docs/integrate/business-dates/) explains the boundary rules.

1. Discover the selected context's [model and type](/docs/api/?api=management#tag/model). Confirm that the type declares an effective period. Having date fields is not enough.
2. Choose live data, a change set or a publication. A publication fixes stored content; the business date then filters that content. These are separate choices.
3. Send the date to the [per-type list or model-aware query](/docs/api/?api=management#tag/objects), using a calendar date rather than a timestamp. For a consumer contract, use the dated read described by its [API reference source](/docs/api/).
4. Inspect the result. A record ending on that day is excluded; one starting on it is included. Open ends remain valid without a bound, and overlapping records can both appear. Do not assume exactly one match.
5. Continue with the returned cursor and the same date and context. If related records must also be constrained, express their dates in the query criteria; expansion alone does not date them.

On `AS_OF_NOT_SUPPORTED`, choose a dated type or remove the date intentionally. Do not retry without the date while presenting the answer as dated. For a mixed consumer lookup, check which returned types the engine actually dated.

## Try the reference contract

**Reference-data example:** this request pages the reference contract's stops valid on 2 November 2026. Obtain a consumer token and use the instance's [all-stops operation](/docs/api/?api=consumer-stops-v1#consumer-stops-v1/GET/api/consumer/stops/v1/lists/all-stops):

```http
GET /api/consumer/stops/v1/lists/all-stops?workspace=graubuenden&asOf=2026-11-02&pageSize=20 HTTP/1.1
Host: <instance>
Authorization: Bearer <consumer-token>
Accept: application/json
```

On success, read `items`, check `asOfApplied` and the `RDM-As-Of-Applied` header, then pass `nextCursor` with the same workspace, date and filters. A pinned extract also sends the same publication selection on every page. The date is a calendar day; it is not interpreted in the client's local time zone.

An empty dated list is a valid answer. A known dated object read by ID outside its period gives `OBJECT_NOT_FOUND`. An invalid consumer date gives `INVALID_AS_OF` with the message **asOf must be one calendar date, written YYYY-MM-DD**; correct the value rather than retrying. On a mixed lookup, retain `asOfApplied` with your result so downstream readers know which public types were dated. The full consumer shapes and filtering rules are in [Reading business objects](/docs/integrate/reading-business-objects/).

---
title: Read through a consumer API
description: Discover a contract, choose its data context and read business objects consistently.
reader: integrator
---

Use this sequence when a downstream system needs a stable business representation. Read [Consumer APIs](/docs/integrate/consumer-apis/) for the contract and permission model.

1. Have an administrator [grant the client](/docs/administer/clients/) the intended consumer API in the workspace. [Get a consumer token](/docs/guide/integrate/get-a-token/); a management role alone does not open these reads.
2. Read the [consumer API index](/docs/api/?api=management). For the reference example, request `GET /api/consumer?workspace=graubuenden` and select `stops`, version 1. Its document is `/api/consumer/stops/v1/openapi.json?workspace=graubuenden`. Read [how the declaration becomes routes and outputs](/docs/integrate/consumer-apis/#from-a-declaration-to-a-running-api), then use the instance's document to confirm its shape. An earlier served version has its own entry marked `deprecated: true`, with `sunset` when announced. Select the version your client implements; deprecated does not mean unavailable.
3. Choose live data for current answers, or a publication for a fixed extract. Use the contract's Publications operation to select an available snapshot. Keep its identity; a business date, if supported, filters that snapshot rather than choosing another one.
4. Read a known object ID, or start a declared list. Check that the answer identifies the intended workspace and publication. Apply only documented narrowing parameters.
5. Process each page and follow its next cursor with the same request scope. Persist completed work before the cursor. A cursor started on the current publication continues on that snapshot if a new one is published.
6. For repeated GET reads, retain the ETag and cached body and send a conditional request. On `304`, keep that body. Batch resolution has no such GET cache response.

**Example:** the reference `stops` API offers [List all-stops](/docs/api/?api=consumer-stops-v1#consumer-stops-v1/GET/api/consumer/stops/v1/lists/all-stops) and [Get by ID](/docs/api/?api=consumer-stops-v1#consumer-stops-v1/GET/api/consumer/stops/v1/objects/{id}). Choose the workspace that declares that contract; other models need not offer it.

If an object is not found, check whether its parameters filtered it out or it exists only in unpublished work. If a publication's contract does not match the requested version, choose a compatible snapshot explicitly. Do not substitute live data without changing the integration's stated guarantees.

## When the version is being retired

Watch `Deprecation` and `Sunset` on the version you use. The model administrator chooses
its notice period; a sunset day does not itself stop service. Arrange migration to a tested
replacement before the administrator removes the version. Each retained version continues
reading current data through its own definition.

`404 CONTRACT_VERSION_NOT_FOUND` means the workspace no longer serves the requested number.
Read `details.servedContractVersions`, rediscover the index and inspect the replacement’s
document. Do not automatically retry another version with the same parser. An older
publication cannot restore a version that the workspace no longer serves. See
[Earlier contract versions](/docs/integrate/consumer-apis/#earlier-contract-versions).

## Work through the reference contract

The `stops` contract is one configuration. Use these exact paths only in a workspace declaring it. Supply a consumer-audience bearer token with the API's workspace grant:

```http
GET /api/consumer/stops/v1/objects/8d90eede-23cf-47c1-8dac-cb37956f5fd5?workspace=graubuenden HTTP/1.1
Host: <instance>
Authorization: Bearer <consumer-token>
Accept: application/json
```

The 200 body is the shared `Stop` object for Tschamut-Selva: the stop number, typed fields, parent, ancestor path, operator, modes, system codes and translations. It is not wrapped in `items`. Check the [complete response](/docs/integrate/reading-business-objects/#a-complete-object-read) before coding a client that expects another shape.

To enumerate stops, use a list instead:

```http
GET /api/consumer/stops/v1/lists/all-stops?workspace=graubuenden&pageSize=1&includeTotal=true HTTP/1.1
Host: <instance>
Authorization: Bearer <consumer-token>
Accept: application/json
```

This answers an `items` array plus `workspace`, `publication` and paging fields. Process the first page, save its next cursor after committing local work, and send that cursor with the same request scope. See the [complete first-page body and continuation rules](/docs/integrate/reading-business-objects/#a-list-page-with-navigation).

To read only stops for one operator, start a new request with `operator=MGB-fo`. The declaration matches operator code or name and requires a matching relationship. The result begins with Tschamut-Selva and counts 13 stops in the reference snapshot. The [parameter example](/docs/integrate/reading-business-objects/#the-same-list-narrowed-by-a-declared-parameter) shows the complete body. Do not reuse the unfiltered cursor.

Finally repeat a GET with its saved ETag in `If-None-Match`. A 304 has no body; retain the previous one. The [unchanged-response exchange](/docs/integrate/reading-business-objects/#reuse-an-unchanged-answer) shows both headers and the absence of a response body. For a missing list or refused filter, correct the declaration name or request rather than accepting an empty extract.

*Source: opentransportdata.swiss, Service Points (Didok), Federal Office of Transport / SBB, snapshot 2026-11-02. Wikidata, CC0.*

---
title: Resolve a file of codes
description: Resolve keyed source rows and keep missing, ambiguous and rejected results separate.
reader: integrator
---

Use consumer resolution to identify records without changing them. Read [Looking up and resolving](/docs/integrate/looking-up-and-resolving/) for scores, targets and limits.

1. Discover the contract and obtain a consumer token with the appropriate workspace grant. Inspect the contract's [resolution operation](/docs/api/) and declared parameters. Choose live data or one publication for the entire file.
2. Keep each source row's own reference. Decide which known facts narrow the question, such as public type or source system. Put shared facts in defaults and override them only where a row differs.
3. Build bounded batches, at most the configured maximum (1,000 by default). Each item supplies a query or an existing record ID, never both. Preserve multi-value terms as JSON values; do not split commas inside actual codes.
4. Submit the read through Batch resolve. **Example:** the reference contract's [Batch resolve](/docs/api/?api=consumer-stops-v1#consumer-stops-v1/POST/api/consumer/stops/v1/resolve) can resolve the fictional Regional ticketing system's codes to stops. If another representation is needed, request one declared target parameter.
5. Reconcile outcomes in source-row order. Store found identities; return no-match and target-not-found items for source correction. Return ambiguous source or target items for disambiguation. Keep request errors separate from valid questions with no answer.
6. Retry corrected questions using additional known facts, without forcing the first tied match. A broad-query refusal needs more specific terms. A batch-size refusal needs smaller batches; a publication mismatch needs a compatible baseline.

**Reference-data example:** `T-9999` is deliberately unmapped and `T-0300` deliberately points to two stops. Both are fictional codes. A reliable integration preserves that distinction instead of inventing an answer.

## Try two rows from the reference world

The reference declaration offers Resolve because it declares both Get by ID and XREF. For a file of known stop numbers and supplier codes, send a bounded read like this. The mode default narrows both questions to records with a matching train mode; an item can override a default parameter.

```http
POST /api/consumer/stops/v1/resolve?workspace=graubuenden HTTP/1.1
Host: <instance>
Authorization: Bearer <consumer-token>
Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json

{
  "defaults": {"mode": "TRAIN"},
  "items": [
    {"ref": "row-1", "query": "8505173"},
    {"ref": "row-2", "query": "T-9999"}
  ]
}
```

The complete [response body](/docs/integrate/looking-up-and-resolving/#resolve-a-small-file-in-one-request) has two outcomes, in that order. Row 1 is `found`, with Tschamut-Selva's full object and `matchScore: 900` from the declared stop-number rule. Row 2 is `not_found` with `NO_MATCH`; the fictional code has no mapping. The counts are one found and one not found. An HTTP 200 is not a reason to mark both source rows as resolved.

For another system's representation, use a declared target such as `to.system=wikidata-stations` on a single lookup or as a resolution parameter. The [full crosswalk example](/docs/integrate/looking-up-and-resolving/#a-crosswalk-from-a-stop-number-to-another-systems-code) explains why the resulting code is a `target` separate from the source stop. If no unique target exists, correct the mapping or target restriction; do not substitute the source's code.

Keep each row's original reference, input, outcome and chosen publication together for reconciliation. A later retry against live data may legitimately resolve differently after a steward corrects the mappings.

*Source: opentransportdata.swiss, Service Points (Didok), Federal Office of Transport / SBB, snapshot 2026-11-02. Regional ticketing codes are fictional.*
guide/src/content/docs/guide/integrate/s:
---
title: Submit a bulk change
description: Prepare a bounded batch, inspect its preview and reconcile every outcome.
reader: integrator
---

Use a batch when your source supplies several changes together. Read [Writing in bulk](/docs/integrate/writing-in-bulk/) for policies and limits.

1. Read the target workspace's [model and capabilities](/docs/api/?api=management#tag/model). Decide whether changes go live or into a change set. Keep the model release and current version claims.
2. Prepare items in dependency order: parents before children, then relationships that need those records. Use public IDs or declared unique keys. Choose atomic if nothing may apply on a refusal, or independent if valid items may apply separately.
3. Submit through the [batch operation](/docs/api/?api=management#tag/jobs), with an idempotency key saved beside the exact request. Choose background preview if you need to review the changes, including cascading deletion impact. Inline execution cannot preview.
4. Follow the returned [job](/docs/integrate/jobs/). In a preview, inspect proposed outcomes, the policy result and whether coverage is complete. A sample does not prove the remaining items are valid. Confirm through the [job confirmation operation](/docs/api/?api=management#tag/jobs), or cancel without applying changes.
5. After execution, page every item outcome. Record committed IDs and versions, correct rejected source items and inspect why unprocessed items stopped. A successful HTTP response alone does not mean the batch applied completely.
6. If the response was lost, replay the exact keyed request. If data was refused for stale versions or changed deletion impact, reread or preview before building a corrected request with a new key. Never change a request under an existing key.

For independent work, retain earlier committed outcomes when a job fails or is cancelled. For an atomic refusal, nothing from the batch applied. Check which case occurred before planning a retry.

## Keep a reconciliation ledger

For each submitted batch, save the exact request, idempotency key, workspace, model release, job ID and your source-row references. Record the policy and whether it was preview or execution. Keep the credentials separately. The [batch and job operations](/docs/api/?api=management#tag/jobs) define the request and result fields.

After confirmation, wait for a final job state and page item outcomes until there is no continuation. Separate applied changes, unchanged applied items, rejected items and unprocessed items. For example, if an independent batch loads a parent but refuses a child, keep the committed parent's ID. Correct the child and any dependent relationships without blindly recreating that parent.

A correction is a new request with a new key. A network retry is the same saved request with the same key. If the old key has expired, first reconcile IDs, unique keys and versions against current data: the server can no longer recognise it as a replay. Cancel a pending job when abandoning it, then inspect what committed before cancellation. Cancelling or deleting your local ledger does not undo those changes.

## Change relationship values from a grid selection

Use this sequence when an integration needs to set one scalar value across many connections,
possibly linking missing pairs. It uses the synchronous
[grid-change operation](/docs/api/?api=management#tag/relations/POST/api/v1/relations/grid-change),
not the job submission and confirmation sequence above. Read
[Relationships and their values](/docs/integrate/relationships-and-their-values/) for the
read models, permissions and version rules.

1. Read the model and the
   [grid](/docs/api/?api=management#tag/relations/GET/api/v1/workspaces/{workspace_key}/relation-grid).
   Keep the workspace, application, relationships-table view and context. Confirm that the
   binding carries the attribute you intend to change. JSON values cannot use this operation.
2. Choose source rows either by `fromObjectIds`, or by `allMatching: true` with the grid's
   search and filters, minus `exceptObjectIds`. Use exactly one selection method. Search,
   filters and exceptions belong only to all-matching selection. Each body filter includes
   `field`, `operator` and its lexical `value`; operators have the same meaning as in the grid read.
3. Choose 1–50 `toObjectIds`. These are the column records to affect, not every column the
   workspace could supply. Preserve the intended column IDs when a grid read reports more
   matching columns than it can show. A relationship-value filter matches through a connection
   to these selected columns.
4. Send `dryRun: true` with the value and `linkMissing` choice. Null clears the named attribute;
   false sets a Yes or no value to No. Missing connections are left alone unless
   `linkMissing: true` asks to create them with that value.
5. Read `change`, `same`, `missing`, `linked` and every `refused` item. Use each item's
   `fromObjectId` and `toObjectId` to identify the pair in your source data, including refusals
   for existing relationships. A refused new link has `relationId: null`. The preview checks all
   selected pairs, not a sample. A 200 preview with refusals is not permission to apply a
   partial result. Correct the selection, model rule or value first.
6. Send the reviewed selection with `dryRun: false`. The operation checks current data again
   and applies all changes together. It does not accept a saved preview token or a relationship
   version per pair: an intervening live edit can change what the selection matches. If exact
   per-connection version claims are required, use the batch sequence below.
7. Reread the result, including rows hidden by a filter on the old value. For a change set,
   supply `changeSetId` and `expectedChangeSetVersion` on both requests. Keep the apply's returned
   `changeSetVersion`; the dry run does not advance it. Review and publish separately.

**Reference-data example:** the Network application's `stop-operators` grid reads the
stop-to-operator binding. It carries Local name (`local-name`), Primary contact (`is-primary`)
and Inspected on (`inspected-on`). To preview setting Primary contact on Tschamut-Selva's
connection to Matterhorn Gotthard Bahn (fo):

```http
POST /api/v1/relations/grid-change HTTP/1.1
Host: <instance>
Authorization: Bearer <management-token>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "workspaceKey": "graubuenden",
  "applicationKey": "network",
  "viewKey": "stop-operators",
  "fromObjectIds": ["8d90eede-23cf-47c1-8dac-cb37956f5fd5"],
  "toObjectIds": ["f94ef862-2a95-4675-9e31-6b1d0a03317f"],
  "attributeTypeKey": "is-primary",
  "value": true,
  "linkMissing": false,
  "dryRun": true
}
```

The reference instance returns this preview: the connection exists and has no Primary contact value.

```json
{
  "dryRun": true,
  "change": 1,
  "same": 0,
  "missing": 0,
  "linked": 0,
  "refused": [],
  "changeSetVersion": null
}
```

For a filtered selection, replace `fromObjectIds` with, for example:

```json
{
  "allMatching": true,
  "exceptObjectIds": [],
  "search": "",
  "filters": [{"field": "relation:is-primary", "operator": "isNull", "value": "true"}]
}
```

This is a selection excerpt, not a whole request: retain the workspace, view, column IDs,
attribute, value and preview choice from the request above. It selects source records with an
existing connection to one of those columns whose primary value is empty. It does not select
unlinked pairs merely because they have no primary value.

An apply refusal is `RELATION_BATCH_REFUSED` (409 for a stale version, otherwise 422), with
item codes and messages in `details.items`, and writes nothing. Reconcile each refused pair
using its endpoint IDs, just as in the dry run; keep its relationship ID when present. The
[grid-change operation](/docs/api/?api=management#tag/relations/POST/api/v1/relations/grid-change)
describes the result fields. `422 INVALID_GRID_CHANGE` means the attribute,
value or endpoint type is invalid. Model or request-shape errors must be corrected, not retried
unchanged. `413 BATCH_TOO_LARGE` reports the `ATOMIC_JOB_MAX_ITEMS` ceiling, including during
a dry run. The limit counts values that would change plus missing pairs to link, not source
rows. Narrow rows or columns, or coordinate a limit change with the operator.

## Change values on known relationship IDs

1. Read each relationship's full attributes and `relationVersion`, keeping its workspace or
   change-set context. Use the relationship's version, not its endpoint's or mapping set's version.
2. Submit the [relationship-value batch](/docs/api/?api=management#tag/relations/POST/api/v1/relations/batch)
   with one item per relationship. Supply its `id`, `expectedVersion` and only the attributes
   to set or clear. The batch merges these values; null clears a named value and omitted
   attributes stay. A single [relationship PATCH](/docs/api/?api=management#tag/relations/PATCH/api/v1/relations/{relation_id})
   instead replaces the full attribute set.
3. For Live, name `workspaceKey`; for a change set, include `changeSetId` and
   `expectedChangeSetVersion`. On success, retain returned relationship versions and any
   `changeSetVersion`. Results follow input order.
4. On `RELATION_BATCH_REFUSED`, reconcile `details.items` by index, relationship ID and item
   error code. Each item also carries `fromObjectId` and `toObjectId` when the relationship
   still exists, so you can identify its pair in your source data. If the relationship cannot
   be found, use the index and relationship ID instead; endpoint IDs are absent. A stale item
   makes the response 409, other refusals 422, and nothing applies.
   Read current values before sending corrected version claims. Repeating an ID is
   `DUPLICATE_BATCH_ITEMS`; an oversized request is `413 BATCH_TOO_LARGE` under `BATCH_MAX_ITEMS`.

This direct batch has no background job or job-confirmation step. After a lost response, read
the relationships to reconcile their state before sending another write.

*Reference names and identities: Source: opentransportdata.swiss, Service Points (Didok), Federal
Office of Transport / SBB, snapshot 2026-11-02. Relationship values are sample data; the preview above was captured from the reference instance without applying it.*

---
title: Subscribe a webhook and verify it
description: Prepare a receiver, verify signatures and recover delivery without missing changes.
reader: integrator
---

Use a webhook when refiroo should send declared events to your endpoint. Read [Consumer events and webhooks](/docs/integrate/consumer-events-and-webhooks/) for payload timing, ordering and retry rules.

1. Confirm with the operator that webhook subscriptions are enabled. Obtain Integration administration in the intended workspace. Inspect the contract's Events operation and choose the events and filters. For the reference model, inspect [stops Events](/docs/api/?api=consumer-stops-v1#consumer-stops-v1/GET/api/consumer/stops/v1/events). Do not assume another model has that event.
2. Prepare an HTTPS receiver that retains raw request bytes, verifies signatures before handling data and acknowledges durably accepted work within 10 seconds. Make event handling repeatable by event ID. Accept both selected formats and batch sizes only as agreed; allow an oversized single object beyond the normal 1 MiB batch boundary.
3. Create the subscription through the [subscription operation](/docs/api/?api=management#tag/consumer%20subscriptions), selecting the workspace, contract, event names, receiver, filters, representation and batching. Supply `contractVersion` to select a served earlier version; omitting it selects the current version. Read [Earlier-contract subscriptions](/docs/integrate/consumer-events-and-webhooks/#keep-a-receiver-on-an-earlier-contract) before choosing. Save the one-time signing secret directly to protected receiver configuration. For browser setup, open **Settings › Connections › Webhooks**. See [Clients for other systems](/docs/administer/clients/) for client access.
4. Verify a delivery using its timestamp plus a dot plus the raw body bytes, with HMAC-SHA256 keyed by the secret exactly as issued. Reject stale timestamps and compare each comma-separated signature in constant time. Accept if one supported signature verifies. Return a 2xx after storing the work safely.
5. Inspect the [delivery log](/docs/api/?api=management#tag/consumer%20subscriptions). Check successful acknowledgment and your local deduplication record. A timeout can cause repeat delivery even if your receiver processed the first request. Automatic retries can contain newer object values for the same event.
6. Rotate the signing key with an overlap, install the new secret in the receiver, verify it works and let the old key end. Keep multi-signature support: it is needed during rotation and on retries.
7. If delivery pauses, read its reason before resuming. Correct the receiver or filter and continue from the first unacknowledged event. If events expired, follow the recovery choices below. Reset skips the undelivered range; a publication older than the reset is insufficient on its own.

Manual resend repeats a stored event in its original format, with the same event ID and a manual-redelivery indication. It is one attempt and does not repair the ordinary delivery checkpoint. Use it deliberately when testing or recovering receiver processing, and retain ordinary deduplication for automatic retries.

## Use the reference event end to end

The `stops` declaration watches code, name and validity outputs through `stops-changed`. Read its [declaration and complete event page](/docs/integrate/consumer-events-and-webhooks/#a-declaration-and-the-event-it-exposes). A height-only edit does not exercise this watched event; a name change does. Use an intentional change in a suitable workspace when testing your receiver.

With a management token holding Integration administration in that workspace, create an identity-payload subscription:

```http
POST /api/v1/consumer-subscriptions HTTP/1.1
Host: <instance>
Authorization: Bearer <management-token>
Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json

{
  "name": "Stop mirror",
  "consumerApi": "stops",
  "workspaceKey": "graubuenden",
  "events": ["stops-changed"],
  "url": "https://receiver.example/refiroo-events",
  "payload": "identity",
  "format": "rdm",
  "maxEventsPerBatch": 1
}
```

Replace the reserved example receiver address with your own HTTPS endpoint. The successful creation returns 201 with the subscription and a one-time `signingSecret`. Store that exact secret in the receiver; do not log it. Retain the subscription's ID, version and acknowledgment position. Consumer grants for reading data and Integration administration for subscriptions are separate permissions.

When a matching change commits, the receiver gets the [complete signed request shown here](/docs/integrate/consumer-events-and-webhooks/#the-actual-webhook-request-shape). Its RDM envelope holds `deliveryId`, `subscriptionId`, the API, version, workspace and an `events` array. Identity payloads carry enough identity to fetch current data but omit the full object. Select `payload: full` if your receiver needs the current shared object in the event instead.

Apply the [verification function](/docs/integrate/consumer-events-and-webhooks/#verify-the-bytes-before-decoding-json) to raw bytes before JSON decoding. The page's demonstration key and dated timestamp reproduce the sample signature only; the real receiver uses its actual secret and current time. Confirm that changing a single body byte fails verification and that an old timestamp is refused. Then durably queue the verified event, make processing repeatable by event ID and acknowledge with a 2xx.

Inspect the delivery log and your receiver's stored event ID together. If processing failed after acknowledgment, use a deliberate manual resend and account for its same event ID. If the sender is retrying, repair the receiver and allow the ordered retry to finish. If the subscription has expired events, rebuild its baseline using the sequence below; a manual resend does not repair its ordinary checkpoint.

## Recover an expired subscription

Choose one recovery boundary explicitly. Keep deliveries durably queued while rebuilding a baseline, and make replay safe by event ID.

- **Keep a retained publication as the baseline.** Select a compatible publication with a non-null `eventSequence`. Create a replacement subscription with `startAfter` equal to that sequence, rather than accepting its default of today's head. If that position is still available, load the publication's lists and then reconcile queued events. Retire the old subscription after the replacement works. An expired position is refused: choose another usable baseline, not an arbitrary later number.
- **Reset the existing subscription.** Read its current version and resume with reset. Record its new acknowledgment position, then arrange a fresh baseline at or after that position: for example, a new publication made after the reset, or a live export taken after it by a suitably authorised management client. Load that baseline and reconcile the queued events. Do not load an older publication and discard its intervening changes.

The [load-and-follow sequence](/docs/guide/integrate/load-then-follow-changes/) explains baseline checkpoints. When replaying queued notifications after loading the baseline, prefer current-object reads for creates and updates so an older notification cannot replace newer baseline values. Deletions remove local objects. A filtered mirror also needs reconciliation of surviving objects that left its scope.

## Change or retire the connection

To move the receiver, deploy its secret and durable queue/deduplication state at the new endpoint, then edit the URL with the subscription's current version. An edit restarts any pending delivery from the unacknowledged point. Verify acknowledgments at the new receiver before decommissioning the old one; allow for a request already in flight.

A subscription retains its accepted contract while that version remains served. A model release
that stops it can suspend delivery with `CONTRACT_VERSION_CHANGED`; missing events or filters
produce `MODEL_CHANGED` findings instead. Read the replacement document and update the receiver
before resuming on the current version. A sunset date alone does not pause delivery.

Suspend for a temporary stop. Resume without reset after fixing the cause if its unacknowledged range remains available. To retire it, save the delivery records you need, then delete it with the current version through the [subscription operations](/docs/api/?api=management#tag/consumer%20subscriptions). Deletion also removes the delivery log; it does not reverse work already accepted by the receiver. Remove unused receiver secrets and local schedules once the connection is retired.

---
title: Add a record type and fields
description: Define where a type stands, add typed fields and reuse existing attributes.
reader: model-admin
---

Work in an editable draft with **Model authoring** access. If needed,
[create a draft](/docs/guide/model/create-a-model-draft/) first.
[The model editor](/docs/model/the-model-editor/) explains the panes and saved steps.

## Add the type

1. Select the application that should list the type. If the draft is empty, use **Application**
   to add one first, enter its name and apply it.
2. In the application's **Object types** section, choose **Object type**. In **Add an object type**,
   enter **Name** and, if needed, **Plural name**. Leaving the plural empty uses the name with an s;
   fill it explicitly when that would read incorrectly.
3. Choose **Stands**: **At the top level** for independent records, or **Under** a type for children.
   For children, choose the **Containment relation**. If creating one, fill both **Relation name
   (from the parent)** and **Reverse name (from the child)**. These describe the same connection
   from each end.
4. Choose **Apply**. The type appears in the model pane and application table. A new type gets
   a generated table view and record page. Check where it stands before adding fields. If Apply
   is unavailable, complete the required names and choices; read any refusal before trying again.

![Add an object type dialog showing its parent and containment relation fields](/docs/screens/model-hierarchy-dialog.png)

*Above: Platform is proposed Under Stop in Network. Both containment names still need filling;
the captured dialog was cancelled, so no Platform type was added.*

Containment defines record hierarchy, not merely indentation in the editor. Use **Move to…**
when you need to change placement; moving a released type used by data may need migration.

## Add fields with the right value types

1. Select the type and open **Attributes**. Review the existing rows before creating another field.
2. Choose **New attribute**. Enter **Name** and select **Value type**: for example **Text**,
   **Long text**, **Whole number**, **Decimal number**, **Yes or no**, **Date**, **Date and time**
   or **JSON** for structured values.
   Choose for the value's meaning, not its appearance in a spreadsheet. A code containing leading
   zeroes may need text, even if every character is a digit.
3. Review **Features**. **Searchable** includes the field in record search. **Filterable** allows
   filtering; the view decides which filter controls it shows. **Unique** prevents another record
   in the workspace from holding that attribute value. It is an attribute-wide rule, including
   other types that share the attribute. **Sortable** is still shown, but ordinary non-structured
   fields sort from list headers regardless of that checkbox.
4. Choose **Required** if records of this type must hold a value. Consider existing records:
   making a field mandatory does not fill it for them. Choose **Apply** and wait for the row.
5. Check its value type, Required and Unique settings. The new row is marked **New**, its type
   may be **Changed**, and the header's draft version advances. Expand **Issues and history**
   to see the saved step. No live record has acquired a value from adding the definition alone.

![New attribute dialog with name, value type, features and Required](/docs/screens/model-field-dialog.png)

*Above: Step-free access is being added to Stop as Yes or no, with Required unticked.*

![Attributes table showing the new field and the updated draft version](/docs/screens/model-field-added.png)

*Above: Step-free access is New, Stop is Changed and Guide draft has reached version 2.*

## Reuse or adjust a field

Choose **Attach an existing one…** when the same field definition already exists. Review **Shared
with** before changing its definition: renaming a shared attribute affects every type that uses it.
Required and Read-only can differ by type. Read-only prevents ordinary value editing; it does not
supply a value automatically.

Select an editable setting cell, choose the value and use **Save**, or **Cancel** to leave it
unchanged. A refusal on a released field means you must review its existing data and the migration
requirement rather than forcing the edit. The visual editor refuses a released field’s
value-type change when it affects stored values. Ask a specialist model author to prepare
that change in [the JSON view](/docs/guide/model/edit-a-draft-as-json/), save and compare
the draft, and install the target release. Then
[review the workspace migration](/docs/guide/model/migrate-a-workspace/) before converting
data. A draft save alone changes no stored record values.

![Required setting opened in place with Save and Cancel](/docs/screens/model-type-required-edit.png)

*Above: Abbreviation's Required choice is open on Stop. This capture was cancelled without changing it.*

Check [Issues](/docs/guide/model/fix-issues-before-installing/), then
[arrange the layout](/docs/guide/model/arrange-applications-and-views/) before releasing.

A list of allowed records is a relationship to a list type, rather than another field value
type. **Turn into a list type…** on an attribute asks for the relationship's name and which
records may be chosen. Configure its candidate criteria as described in
[Add a relationship](/docs/guide/model/add-a-relationship/#limit-which-records-can-be-chosen).
After adding fields, open the type’s **Settings**. Edit **Display attribute** to choose which
attached field names records in lists, links and titles, or choose **None: records are named
by their name**. Edit **At least one of** to select fields of which one must hold a value;
clear the selection to remove that requirement.

For business validity, attach two **Date** fields, then edit **Effective period**. Select
**Starts on** and **Ends on**, and **Apply**. The fields must differ; the end is exclusive and
must be later than the start when both are filled. Empty dates leave that end open. Adding
the rule does not repair existing dates: review compatibility before activation.

![Type Settings with display attribute, effective period and grouped requirement](/docs/screens/model-type-settings.png)

Default values still need a specialist; see [the JSON view](/docs/model/json-view/).
Text-format and length rules are not offered by these controls.

---
title: Add a relation matrix
description: Choose row, cell and column types and the actions people can use in a matrix.
reader: model-admin
---

Open a draft with **Model authoring**. A matrix needs row records related to cell records that
stand under column records. See [Applications and views](/docs/model/applications-and-views/).

1. Select an application and choose **Add a relation matrix…** from its menu, or **Relation
   matrix** in its panel. The form has a preview beside it.
2. Choose **Rows**, then **Each cell shows**. Read the explanation of the relationship offered.
   If a type is missing, check its allowed relationships and the cell type's parent structure.
3. Choose **Columns**. There is one column per record of a type the cell records sit under.
   Choose **Column heading** to identify those column records clearly.
4. Choose and order **Fields in a cell** and **Row columns**. Use the add, remove and up/down
   controls to inspect the intended order. The first text or number cell field is used for the
   cell display; if none is available, it uses the record name.
5. Set **What people can do in a cell** from the offered **Create**, **Edit**, **Link existing**
   and **Unlink** choices. Availability depends on the declared structure. A checked action
   still needs the person's record or relationship permissions at runtime.
6. Enter **Name**, inspect the preview and choose **Apply**. Review **Issues** before installing.
   A preview is a design aid, not proof that every user has permission to perform its actions.
7. For an existing relation matrix, open its row in **Views** and choose **Change…**. Use
   **Rename…** for its label or **Remove relation matrix** to remove the view. Removing the
   view does not delete the data it displayed. **Undo** can restore the draft step.

## Choose the cell actions

For an existing view, select the application, find the matrix in **Views**, open its menu and
choose **Change…**. In **What people can do in a cell**, select any offered combination:

- **Create** makes a record and connects it to the row. The creation form uses the relationship's rules and the groups already holding this view's
  records to suggest where it belongs under the column. It can propose a missing group,
  without a model change; the person checks the proposal or chooses another eligible group.
  See [Where new records go](/docs/use/importing-and-exporting/#matrix-cells-and-new-records). Create is offered only when **Fields in a cell**
  includes every required field, and creation needs no other required incoming relationship
  beyond the one this cell supplies. Parent containment is handled separately.
- **Edit** allows editing the displayed record fields. It is offered when at least one selected
  cell field is writable.
- **Link existing** connects a record already under the column. It is offered in the editor,
  but each candidate must satisfy the relationship rules when someone uses the matrix.
- **Unlink** removes a connection and keeps the record. It is not offered for a required
  relationship.

Choose **Apply**, review **Issues**, then install and activate the release through your usual
[model release process](/docs/model/releases/). Check the actions after changing
row types or cell fields: dependent choices can be reset or removed when they no longer fit.

For a translation matrix, Create and Edit can support one name per language. For a mapping
matrix, Create and Link existing let people choose between a new code and reuse of an existing
code. Reuse creates another relationship to the same record, which keeps its identity for
connected systems after publication. These are model choices, not separate kinds of application.
A filled one-per-cell matrix suppresses Create even when the view enables it; see
[Relation matrices](/docs/use/relation-matrices/#what-you-can-change-from-a-cell).

![Relation matrix choices with ordered cell fields and a preview](/docs/screens/model-view-matrix-dialog.png)

*Example: Municipality rows connect to System code cells, which stand under System columns.*

A **Not applied** notice leaves the attempted change unapplied; read its reason and correct
the structure or choices. Saving this view in a draft does not change the live application.

Adding a matrix also adds any type listings it needs to the application in the same step.
Records retain their owning applications. Removing the matrix can remove listings needed only
by that view; a released listing in use can require migration. Inspect the removal confirmation
and Issues rather than assuming the view is the only affected definition.

---
title: Add a relationship
description: Allow two record types to connect, with forward and reverse names and the intended limits.
reader: model-admin
---

Allow a relationship in a draft before people can create it between records. You need **Model
authoring**. A relation type gives the connection its meaning; an allowed pair determines which
types it may join. See [Types, attributes and relations](/docs/model/types-attributes-relations/).

## Inspect existing connections

1. Open the draft and select the type at the intended **from** end.
2. Choose **Relations**. Read **From → to**, **Cardinality**, **Required** and **Which records**.
   The list includes incoming as well as outgoing relationships, so use the direction column
   rather than assuming every row starts from the selected type.
3. If the connection already exists, inspect its row instead of creating a second relation type
   with the same meaning. **Which records** can limit the permitted endpoints beyond their types.

![Relations table showing directions, cardinalities, requirements and endpoint restrictions](/docs/screens/model-relations.png)

*Above: Stop has outgoing relationships to Mode and Operator, incoming containment from Municipality
and incoming system-code relationships restricted by their parent systems.*

## Allow the pair

1. Choose **Allow a relation…**. Select **To**, the target record type.
2. Under **Relation type**, reuse an existing meaning where appropriate, or choose **A new relation
   type**. For a new one, enter **Name (from …)** and **Reverse name**. Read them as sentences from
   both ends so people understand the same relationship whichever record they open.
3. Set **Cardinality** using the from and to types shown below. Do not infer it from the plural
   wording of a label.
4. Review **Required**. This is a dependent-ownership rule, not a general request that every source
   record have a target. For the supported required one-to-one or one-to-many connection, the
   target is created with its owner relationship. **Many to one** cannot be required. Leave it
   unticked for an optional association.
5. Choose **Apply**. Check the new row's direction and limits, its **New** mark and the saved
   history step. If refused, correct the named combination or migration problem. **Cancel**
   leaves the draft unchanged.

| Cardinality | What it permits |
| --- | --- |
| Many to one | Each source has at most one target; a target may serve many sources. |
| One to many | A source may have many targets; each target has at most one source. |
| One to one | At most one at each end. |
| Many to many | Neither end is limited to one by this setting. |

![Allow a relation dialog with target, forward and reverse names and cardinality](/docs/screens/model-relation-dialog.png)

*Above: Stop to Operator is given the new names Inspected by and Inspects, with Many to one and
Required unticked. It is separate from the existing Operated by relationship.*

![Relations table with the newly allowed relationship marked New](/docs/screens/model-relation-added.png)

*Above: Inspected by now appears beside Stop's released relationships. No actual inspection
relationship between records was created by this draft step.*

## Check the whole structure

Choose **Open the relationship matrix**, or **Relationship matrix** in the model pane. Rows are
from types and columns are to types. Select a cell for that ordered pair. Arrow keys move between
cells and Enter selects a pair. Containment is labelled **contains**.

![Relationship matrix with from types as rows and to types as columns](/docs/screens/model-matrix.png)

*Above: Guide draft's matrix shows the containment chain and permitted system-code mappings. The
new Inspected by relation is also listed in the model pane.*

For parent-child hierarchy, use the type's **Stands** and containment controls described in
[Add a record type and fields](/docs/guide/model/add-a-record-type-and-fields/).
Then [check issues](/docs/guide/model/fix-issues-before-installing/) and preview the type's generated
relationship panels before activation.

## Limit which records can be chosen

1. On **Relations**, open the **Which records** cell, or the row menu's
   **Which records may be chosen…**. The criteria editor separates the two ends; check which
   type's choices you are changing.
2. Add criteria on the name, a field or a field of an ancestor. Choose the condition and value
   for the intended end. Several criteria are combined with “and”; several **is** choices on
   one field are alternatives.
3. Apply the change and inspect the row's summary. These conditions restrict new choices in
   every record picker, not just one panel. Existing relationships remain if a record later
   stops meeting the condition. Recheck Issues before activation.

A relation type's names and reverse name describe the connection from both ends. Its key and
reverse key are stable once released; changing its wording does not create a new identity.
In **Relationship matrix**, selecting a pair opens its relations' menus and the action to allow
another; resize the selected-pair panel if the choices need more room.

## Choose what each relationship carries

1. On **Relations**, edit the pair’s **Carries** cell or choose **Attributes of the relationship…**
   from its menu. If there are no attribute types, create the shared definitions first.
2. Select the **Attributes** whose values belong to the connection itself, then **Apply**.
   Carries now names them; an empty selection reads **Nothing**. Endpoints’ fields are unchanged.
   Select shared definitions of the right value type: a date stays a date, and a Yes or no value
   becomes a checkbox. Check the from and to types in the dialog title: this choice applies to
   that directed pair, not every pair using the relation type.
3. To revise limits together, choose **Cardinality and required…** and apply the intended
   combination. Released pairs may withhold these structural actions. Use the refusal and
   compatibility check to decide whether a migration is necessary.
4. Select the shared **Relation type** to review both names and its **Settings**. Change
   **Oriented** only after reviewing its effect on record deletion; see
   [relationship settings](/docs/model/types-attributes-relations/#visibility-help-and-relationship-settings).

![Allowed relationship showing Carries beside number limits and candidate criteria](/docs/screens/model-relation-carries.png)

After installation, check the relationship's columns on a record or in a matrix cell. To give
people a dedicated view for these values, [add a relationships table](/docs/guide/model/add-a-relationships-table/).
To expose them to another system, [choose them in a consumer API's related block](/docs/guide/model/define-a-consumer-api/).
Each connection holds its own values; selecting Carries creates no values on existing connections.

**Remove relation type** also stops allowing that relation between its listed pairs. Read the
confirmation’s pair list before accepting. Removing a definition from a draft does not delete
live connections immediately; stored use can prevent the change or require a migration.

---
title: Add a relationships table
description: Put both ends of a relationship and its own values in rows or a grid.
reader: model-admin
---

Add a relationships table when people need to maintain values belonging to connections between
records. Work in a draft with **Model authoring**. First [allow the relationship](/docs/guide/model/add-a-relationship/)
and choose what it carries. Read [columns and grouping](/docs/model/applications-and-views/#relationships-tables-columns-and-grouping)
for the model rules, and [Relationships tables](/docs/use/relationship-tables/) for the
result people use.

## Choose the relationship and columns

1. Select an application in the draft and choose **Add a view…**.
2. In **Kind of view**, choose **Relationships table: each relationship in a row, with its own attributes**. If it is absent, allow a relationship
   between two types first. Containment is not offered for this view.
3. In **Relationships**, choose the directed pair and relation. Read the arrow: the from end
   supplies grid rows, and the to end supplies column groups. The view reads this one pair,
   even when the relation type also connects other pairs.
4. In **Columns of the from record** and **Columns of the to record**, select and order the
   fields that identify each end. Keep at least one in each. Name and scalar fields are
   offered; fields holding JSON are not endpoint-column choices. The initial choice is Name
   and, where available, a unique scalar field. Changing Relationships resets these choices.
5. Under **Attributes of the relationship**, select the values to show. Only attributes carried
   by this pair are offered. An empty choice is allowed. Change the pair's **Carries** first if
   a needed value is missing. For a grid, choose the attributes people need under each column group.
6. Set **Layout** to **One row per relationship** or **Grid: each record once, a column group per
   related record**. Rows show existing connections. A grid also exposes gaps where people can
   link records. The first selected to-record field labels each grid column group.
7. For rows, **Head the rows by** chooses **Nothing: one list**, **The from record** or **The to
   record**. Group headings include counts. This choice does not group the grid.
8. Enter **Name** and choose **Apply**. Check the saved step, **Views** and **Issues**. The
   application lists either endpoint type if it was not already listed. No data is created.

![Add a relationships table with its directed pair, endpoint fields, relationship attributes and Layout choices](/docs/screens/model-add-relationships-table-layout.png)

*Above: Add a view to Network in a reference-model draft, with Stop to Operator through
Operated by, endpoint columns and the three relationship attributes. Layout is an open list
showing both choices, with Grid selected. Head the rows by and the name Stops of each operator
are also visible. This dialog has not been applied.*

## Understand the initial reading choices

The form derives filters from selected fields marked Filterable. It offers sorting by both
record names, selected endpoint fields and selected non-JSON relationship attributes, starting with the
from record's name. The reading size starts at 20. Filters, sort declarations and reading size
are not separate fields in this dialog. A specialist can adjust them in the
[JSON view](/docs/model/json-view/); the model checks their references and permits reading sizes
from 1 to 100.

In grid layout, people also get each endpoint type's main-view filters. They can narrow records
and choose displayed fields without changing the model. Their choices stay in that page's address.

## Change the layout and activate

1. In **Views**, open the relationships table's menu and choose **Layout…**.
2. Select either layout and **Apply**. This changes the presentation of the same relationship;
   it does not duplicate or remove its connections.
3. Review **Issues**, then [install and activate the release](/docs/guide/model/install-and-activate-a-release/).
   Open the view in a workspace using the release and check its fields and available actions.

**Not applied** means the draft step was refused. Read the named issue and correct the pair or
field choices. **Cancel** leaves it unchanged. A publication is read-only, and live editing
still requires the person's data permissions; adding a view does not grant them.

**Remove relationships table** removes this presentation. Its confirmation also lists types
that stop being listed because only this view needed them. Review that list and any migration
warning before applying. The view does not own the stored relationships.

---
title: Add a table, tree or mapping grid
description: Add a collection view and choose its hierarchy or matching relationship.
reader: model-admin
---

Work in a draft with **Model authoring**. A view gives people a way to work with existing
types; adding it does not create records. Read [Applications and views](/docs/model/applications-and-views/)
for the structural rules. For cells at row and column intersections, use
[Add a relation matrix](/docs/guide/model/add-a-relation-matrix/) instead.

## Start with the application

1. Select the application and choose **Add a view…** from its menu.
2. Choose **Kind of view**. Only suitable kinds are offered. A table needs a type; a tree
   needs a listed type that permits records without a parent; a mapping grid needs an optional
   non-containment relationship. Add those definitions first if the kind is missing.
3. Complete the form for that kind below. Enter **Name**, then **Apply**. Check **Views** and
   **Issues**. **Not applied** means the step was refused: read its reason and revise the
   choices. **Cancel** leaves the draft unchanged.

## Table

Choose **Table: the records of one type in rows**, select **Type**, and enter **Name**.
The application also lists the type if necessary. Columns, filters and sorting start from
its attributes. After Apply, select the type and open **Preview**, **Edit layout**, **Table**;
choose this view in **View** to [arrange it](/docs/guide/model/choose-table-columns-filters-and-sort/).

## Tree

1. Choose **Tree: records under the records that contain them**.
2. Select **Top of the tree**. These are types that can stand without a parent. The tree
   includes the types beneath them that this application lists. List missing child types in
   the application before adding the tree.
3. Set **Each record reads** to Name or a field shared by every shown type. **Second line**
   adds another shared field; **None** removes it.
4. Set **Records under a record are ordered by**. The form applies that one field to child
   types. It starts with Name. More detailed per-type or descending ordering needs a specialist.
5. For an on/off control, choose a common Yes or no field in **Switch a record on and off with**.
   Choose None for no availability action. A read-only field cannot support this action.
6. Enter the name and Apply. Review Issues. The form sets availability actions only; do not
   expect Create, Rename or Move just from choosing a tree. Ask a specialist to declare those
   separately when needed.

![Add a view with Tree selected and roots, label, second line, order and availability choices](/docs/screens/model-add-tree-view.png)

## Mapping grid

1. Choose **Mapping grid: records of one type matched to records of another**.
2. In **Matches records through**, choose the permitted relationship and its two types.
   Containment and required ownership are not offered.
3. In **Rows are**, choose the first or second type. This decides which end chooses records
   at the other end. Changing the relationship or row end resets the column and search choices
   to Name: select them again afterwards.
4. Choose and order **Columns of a row** and **Columns of the matched record**. Keep at
   least one in each list. Fields holding JSON are not offered. In **Columns of a row**,
   **From the parents** offers the types the row can stand beneath. Add one to show the name
   of each row record's nearest parent of that type, even several levels above it. The type's
   name heads the column. These parent names give context but are not searched when people
   search the grid's rows.
5. Choose **Find a record to match by**. Name and searchable attributes of the matched type
   are offered. This controls candidate searching, not a relationship’s eligibility rules.
6. Enter the name, Apply and check the resulting view and type listings. The new grid starts
   with 20 rows per page. A specialist can change that reading size.

![Add a view with Mapping grid selected, relationship, row end and display/search fields](/docs/screens/model-add-mapping-grid.png)

## Change or remove a view

In **Views**, open a tree or mapping grid’s menu and choose **Change…**. Apply changes and
review the saved step. On a tree, the form rebuilds actions from its availability choice:
review any actions a specialist had previously declared. New trees start with 50 records per
branch page; the change form preserves an existing reading size.

**Rename…** changes the label. **Remove view** removes the view and can stop listing types
only it needed. Review the confirmation and remaining listings. Stored data remains. Use
**Undo** to restore the draft step. Review the application’s **Default view** in Settings
when changing its views, then [install and activate](/docs/guide/model/install-and-activate-a-release/)
when the draft is ready. People keep the current views until activation.
guide/src/content/docs/guide/model/arran:
---
title: Arrange applications and views
description: Create an application, list shared types and choose the next navigation or layout task.
reader: model-admin
---

Arrange a draft so people can find the types and views they need. You need **Model authoring**.
Any application can use a view when its structure fits. See
[Applications and views](/docs/model/applications-and-views/) for listings and view rules.

1. In the model pane, choose **Add**, **Application…**. Enter **Name** and, if useful,
   **Description**, then apply. In an existing application, select its row instead.
2. Check **Object types** and **Stands** to see what it lists and where records belong. Use
   **Object type** to create a definition, or **List an existing type…** to list a shared type
   here. Check the intended type before applying: listing it does not copy its records.
3. Open a listed type's menu. Use **Stop listing in this application** where offered to remove
   only that listing. For containment or a move between applications, use
   [Split, merge and move types](/docs/guide/model/split-merge-and-move-types/) instead. Released
   listings and placements can be refused when data uses them; read the impact before proceeding.
4. Inspect **Views**, including each view's kind, **Shows** and state. **Rename…** changes a
   view's label. To add or configure a relation matrix, follow
   [Add a relation matrix](/docs/guide/model/add-a-relation-matrix/).
5. Use [Group collections in navigation](/docs/guide/model/group-collections-in-navigation/) for
   sidebar sections, their order and initial folded state. This does not change record parents.
6. Use [Preview a type](/docs/guide/model/preview-a-type/), then
   [Edit a record page](/docs/guide/model/edit-a-record-page/) or
   [Choose table columns, filters and sort](/docs/guide/model/choose-table-columns-filters-and-sort/)
   for screen layout. Use [Add a table, tree or mapping grid](/docs/guide/model/add-a-view/)
   for the other view forms.
7. Check **Issues** and review the saved steps before installing. A **Not applied** notice means
   the attempted step was refused; correct its named problem. **Undo** reverses unwanted saved work.

![Application editor listing types, views and navigation groups](/docs/screens/model-editor-application.png)

![Application view list with table, tree, mapping-grid and relation-matrix kinds](/docs/screens/model-editor-systems-views.png)

*Example: an application in the Graubünden model declares all four view kinds. These are choices
in that model, rather than features reserved for the subject of that application.*

The live workspace keeps its current navigation and layouts until the release is activated.

To choose the opening view, edit **Default view** under the application’s **Settings**, select
one of its views, then **Save**. To remove a non-matrix view, choose **Remove view**. Read
“Types only it needed stop being listed here.” before confirming: review the application’s
listings as well as the view list afterwards. Removal changes navigation, not the stored
records. Restore an unwanted draft change with **Undo**.
guide/src/content/docs/guide/model/chang:
---
title: Change a model with the assistant
description: Describe a model change, review the proposal and complete a migration or a staged record move.
reader: model-admin
---

Use this task to change the structure of an active workspace from words. Read
[Model changes with the assistant](/docs/model/ai-model-changes/) for permissions and the two
ways records can move. You need the assistant enabled, permission to send the data it needs,
and the rights to author, install and release the model and work in change sets.

Your words, the model and any whole workbook you attach go to Claude Code; it can read workspace
records as needed. Turns can cost money, and tasks, files and session transcripts are kept for
