from that webhook instead. Share the new key securely with its receiver and use the chosen overlap
to maintain verification during handover. These actions do not replace a client's secret.
Changing the encryption key used to store secrets is a separate operator procedure in
[Secrets and keys](/docs/run/secrets-and-keys/); coordinate that work with the operator.

## Check the security model

A security reviewer, administrator or integrator needs to understand where access is enforced
and how to assess the deployment. Begin with [Security, audit and privacy](/docs/about/security-and-trust/),
then compare the intended access with [Roles and grants](/docs/administer/roles-and-grants/) and
[Audit](/docs/administer/audit/). Include direct, group and installation-wide grants, writes
narrowed to types, background work and the separate grants for consumer APIs.

The service enforces permissions across browser and integration operations. Hiding a button is
not the security boundary. Deactivation and revoked permissions affect later requests and job
steps. Use the [Security checklist](/docs/run/security-checklist/) with the operator for HTTPS,
credential storage and deployment controls. Integrators can continue with
[the security model for integrations](/docs/integrate/security-model-for-integrators/).
This review connects the documented rules and evidence; it is not a separate security-checking
screen in refiroo.

## Move people to the organisation's sign-in provider

A security administrator [adds a sign-in provider](/docs/guide/administer/add-a-sign-in-provider/)
and tests complete sign-in, then [links an existing person](/docs/guide/administer/link-a-provider-person/)
where needed to preserve their grants and history. Review any provider-group mappings as well
as direct grants. Changing the provider's credentials requires coordination with its owner;
[Sign-in](/docs/administer/sign-in/) explains the recovery path.

[Require a second factor](/docs/guide/administer/require-a-second-factor/) for local accounts
and prepare recovery before losing a device. When provider sign-in is proven,
[turn off ordinary local sign-in](/docs/guide/administer/turn-off-local-sign-in/) only after
testing the retained local administrator route. That switch keeps accounts, roles and existing
second-factor requirements. Test both intended sign-in and recovery afterwards.

## Tailor a responsibility and remove access when it ends

[Create a custom role](/docs/guide/administer/create-a-custom-role/) from an existing role or
from nothing, choose its action groups, then grant it in the intended scope. Changing it later
affects every holder; copying a role does not keep the copy linked to its source. Review the
[permissions reference](/docs/administer/permissions-reference/) and the recipient's effective
access after changing it. Remove all grants before deleting an unwanted custom role.

When a person leaves, [People and groups](/docs/administer/people-and-groups/) connects
account deactivation, membership and retained attribution. Removing one grant can leave other
access in place. Deactivation stops the next request without erasing data history; refiroo
refuses changes that would remove the last active security administrator.

## Configure publication review and system delivery

[Set an approval policy](/docs/guide/administer/set-an-approval-policy/) with the workspace's
administrator, then use [Change with approval](/docs/journeys/change-with-approval/) for an
actual proposal and decision. A changed policy affects waiting decisions too; inspect the
current policy rather than assuming the one used during preparation still applies.

For event delivery, [create a webhook](/docs/guide/administer/create-a-webhook/), agree its
signing key with the receiver and inspect a real delivery. If it stops,
[find out why a webhook paused](/docs/guide/administer/find-out-why-a-webhook-paused/) before
resuming or resetting. Reset can skip changes; restore the receiver's baseline when needed.
See [Webhooks](/docs/administer/webhooks/) for disabling, deleting and rotating delivery keys.

## Control assistant access and inspect AI use

[Manage agent access](/docs/guide/administer/manage-agent-access/) to inspect external-assistant
registrations, clients and call records, or stop an unwanted connection. Its read-and-prepare
ceiling still applies when the underlying person's grants are broader. Ending a personal
connection and blocking an assistant have different scopes.

With **Operations**, [check the AI provider](/docs/guide/administer/check-the-ai-provider/),
read the send policy and inspect calls and costs. Server settings are changed by the operator,
not by this page. [AI administration](/docs/administer/ai/) explains retained records and
separately enabled features; [Work with an assistant](/docs/journeys/work-with-an-assistant/)
connects them to their actual tasks.
guide/src/content/docs/journeys/receive-:
---
title: Receive notices
description: Connect outgoing mail setup with personal email choices, digests and workspace following.
reader: steward
---

Use these journeys to hear about work that needs attention without continually opening each
proposal or job. Administrators provide outgoing mail; each person chooses email for their own
inbox. Inbox notices and workspace following also work without mail. These features do not require
an assistant or AI configuration.

## Send mail

A security administrator connects the instance to an outgoing mail server so people can receive
account links and the notices they choose. Start with [Mail](/docs/administer/mail/), then
[set up mail](/docs/guide/administer/set-up-mail/) and send a test message. Check that it reaches
the intended mailbox and that its application link points to the address people can open.
The server accepting a message does not prove it reached the inbox.

Ordinary messages wait for background delivery. Inspect waiting, sent and failed entries on the
Mail page; temporary failures retry, while permanent failures or exhausted retries need attention.
The reason distinguishes connection, secure connection, login and recipient problems. Correct the
cause with the mail administrator or operator. [Sign-in and mail setup](/docs/run/sign-in-and-mail-setup/)
explains the operator's part. Removing settings stops sending but does not immediately erase the
waiting queue. Stopping an individual message does not revoke a password link already created.

For a person receiving a new-account or reset link, follow it once to set a password and then sign
in. An expired or used link needs a fresh one; an existing second factor remains required.
Read [Account](/docs/use/account/) for personal sign-in security. For optional inbox email,
continue with the next journey.

## Notification digests and following a workspace

A person starts with [Inbox and approvals](/docs/use/inbox-and-approvals/) to understand the
notices and the work they open. Then read [Notification settings](/docs/use/notifications-settings/)
and [set up email notices](/docs/guide/use/set-up-email-notices/). Email starts off. Where mail
is configured and the account has an address, enable it and choose **At once**, **Digest** or
**Off** for each kind. These preferences do not remove notices from the inbox.

A digest can come every morning or on Mondays at 07:00 in the browser's time zone. Check the
saved zone and next digest time. It counts eligible unread, unhandled notices and lists the newest
50 with links; an empty digest is not sent. Reading or handling a notice before delivery can remove
it from the message. The email contains kinds, times, counts and links rather than record, workspace,
file or people's names. Digest notices do not use immediate mail's 24-hour cutoff.

To hear about another person's publication, [follow a workspace](/docs/guide/use/follow-a-workspace/)
from its Home card. Following needs Browse and adds inbox notices; email copies depend on your
choices above. Your own publications do not send you follower notices. Open a notice to inspect
its publication where it is still available and you still have access. The notice can remain after
its destination is no longer openable.

Stop following from Home or notification settings when no longer needed. Losing Browse or account
deactivation pauses notices while keeping the choice, so they can resume if access returns.
If email does not arrive, check the inbox, address, mail availability and saved choices before
assuming publication or approval failed. A refused settings change keeps the previous preferences.
guide/src/content/docs/journeys/run-the-:
---
title: Run the service
description: Start refiroo, recover safely and inspect the deployment and its configuration.
reader: operator
---

These journeys are for operators keeping refiroo available and understanding what the deployment
actually runs. Operators need the appropriate server or platform access for installation work;
the application's Operations permission opens deployment diagnostics. It does not grant reference
data editing or security administration.

## Run the service, and recover from an expected refusal

An operator begins with [Install with Compose](/docs/run/install-with-compose/),
[The database](/docs/run/database/) and [Configure refiroo](/docs/run/configure/) to prepare
persistent storage, PostgreSQL and the instance's settings. Start the service, then use
[Health and startup checks](/docs/run/health-and-startup-checks/) to decide whether it is ready
for traffic. Liveness means that the process answers; readiness also needs the database and at
least one workspace it can serve. Readiness alone does not prove every workspace is available.

If startup refuses or enters maintenance mode, read the stated cause, resulting service state
and recovery action. [Troubleshooting](/docs/run/troubleshooting/) connects database connectivity,
collation, missing extensions, migration revisions and model problems to their safe remedies.
Correct the named setting or dependency, then restart where instructed and check readiness again.
Do not edit migration revision rows or stored model documents to suppress a refusal.
[Upgrades](/docs/run/upgrades/) covers migration and unsupported stored-release recovery.

Once serving, use [Monitoring](/docs/run/monitoring/) to inspect workspace and process readiness,
background threads, connection pools and request diagnostics. During a database outage, a process
can remain live while unready. Restore connectivity and allow workers to recover; repeatedly
restarting healthy processes does not restore PostgreSQL. With several processes, follow
[Several processes](/docs/run/several-processes/) for their shared database and file storage.

Complete the recovery preparation with [Back up and restore](/docs/run/backup-and-restore/).
Restore a backup into a separate database and run the documented restore check there, then inspect
the recorded rehearsal outcome. The check must not target the live database. A failed rehearsal
is evidence to resolve before depending on that backup, rather than proof of a working restore.
Preserve the concise error and correlation references when escalating a failure.

## Check what a deployment runs and how it is configured

An operator identifies the running application version, supported model languages, model release
and source information before diagnosing a mismatch or planning maintenance.
[Monitoring](/docs/run/monitoring/) connects the deployment pages with process and workspace
information. [Configure refiroo](/docs/run/configure/) explains the settings catalogue, current
values, defaults, and whether a value came from the environment.

The pages inspect configuration; they do not edit environment settings. Change those in the
server or platform configuration and restart as documented. Secret settings show whether they
are present rather than revealing their values; the database address masks its password.
After a model activation, check the selected workspace's running release rather than assuming
all workspaces run the same one.

Use [Licence and source](/docs/run/licence-and-source/) to verify the running version's source
link, especially for a modified installation. If behaviour still disagrees with configuration,
return to [Troubleshooting](/docs/run/troubleshooting/) with the version, time, failing action,
workspace and diagnostic reference, excluding credentials and full environment files.

## Open a production installation over HTTPS

Start with [What you run](/docs/run/overview/) and
[Install with Compose](/docs/run/install-with-compose/), then choose automatic public
certificates, your organisation's certificate files or an existing HTTPS balancer in
[Serve over HTTPS](/docs/run/https/). Automatic issuance and renewal needs a public DNS name
and reachable port 443; port 80 is optional for redirects. Preserve certificate storage and
check renewal through the public address. Private names need a different certificate route.

[Set up sign-in and mail](/docs/run/sign-in-and-mail-setup/), test a complete sign-in and
recovery path, then complete the [production checklist](/docs/run/production-checklist/)
and [security checklist](/docs/run/security-checklist/). A healthy container does not establish
that every workspace, public sign-in, notification or receiver works. Keep the outcomes for
your installation and correct failed checks before admitting traffic.

## Upgrade and recover a failed cutover

Follow [Upgrades](/docs/run/upgrades/) to record the running source, supported model languages,
private configuration, backup and file archive before maintenance. Check the new deployment's
readiness, workspaces, sign-in and retained files before reopening writes. An unsupported stored
model needs the documented raising review; a database migration refusal needs its stated remedy.

[Model releases and rollback](/docs/run/model-releases-and-rollback/) distinguishes a compatible
model activation from application rollback. Restoring an older application requires its matching
pre-upgrade database and configuration; changing the bootstrap model file does not switch
existing workspaces. Do not repair a cutover by editing migration revision rows.

## Back up, rehearse and move to another host

[Back up and restore](/docs/run/backup-and-restore/) connects a consistent PostgreSQL and
job-file backup to its source version and protected keys. Rehearse the restore in an isolated
database and inspect the recorded result before relying on it. Include the public sign-in path
and file downloads when testing a replacement host; a database-only check does not establish those.

Use the same runbook's host-move sequence to stop writers, take the final consistent copy,
restore, verify and cut over the public address. Preserve the recovery material until the
replacement is proven. Retire the old host after cutover so it cannot resume competing work.
A missing sealing key prevents recovering stored secrets from their encrypted values alone.

## Replace secrets and watch growing storage

[Secrets and keys](/docs/run/secrets-and-keys/) identifies client credentials, signing material,
cursor keys and the sealing key before choosing the replacement procedure. Check which processes
share them and coordinate with the administrator and receivers. Retain the key matching a backup;
replacing a value blindly can make stored credentials unreadable or invalidate saved positions.

[The database](/docs/run/database/) covers connection budgets and growth. Combine it with
[Background jobs](/docs/run/background-jobs/), [Webhook delivery](/docs/run/webhook-delivery/)
and [Monitoring](/docs/run/monitoring/) to watch files, queues, delivery results and retained logs.
Change retention deliberately; it can remove diagnostic detail without removing reference data.
[Several processes](/docs/run/several-processes/) requires shared identity and file storage.
Measure the actual workload before making capacity or recovery-time promises.

## Enable optional AI or prepare a developer instance

Read [AI operation](/docs/run/ai/) before [Set up AI](/docs/run/set-up-ai/). Choose the provider,
built-in assistant and external-agent connection separately, set a send policy and credentials,
apply the configuration, then verify each enabled path. Inspect calls and task retention as well
as service readiness. Disabling a feature stops future use; it does not erase published records,
history or all retained task material. Follow the same page for replacement credentials or cleanup.

For local source work instead, follow [Developer instance](/docs/run/developer-instance/).
It has a different support boundary from the reference installation. Use
[Command-line tools](/docs/run/command-line/) for the documented maintenance commands, and
[Troubleshooting](/docs/run/troubleshooting/) to prepare concise diagnostics when a recovery fails.
guide/src/content/docs/journeys/shape-a-:
---
title: Shape a model
description: Connect model design, workbook loading, releases and workspace migrations.
reader: model-admin
---

These journeys are for model administrators shaping the types, fields, relationships and views
that people use. Applications are declared by the model; they can be changed, replaced or removed.
Start with [Models](/docs/model/models/) for the difference between a draft, an installed release
and the release running in a workspace.

Model authoring, model release and workspace administration permissions serve different purposes.
They do not automatically grant permission to read or change reference data. Each linked task
explains its required access and deployment settings.

## Create and activate an application-model release

A model administrator turns a reviewed design into the definitions a workspace runs.
[Releases](/docs/model/releases/) connects the lifecycle: create or import a draft, validate it,
compare its differences and stored-data compatibility, then install an immutable release.
[Install and activate a release](/docs/guide/model/install-and-activate-a-release/) takes that
release into the intended workspace. Saving, installing and activating are separate outcomes.

An incompatible release does not become active. Resolve its data problems or use the reviewed
[migration](#move-a-workspace-to-another-release) path. If another activation wins first, refresh
the state and review again. Use [Compare releases](/docs/guide/model/compare-releases/)
when checking differences, or [Export a release](/docs/guide/model/export-a-release/) to reuse it
elsewhere. Read-only inspection remains available when model administration is switched off.

## Administer workspaces

A workspace administrator, or an authorised integrator, creates a separate place for data,
gives it a stable key and a label, and chooses the release it runs.
[Managing workspaces](/docs/model/managing-workspaces/) leads to
[Create a workspace](/docs/guide/model/create-a-workspace/) and
[Make a workspace the default](/docs/guide/model/make-a-workspace-the-default/).
Changing the default affects requests that omit a workspace; an explicit choice stays explicit.

When a workspace is no longer used, [retire or delete it](/docs/guide/model/retire-or-delete-a-workspace/).
Retirement preserves reads and refuses changes. The default cannot be retired; deletion also
requires an empty workspace with no publications. A refusal names what still prevents deletion.
Choose another default or retain the workspace for reading as appropriate.

## Define a consumer API in the model

A model author defines the business objects other systems should read without exposing their
storage structure. Start with [Consumer APIs](/docs/model/consumer-apis/), then
[define a consumer API](/docs/guide/model/define-a-consumer-api/) over the chosen types, fields,
related records, lists, lookup rules and events. Validate each reference and review the generated
[schema and message example](/docs/guide/model/see-a-consumer-apis-documents/).

Compare the consumer contract before installing and activating the release. A breaking change
needs a higher contract version; activation refuses it otherwise. An operation is available only
when declared. Coordinate changed contracts with integrators, who can then
[read through the consumer API](/docs/guide/integrate/read-through-a-consumer-api/).

**Example:** the reference model's stops consumer API exposes stops with names and codes drawn
from connected records. Another model can expose entirely different business objects.

## Design a model in the editor

A model administrator [creates a model draft](/docs/guide/model/create-a-model-draft/), then uses
[the model editor](/docs/model/the-model-editor/) to shape applications, types, reusable fields,
relationships, navigation and pages. Each edit has issues and a history; inspect them as the model
grows and [undo or review steps](/docs/guide/model/undo-and-review-the-draft-history/) where needed.
Preview pages before installation, without writing reference data from the preview.

A draft can temporarily be invalid, but an invalid draft cannot be installed. Released keys are
stable; a removal or structural change affecting stored data can require migration. If a colleague
changes the draft first, review their steps before retrying your edit. Finish through
[installation and activation](/docs/guide/model/install-and-activate-a-release/), then work with
records under the changed model to check the result.

## Onboard a workbook

A model administrator turns a workbook into a reviewed model and a repeatable loading profile.
Read [Workbook onboarding](/docs/model/workbook-onboarding/), then
[start a draft from a workbook](/docs/guide/model/start-a-draft-from-a-workbook/).
Inspect sheets, tables and lists; accept, change or reject proposals, or map columns by hand.
[Map a column](/docs/guide/model/map-a-column/) and
[read lists in a sheet](/docs/guide/model/read-lists-in-a-sheet/) explain the choices.
A proposal does not apply itself.

[Check the workbook with a dry run](/docs/guide/model/check-a-workbook-with-a-dry-run/) to inspect
what every row would do without writing records. Resolve missing values and mapping problems,
install and activate the model, then [load into a change set](/docs/guide/model/load-a-workbook-into-a-change-set/).
Review its differences and publish. Installation saves definitions and the loading profile;
it does not make the file's records live.

## Load the next version of a workbook

A steward or model administrator uses the saved profile to repeat the load without rebuilding
the mapping. [Load the next version of a workbook](/docs/guide/use/load-the-next-version-of-a-workbook/)
connects uploading the next file, inspecting differences, accepting column renames or ignoring
new columns, and checking again. Read the report before loading into a new change set.

Missing records are reported and kept unless the profile explicitly deletes them. A deleting
load needs a change set so the removals and their relationships can be reviewed. A changed model
release can invalidate a profile binding; fix the named binding rather than loading around it.
Finish by [reviewing the changes](/docs/guide/use/review-what-a-change-set-changes/) and publishing.

**Example:** a newer workbook of stop names or external codes can correct existing records and
add others. A stop absent from that file is not automatically deleted.

## Run a workspace on a model of its own

A model administrator installs the desired release and
[creates a workspace on it](/docs/guide/model/create-a-workspace/) or
[changes an existing workspace's model](/docs/guide/model/change-a-workspaces-model/)
after its compatibility review. Other workspaces keep their models. Switching workspace changes
the available applications and views as well as the records; shared labels do not imply shared data.

To evolve that workspace's definitions, [edit its model](/docs/guide/model/edit-a-workspaces-model/)
and apply the reviewed draft there. A page built under a replaced release must reload before
saving. If one workspace's model cannot be served, inspect its explanation and recovery options;
other workspaces can remain available. [Releases](/docs/model/releases/) also explains retiring
unused choices and deleting releases that nothing refers to.

## Move a workspace to another release

A model administrator uses [Migrations](/docs/model/migrations/) when the target release needs
conversions or changes the existing data cannot adopt unchanged.
[Migrate a workspace](/docs/guide/model/migrate-a-workspace/) connects the preview, type and field
mapping, inspection of every loss, correction of blockers and explicit confirmation. Cancelling
changes nothing. The data conversion and release switch succeed together or neither does.

An intervening write makes the review stale: preview again instead of confirming an older result.
Open change sets stay on their release; move them separately or review a workspace migration with
publication as one operation. Existing publications keep their model and content. If a workspace
cannot open because its stored model uses an unsupported language version, follow the specific
recovery in [Managing workspaces](/docs/model/managing-workspaces/); an ordinary migration and
raising an unsupported stored release are different operations.

## Move data between workspaces whose models differ

A model administrator or steward needs a mapping between the source and target definitions,
rather than assuming record types mean the same thing. Start with
[Model mappings](/docs/model/model-mappings/), then
[move records to another model](/docs/guide/model/move-records-to-another-model/).
Complete the proposed mapping, choose the records, and inspect the dry run's created, updated and
refused items. Confirm a copy or move into the target's change set, then review and publish it.

A move also prepares reviewed deletion in the source; publish the target copy before that deletion.
Relationships whose other end stays behind are carried only when the counterpart can be found
in the target, otherwise they are dropped and reported. Matching and remembered counterparts let
later transfers update records rather than duplicate them. A changed mapping or release needs a
fresh review. Nothing rejected in the dry run should be treated as successfully moved.

## An account of a model change

A model administrator with **Model release** and **Use AI proposals** in the workspace can ask
for an explanation before activating a release or applying a draft. A configured AI provider
is required; enabling only the built-in assistant does not offer this account. Follow
[Explain a model change](/docs/guide/model/explain-a-model-change/).

Open the activation dialog or **Apply to this workspace** and read the compatibility checks.
Under **What this change does**, choose **Explain this change**. Nothing is sent before that
request. The provider receives the model's differences, rule failures, consumer-contract effects
and record counts, without record values or names. Requests can incur charges; the same facts
are reused for up to an hour. Call records remain; request text is kept only if enabled.
Read [AI and your data](/docs/use/ai-and-your-data/) for full access, disclosure, cost and retention rules.

Review the account and follow each numbered citation to the facts refiroo computed. These include
blocked activation and the counts of affected records, not a promise that the change is safe.
The explanation is English only, is not attached permanently to the release and takes no
follow-up question. It appears in activation and Apply, rather than installation or migration.
[Accounts of model changes](/docs/model/model-change-accounts/) explains its rules and limits.

![An account beside the model checks, with numbered citations and facts](/docs/screens/model-account-facts.png)

*Above: the Apply dialog for a change to the Graubünden reference model. The account cites the facts below it.*

If the provider fails, read the facts alone or choose **Try again**. Fix an invalid or newer draft
before asking again. Asking does not apply or activate anything, and an explanation cannot remove
a compatibility refusal. Continue through the normal activation review, or use
[the migration path](/docs/guide/model/migrate-a-workspace/) when the existing data needs conversion.

## Add types, fields and relationships

With **Model authoring**, [add a record type and fields](/docs/guide/model/add-a-record-type-and-fields/),
[reuse and change attributes](/docs/guide/model/reuse-and-change-attributes/) and
[add a relationship](/docs/guide/model/add-a-relationship/). A shared attribute change affects
all its attachments. Review required values, allowed parents and relationship candidates, then
[fix issues before installing](/docs/guide/model/fix-issues-before-installing/).
[Turn an attribute into a list](/docs/guide/model/turn-an-attribute-into-a-list/) when values
should become maintained records. Released values can need migration; a saved draft does not
populate that list or convert Live.

## Arrange navigation, views and record pages

[Find your way around the editor](/docs/guide/model/find-your-way-around-the-editor/), then
[arrange applications and views](/docs/guide/model/arrange-applications-and-views/) and
[group collections in navigation](/docs/guide/model/group-collections-in-navigation/).
[Add a view](/docs/guide/model/add-a-view/) for another way to read a collection, or
[add a relation matrix](/docs/guide/model/add-a-relation-matrix/) when its structure supports one.
Removing a navigation group keeps its collections; hiding a page panel keeps its stored values.

[Edit a record page](/docs/guide/model/edit-a-record-page/) to arrange fields and panels, and
[choose table columns, filters and sort](/docs/guide/model/choose-table-columns-filters-and-sort/)
for a view's defaults. [Preview a type](/docs/guide/model/preview-a-type/) against populated and
empty records before installation. Preview cannot write records. An invalid draft needs its
issues repaired first. [The specialist workbench](/docs/model/json-view/) owns supported
settings without visual forms; ask a specialist to
[edit that draft](/docs/guide/model/edit-a-draft-as-json/) where needed.

## Refine a draft without losing identity or colleagues' work

[Rename or re-key an element](/docs/guide/model/rename-or-re-key-an-element/) distinguishes a
label change from a stable identity: released keys are fixed even without records.
[Split, merge and move types](/docs/guide/model/split-merge-and-move-types/) reshapes definitions;
[remove an element](/docs/guide/model/remove-an-element/) first reviews affected uses and data.
Neither changes Live simply by saving the draft. Plan a migration when released data blocks a change.

[Work on a draft with others](/docs/guide/model/work-on-a-draft-with-others/) explains reviewing
a colleague's newer steps before retrying an edit. Use
[Undo and draft history](/docs/guide/model/undo-and-review-the-draft-history/) for an unwanted
saved step. [Delete a draft](/docs/guide/model/delete-a-draft/) only after preserving needed
work: its history and attached workbook go with it; installed releases stay.

## Recheck a workbook design or a saved mapping

[Propose again with a newer workbook](/docs/guide/model/propose-again-with-a-newer-workbook/)
keeps the distinction between design proposals, accepted draft edits and a fresh dry run.
Inspect changed columns and skipped sheets, then return to the normal loading and review path.

For transfers, [edit a mapping row](/docs/guide/model/edit-a-mapping-row/) and
[choose what moves](/docs/guide/model/choose-what-moves/) before reviewing a fresh complete dry
run. [Delete a model mapping](/docs/guide/model/delete-a-model-mapping/) only when future
transfers no longer need it; deletion does not undo earlier copies or moves.

## Maintain released contracts and definitions

[Raise a contract version](/docs/guide/model/raise-a-contract-version/) before activating a
breaking consumer change, and coordinate it with callers. This does not raise the model language:
[Raise a model language version](/docs/guide/model/raise-a-model-language-version/) is the
separate review for a stored model outside the supported window. Keep retained publications and
their definitions in the recovery plan.

[Retire or delete a release](/docs/guide/model/retire-or-delete-a-release/) hides unused choices
or permanently removes an unreferenced release. Existing references can prevent deletion.
Retirement does not stop workspaces already using a release. Review current use rather than
treating an older version as automatically disposable.
guide/src/content/docs/journeys/work-wit:
---
title: Work with an assistant
description: Find records in words, review AI proposals and connect an assistant that prepares changes.
reader: steward
---

Choose the help that fits your task. A provider proposes mapping targets, turns questions into
list filters and explains changes. The built-in Claude Code assistant prepares models and data
from words or a workbook. An external assistant connects separately through the Model Context
Protocol (MCP). Your operator enables each separately.

Built-in actions need **Use AI proposals** in the workspace and the permissions for the task.
Your words and the information allowed by the instance's send level are sent to the configured
service; an external assistant instead receives what its grants allow it to read. Requests can
incur charges. refiroo keeps call records and, for built-in tasks, the workbook and proposal for
the configured retention period. Read [AI and your data](/docs/use/ai-and-your-data/) for the full
access, disclosure, cost and retention rules before starting.

## Use AI proposals

An operator enables the assistant or provider in the server configuration, chooses how much
information may be sent, and restarts the service. [Running AI](/docs/run/ai/) explains the
settings and failure recovery. A configuration that cannot work refuses startup and names the
setting to correct.

With **Operations**, open **Settings › This instance › AI** to inspect which help is on and
what may be sent. [Check the AI provider](/docs/guide/administer/check-the-ai-provider/) leads
through **Send a test request**, which contains no reference data, then the call records and
30-day totals. A refused key, unreachable service or unreadable answer is recorded as a failure.
An absent provider does not disable an independently enabled built-in assistant. Neither enabled
means no built-in AI action and nothing sent by those features.

## Targets for unmapped values

A steward with **Use AI proposals** and **Work in change sets** opens a mapping grid and chooses
**Propose targets**. This needs a provider and permission to send record values. Follow
[Propose targets](/docs/guide/use/propose-targets/) to choose an existing or new change set,
start the job and inspect the outcome. The grid's search and chosen parent bound the sources.
The provider receives source names and displayed fields, with only eligible target candidates:
all up to 100, otherwise each source's 20 closest by name.

Use **Show proposed** and the **Proposed** filter to review the mappings, confidence and reasons.
A low-confidence or missing answer leaves its source unmapped; a source changed meanwhile is
left alone and counted. **Stop** keeps proposals already saved. Correct a target with **Change**
and **Save mapping**; the replaced mapping loses its AI mark. Validate and publish through the
workspace's normal approval process. Live stays unchanged until publication, and published
history records the AI origin and publisher. See [Mapping grids](/docs/use/mapping-grids/#targets-proposed-by-ai).

## Load a workbook, or change records, with the assistant

A steward starts from **Import** on a collection, or the workspace's **Ask about these records…**.
The built-in assistant needs permission to send values, **Use AI proposals**, **Bulk and import**
and **Work in change sets** to accept and load. Model work also needs the appropriate model
permissions. Follow [Load a workbook with the assistant](/docs/guide/use/load-a-workbook-with-the-assistant/)
or [Change records with the assistant](/docs/guide/use/change-records-with-the-assistant/).

Give a file and a few words, or words alone. Review the proposed types, fields, relationships,
questions and **Checks**. For a workbook, **What the load does** shows new records, existing
records matched, new relationships, refused items and rows read. Open a type's row for example
records with their source cells; inspect repeated-name findings and **Where each part of the
file goes**. Unexpected new records can mean an intended update failed to match them. Answer
questions, tell the assistant what to change or edit its draft in the model editor. If the draft
changed after the check, acceptance checks every record and relationship again first.
[Review the assistant's workbook design](/docs/guide/model/review-an-assistants-workbook-design/)
explains this review.

![Workbook proposal showing what the load does, its results by type and the choices before acceptance](/docs/screens/use-assistant-proposal.png)

*Above: the workbook proposal for the Graubünden reference data, showing What the load does
and the table of results by type. Below it, Questions marks the assumed answer, and the acceptance
bar explains that the checked records go into a new change set. Nothing is loaded or published yet.*

A words-only proposal that says **No change to the model.** uses **Accept**. It has no model
draft and prepares a change set on the workspace’s current release, installing and activating
nothing. A workbook proposal uses **Accept and load to change set**: the engine installs the model if it
changed and loads exactly the checked records and relationships into a change set as one batch,
without another assistant turn. Nothing is activated or published. If any item is refused,
none of the batch is loaded and its change set is discarded; read the reason and correct the
proposal. A release installed before a failed load can remain installed. Review and publish
the successful change set through the normal approval process. If it uses a different model
version, review offers migration and publication together; a model administrator with
publication permission previews it and confirms **Migrate and publish**. The assistant saves no import profile: send the next file to it again.
Model-only and record-move proposals keep **Accept the model** and their separate endings.

**Stop** ends the turn, not the task. A stopped load discards the change set being loaded and
returns to the accepted proposal. A failed or stopped task takes words or a retry. On a wrong
loaded result, **Discard and load again** removes that change set, including manual edits, before
preparing another. For a workbook, review the revised proposal and choose **Accept and load to change set**
again before the replacement is loaded. [Continue an assistant task](/docs/guide/use/continue-an-assistant-task/) covers
these recovery paths and expired tasks.

To reshape the model from words, follow
[Change a model with the assistant](/docs/guide/model/change-a-model-with-the-assistant/).
A whole-type move needs a person's migration preview and confirmation, which changes live data
directly. A model-only change also ends with migration review and confirmation, with no type
moves and every record left as it is. A partial move uses release activation, change-set publication and, when old types are
removed, final activation. These different reviews are explained in
[Model changes with the assistant](/docs/model/ai-model-changes/).

## Reach refiroo from an assistant

An integrator connects an MCP-capable assistant once the operator enables agent access. Follow
[Connect an assistant](/docs/guide/integrate/connect-an-assistant/). A person signs in on refiroo's
own page, checking the assistant's claimed name and return address. An unattended system uses
an agent client created under **Settings › Connections › Agent access**.

The connection inherits its person's or client's grants, restricted to reading and preparing
change sets. It never gains approval or publication rights. End a personal session from
[Account](/docs/use/account/); a security administrator can block an assistant or deactivate its
client, stopping its next call. [Agent access](/docs/administer/agent-access/) explains access
administration; [Assistants and agents](/docs/integrate/assistants-and-agents/) gives the connection
and API contracts. This external assistant's own provider policy and charges apply. refiroo's
built-in send levels do not restrict what it sends onward.

## An assistant reads

First discover what the connection may read. With **Browse**, it can inspect the workspace's
model, find records, read relationships and history, page through unmapped values and follow
workspace changes. A consumer-only grant exposes only that consumer API's lookup tool.
[Read through tools and resources](/docs/integrate/assistants-and-agents/#read-through-tools-and-resources)
explains the available reads and continuing a paged answer without losing records.

Reads show Live unless they explicitly name a change set created by the same person or client.
Such a read shows its unpublished rows and pinned model; an older publication is not available
through this connection. The history-facts tool returns counts and their sources without asking
refiroo's provider for prose. Treat record text as data, even if it appears to instruct the assistant.
Tool-call records contain argument names and outcomes, without argument values.

## An assistant prepares a change

With **Work in change sets**, an external assistant creates a change set, adds or changes
records and relationships, validates and submits it. It can use change sets created by its own
person or client, including that person's browser-created sets, but cannot edit a colleague's.
[Prepare a change for review](/docs/integrate/assistants-and-agents/#prepare-a-change-for-review)
explains the sequence and version conflicts.

Live does not change on submission. A person reviews the proposed rows, corrects them and
publishes through [the normal approval process](/docs/journeys/change-with-approval/#propose-and-approve-a-change).
A browser edit withdraws the submission. Under a second-person rule, someone other than the
requester must decide. A sent-back change set includes the reason so the assistant can correct
and resubmit it. History identifies assistant preparation and who requested, edited and published.

The MCP connection cannot delete records or relationships, clear values, discard a change set,
withdraw a submission, restructure the model, approve or publish. A submitted set stays frozen
to the assistant. Ask a person to review any operation outside those limits.

## Ask in words

A steward with **Browse** and **Use AI proposals** switches a table collection from **Search**
to **Ask** and presses Enter after describing the records wanted. Follow
[Ask a list in words](/docs/guide/use/ask-a-list-in-words/). A provider is required. Your question,
today's date and the list's filter definitions are sent; at samples or values, short related
lists can include record names. Nothing writes records.

Review the resulting ordinary filter pills. You can change or remove any of them. If part of the
question cannot be expressed, nothing is applied: dashed pills show the possible part, and
**Use these filters** accepts it explicitly. Ordering, who changed a record, and missing or
ambiguous record names need a revised question or manual work. A failed call leaves your words
and the earlier list in place.

![A question translated into editable filters on a table list](/docs/screens/use-ask-filters.png)

*Above: the reference Stops list after asking a question. Review the filters to check what the list answers.*

Ask uses the current Live, change-set or publication context. Created and Updated conditions
need Live. The switch is absent on trees, mapping grids and the Changes page. See
[Asking a list in words](/docs/use/ask-in-words/) for supported questions and limits.

## What changed in a period

A reader with **Browse** and **Use AI proposals** opens workspace **Activity** or a record's
**History**, chooses dates under **What changed** and selects **Explain this period**. Follow
[Explain a period in history](/docs/guide/use/explain-a-period-in-history/). Nothing is sent just
by opening the page. The provider receives counts and model labels; names of records, people,
change sets and files are included only at values. Requests can incur costs; the same facts are
reused for up to an hour. See [AI and your data](/docs/use/ai-and-your-data/) for retention.

Read each statement's numbered sources, then use **Show them** to inspect the changes it counted.
The facts cover live changes, including publication, rather than counting unpublished row edits
as live work. A period without changes makes no provider request. If the provider fails, the
facts remain readable. A removed job has no link to open. The account can be wrong and is English
only. [History](/docs/use/history/#what-changed-in-a-period) explains periods and attribution.

## Reuse a checked layout or stop using AI

An assistant load saves no import profile. Send the next workbook of the same layout to the
assistant again. If you already have a separately saved import profile, the engine can check
and load a matching file without an assistant session. Follow [Load the next version of a workbook](/docs/guide/use/load-the-next-version-of-a-workbook/)
and inspect its current mapping and dry run. A saved-layout load can activate a changed draft
when the requester has **Model release**; that differs from the assistant session, which cannot
activate. Read the shown result and next steps rather than assuming every task ends the same way.

To stop a built-in task, [continue or discard it](/docs/guide/use/continue-an-assistant-task/)
with the unpublished-change consequences visible. To stop an external connection, end its
session or ask the security administrator to [manage agent access](/docs/guide/administer/manage-agent-access/).
The operator can disable future built-in help through [AI settings](/docs/run/ai/).
Disabling help does not undo published records or erase history; task retention and the outside
provider's retention are separate. Manual filters, modelling and file-loading paths remain
available within their own permissions and deployment switches.
guide/src/content/docs/model/ai-model-ch:
---
title: Model changes with the assistant
description: Review a model proposed from words or a workbook, and understand how its records move.
reader: model-admin
---

Describe the model you need in words and the assistant proposes a draft for you to review.
You can attach a workbook, but a file is not required. The assistant can add fields, types,
relationships and applications, or propose moving records between types. These are model
capabilities available to any application.

Start with [Change a model with the assistant](/docs/guide/model/change-a-model-with-the-assistant/).
For a file that needs a model and a load, follow
[Review the assistant's workbook design](/docs/guide/model/review-an-assistants-workbook-design/).
The [model editor](/docs/model/the-model-editor/) remains available for direct edits.

## Availability and your data

The built-in assistant uses Claude Code. It is available only when your operator has enabled it
and allows the data it needs to be sent. Your words and the workspace's model go to Claude Code,
with the whole workbook if attached. The assistant reads workspace records as needed, within
your permissions. This is more than sending a few sample rows.

**Change this model…** is offered in an active workspace when you hold **Use AI proposals**,
**Bulk and import**, **Work in change sets**, **Model authoring** and **Model release**, and job
creation is enabled. Installing a changed model also needs **Model release** at instance level.
If the offer is missing, ask your administrator to check these rights and the assistant setup.
The separate AI provider used for explanations does not enable this assistant.

Assistant turns can incur Claude Code usage charges. refiroo records who asked, the outcome,
tokens and cost when reported. Tasks and workbooks normally remain for 90 days after completion
or the last change. Session files and transcripts remain while the task can continue; cleanup
follows publication, discard, confirmed migration or expiry. These are separate from optional
logging of request content. See [About AI in refiroo](/docs/run/ai/) for the full explanation of
access, billing, data leaving the instance and retention, including the provider's own policies.

## Review the proposal before accepting

**The assistant’s proposal** describes the types it would add or change and any records it
would move. Read the counts and **Checks**, not only the summary. The assistant's wording can
be wrong. The engine checks the draft and the data against its rules; that does not establish
that the proposed design means what you intended.

Answer the questions or use **Tell the assistant what to change**. You can also choose
**Open in the model editor** and edit the draft directly. The same assistant reads those edits
when it continues. A second assistant task cannot take over a draft another task holds.

For a workbook load, **What the load does** shows new and matched records, new relationships,
refused items and rows read. Open a type's row for example records with their source cells,
read any **One name twice in one type** finding, and expand **Where each part of the file goes**
to review how the file is used. The assistant reads the file, model and workspace records and
prepares records and relationships for the engine to check; it writes no import profile.

**Accept and load to change set** lets the engine install the changed model and load exactly those checked
records and relationships into a new change set as one batch. No assistant turn runs, and nothing
is activated or published. A draft changed after the check is checked again first; any refusal
then prevents installation and loading. If changed data causes a refusal during the batch, none
of the batch is loaded and the change set is discarded. A release installed before that failure
can remain installed. Correct the proposal in words, review the new check and accept again.
An assistant load saves no profile for the next file; send that file to the assistant again.

Model-only and record-move proposals keep **Accept the model**. A whole-type move still needs
migration confirmation. A partial move still needs publication. Loading an already saved layout
is a separate path: its confirmation can install and activate a model change before importing.
Read the confirmation for the path you are using.

## Only the model changes

When the request changes the model alone, such as adding a view without changing records,
acceptance installs the release and ends with a migration that moves no type. Review
**Preview the migration** and confirm it with **Model release** to put the workspace on the
new model. No change set is created and every record stays as it is.

## Every record of a type moves

A whole type becoming another type, two types merging, or a type moving into another application
can use a migration. The proposal lists what each type becomes and how many records it holds.
Accepting installs the proposed release but moves no record. **Preview the migration** opens
the existing migration review with the proposed choices filled in.

Someone with **Model release** confirms that migration. It changes live data and the workspace's
release together, keeping record IDs, values, relationships and history for the accepted type
moves. There is no change set to submit for approval in this path. Inspect every conversion,
removal and refusal in the [migration preview](/docs/guide/model/migrate-a-workspace/).

## Only some records move

For a split based on a field value, the proposal describes what acceptance prepares: a
release holding the old types beside the new ones, a change set moving the selected records,
and the final release removing the emptied types. The removal note says which records move
and where they go. After accepting, complete the prepared steps:

1. Activate the release holding the new types beside the old. No record moves yet.
2. Review and publish the change set, following the workspace's approval rules. The records
   change type and keep their IDs.
3. Activate the final release, removing the emptied types. If someone has added records to an
   old type meanwhile, activation is refused until that is resolved.

The task shows the next available step and marks completed steps **Done**. If the old types
remain in the accepted model, it shows **Two steps are yours** instead: no final removal is needed.
A whole-type move and a partial move need separate tasks. Splitting thousands of top-level
records can be slow because those records are prepared one at a time.

## Stop, correct or discard

**Stop** ends the current turn. A stopped correction returns to the last proposal, with a
warning if it already changed the draft. A stopped load discards the change set it was making
and returns to the accepted proposal. Before any proposal exists, the stopped task still takes
words telling the assistant how to continue.

A failed task shows its reason. Use **Tell the assistant how to go on**, or **Try again as it was**.
A stopped task offers **Go on as it was**. **Discard this task** ends it and removes its draft;
if it has a loaded change set, that is discarded too. Discard does not reverse a confirmed
migration or an already published change.

For a loaded change set that is wrong, **Discard and load again** removes that change set,
including your manual edits in it. For a workbook load, the assistant then revises the proposal
and checks its records again. Review it and choose **Accept and load to change set** to prepare the replacement
change set. Review the discard confirmation carefully. Once published, the task offers new work through **Change this model…** or
**Ask about these records…**, subject to your current permissions.
guide/src/content/docs/model/application:
---
title: Applications and views
description: Organise shared types into applications, navigation groups and declared views.
reader: model-admin
---

Applications give people named places to work. A model decides which types and views each
application lists. Any application can use any supported view when its structure fits; an
application's name does not give it special capabilities. You need **Model authoring** to edit
these definitions. Start with [Arrange applications and views](/docs/guide/model/arrange-applications-and-views/).

## Listings and navigation

Select an application to inspect **Object types**, **Views** and **Navigation groups**.
The type table shows where records stand and their attribute and relation counts. **List an
existing type…** adds another listing of a shared definition; it does not copy records.
**Stop listing in this application** removes a listing where allowed. Moving containment or
removing the definition has a different effect; see [Types](/docs/model/types-attributes-relations/).

![Application panel with its object types, views and navigation groups](/docs/screens/model-application-panel.png)

Navigation groups have a **Label**, ordered entries (collections and relation matrices) and an **Open**
or **Folded** starting state. A collection, or a relation matrix, can belong to only one group in an
application. A relation matrix placed in a group has an entry of its own, named after the view, and its
row type's entry stays. The matrix symbol uses the row type's colour, and opening the entry
goes directly to the matrix. The matrix also stays among the row collection's view tabs. Without
a group placement, it is available through that collection only. Ungrouped collections appear
at the top. An empty group is valid. Grouping does not change parents, data access or the type's
identity. Follow [Group collections in navigation](/docs/guide/model/group-collections-in-navigation/).

Navigation groups have one level: a group cannot contain another group. Its collection page
lets people search collection and matrix names; it does not show a record count for each entry.
Only collections with a view in this application can be placed in its groups. Group labels
and ordering change navigation without requiring a data migration.

A new navigation group starts open unless **Folded when the sidebar opens** is selected.
A person's later folding choice is remembered in their browser. Within an application, each
group has its own key, and a collection cannot be declared in two groups at once. If validation
names a collection outside the application, add a suitable view there or remove that group entry.

### The group panel

Choose a group in the model pane, or its name in the application's **Navigation groups**
table, to open its panel. It shows the application, starting state and entry count. **Entries**
lists collections and matrices together, in their sidebar order, with **Entry**, **Kind**,
**Opens on** and **State**. The application's group table also lists both kinds in **Entries**.

**Add to group…** lets you search and select several collections and matrices in one dialog.
Their location notes distinguish ungrouped collections, matrices inside a row collection and
entries in another group. Selecting an entry from another group moves it rather than copying
it. Entries already in the destination group are omitted. The whole addition is one history
step, so one **Undo** reverses it. In the application panel, **In no group:** offers
**Add to a group…** with the ungrouped collections already selected.

An entry's row menu offers **Move up**, **Move down**, **Move to another group…** and
**Take out of the group** where applicable. Taking a matrix out removes its separate entry;
it keeps the view in the row collection. A matrix's menu in the application's **Views** table
also offers **Move to group…** when a group exists. The group panel has **Rename…** and
**Start folded** / **Start unfolded**; the group menu orders or removes the group itself.

### A collection's opening view

**Opens on** chooses which of a collection's views opens from its sidebar entry or the group
page. Edit the cell in the group panel when the collection has more than one view, then
**Save**. The choice belongs to that collection in this application; it does not change
another collection's opening view or remove any view tabs. A separate matrix entry always
opens itself and shows **Itself** in this column.

Without a collection choice, refiroo uses the application's **Default view** if it is one of
that collection's views, otherwise its table, otherwise its first view. Choosing that same
fallback in **Opens on** returns the collection to following the default rather than keeping
a separate choice.

## Views

| View | What people use it for |
| --- | --- |
| Table | Read a collection with declared columns, filters and sorting. |
| Tree | Browse and move records through a declared hierarchy. |
| Mapping grid | Connect source and target records through a relationship. |
| Relation matrix | Read or edit related cell records at row and column intersections. |
| Relationships table | Show both ends and the connection’s own attributes in rows or a grid. |

A type created through the editor receives a table view. **Views** lists each view's kind,
what it shows and its state. Use its menu's **Rename…** for a label change.
Choose **Add a view…** in the application’s menu to add a Table, Tree, Mapping grid,
Relation matrix or **Relationships table: each relationship in a row, with its own attributes**. The kind list offers only views for which the model has suitable types and
relationships. Existing trees, mapping grids and relation matrices have **Change…**; ordinary collection table
layouts are arranged from the type’s Preview. A relationships table has its own **Layout…** action. Follow [Add a table, tree or mapping grid](/docs/guide/model/add-a-view/).

Application **Settings** has **Default view**, the view that opens first. Choose an existing
view and Save. A collection's **Opens on** choice takes precedence when opening that collection.
This changes the starting lens, not which types users can access. Icons,
colours and free-form presentation settings still need the [JSON view](/docs/model/json-view/).

## Relationships tables: columns and grouping

A relationships table reads one declared, directed relationship between two types. It shows
the from record, the to record and values carried by their connection. Containment is not
eligible. Both endpoint types are listed in the application when needed; adding the view
creates no records or relationships. Follow [Add a relationships table](/docs/guide/model/add-a-relationships-table/)
for the steps through **Add a view…**.

| Dialog field | What it controls |
| --- | --- |
| Relationships | The permitted pair and relationship, shown with an arrow from one type to the other. Changing this resets the field choices. |
| Columns of the from record | An ordered, non-empty choice of Name or scalar fields attached to the from type. The initial choice is Name and the first suitable unique field, if one exists. |
| Columns of the to record | The same choices for the to type. Their order is the displayed column order; the first labels each grid column group. |
| Attributes of the relationship | Attributes carried by this specific pair, rather than ordinary fields of either record. None is allowed. JSON values can be columns here. |
| Layout | **One row per relationship** lists existing connections. **Grid: each record once, a column group per related record** shows each from record once, with relationship attributes beneath each to-record group. |
| Head the rows by | **Nothing: one list**, **The from record** or **The to record**. Headings collect rows under the selected record. This choice is ignored by the grid. |
| Name | The label people see for this view. |

Endpoint columns cannot repeat and cannot hold JSON. Relationship columns must be declared
on the chosen pair and cannot repeat. The form derives filters from selected fields marked
Filterable, excluding JSON. Sorting includes both record names, selected scalar endpoint fields
and non-JSON relationship attributes. The initial sort is the from record's name and the
reading size is 20. A specialist can adjust filters, sorts and reading size (1–100) in the
[JSON view](/docs/model/json-view/#relationships-table-configuration).
Grid row ordering uses sorts on the from record.

If a saved declaration names a missing type, relationship, undeclared pair or unsuitable field,
**Issues** explains the failed reference. Correct that choice before installing; the
[specialist rules](/docs/model/json-view/#relationships-table-configuration) explain the diagnostic wording.
The view's **Layout…** changes only its presentation. **Remove relationships table** removes
the view and can stop listing types only it needed; read the confirmation. Stored connections
remain. The workspace sees draft changes only after release activation, and the view grants
no data permissions.

## A relation matrix needs a particular structure

Rows must connect to cell records; the cell records stand under column records. The form offers
only suitable choices. **Column heading**, ordered **Fields in a cell** and **Row columns**
determine what is shown. A cell displays its first text or number field, or its record name.
Open the matrix's menu in **Views** and choose **Change…** to set **What people can do in a
cell**. Any offered combination of **Create**, **Edit**, **Link existing** and **Unlink** can
be selected. These actions never grant access by themselves.

Create needs all required cell fields and no other required incoming relationship that the
cell cannot supply, apart from parent containment. Edit needs a writable selected cell field.
Link existing is offered, with individual candidates checked at runtime. Unlink is absent
when the relationship is required. Changing the structure or selected fields can remove
choices that no longer fit.

Create adds a record and its connection to the row. The relationship's candidate rules limit
where it may belong under the column. The form uses those rules first, then the groups already
holding this view's records, to suggest a place. It can also propose a missing group using
other columns as a pattern; accepting it needs no model change. The person reviews the place
and can choose another eligible group. See
[Relation matrices](/docs/use/relation-matrices/#what-you-can-change-from-a-cell). Link existing adds a connection to a shared
record, and Unlink removes only that connection. A filled cell offers Create alongside Link
existing unless a one-per-column uniqueness rule or the row's relationship cardinality limits
it to one. Empty, inactive and history-only cells can still offer Create. See
[Relation matrices](/docs/use/relation-matrices/) for counting states and change-set conflicts.

![Relation matrix form beside its structural preview](/docs/screens/model-matrix-view-dialog.png)

[Add a relation matrix](/docs/guide/model/add-a-relation-matrix/) walks through the form.
Do not confuse it with the editor's **Relationship matrix**, which defines permitted type pairs.
[Record pages and tables](/docs/model/record-pages-and-tables/) covers layout settings. A draft's
navigation and views become active only when its release is applied to the workspace.

## Application settings

The visual **Application…** form includes **Name** and **Description**. In an existing
application, **Settings** lets you change **Default view**. Application and type icons and
existing descriptions need a specialist in the [JSON view](/docs/model/json-view/).
Removing an application is a structural model change; retiring a workspace or release is a
separate administrative task. Check the removal confirmation for types only that application lists.

## Collections and their lenses

Views of the same source type appear as lenses of one collection. A table's source is the type
it lists. A mapping grid's source is the end chosen as its direction; a relation matrix's source
is its row type. A tree belongs to its first declared root type. Adding a second view for one
source type adds a way to work with that collection. Placing a relation matrix in a navigation
group adds a direct entry for that view while keeping the shared row collection.

## Mapping-grid declarations

A mapping grid chooses one permitted relationship and its two endpoint types. In the outgoing
direction its rows are sources choosing targets; in the incoming direction its rows are the
other end and the choices run back towards the source. Choose the direction before choosing
row and target-display fields. Both field lists must be non-empty and contain no repeats.
**Columns of a row** offers the row's own fields and, under **From the parents**, the types
it can stand beneath. Choosing a parent type adds a column headed by that type's name. It
shows the name of the row record's nearest parent of that type, including a parent several
levels above it. This gives context without changing the records being mapped. Row search
looks at source names and the source's displayed attributes; it does not search parent names.
**Columns of the matched record** offers that record's own fields, without parent columns.
Candidate search uses names or searchable attached fields of the type being chosen.

The configured relationship must be an optional association. Containment and required ownership
cannot be used, because replacing a mapping must not change a record's parent or orphan a
dependent. Saving one selected mapping replaces that source's mapping set; it does not change
the underlying relationship's cardinality for other clients.

A grid's model sets a page size of 1–100. The parent scope and coverage choices people select
while using it are temporary filters, not model settings. **Mapped**, **Unmapped** and
**Ambiguous** describe coverage for the configured relationship. **Add a view…** and the view’s **Change…** set its relationship, row end, display columns
and candidate search fields. New grids read 20 rows per page; changing that reading size
still needs the specialist view.

## Relation-matrix rules

A matrix uses one non-containment relationship, in either direction, between row and cell types.
The row, cell and column types must all be listed in the application. Its rows include records
of the row type in the workspace even when another application owns those records. Columns are
records of a type that can contain the cell type, directly or through intervening levels. A cell
record belongs to its nearest ancestor of that column type.

Choose unique, non-empty lists of **Row columns** and **Fields in a cell**. Row columns can include
fields of the row and its ancestor context. The column heading is the column record's name or a
non-JSON field attached to its type. Cell fields must be attached to the cell type. A specialist
can also declare row-search fields, using the name or searchable attached fields, and a page
size of 1–100.

| Cell action | Why it may be unavailable |
| --- | --- |
| Create | Every required cell field needs to be supplied or have a default. The cell must not require an additional owner relationship that the matrix cannot supply. |
| Edit | At least one displayed cell field must be editable. |
| Link existing | The chosen records must fit the binding, its candidate rules and number limits. |
| Unlink | A required owner relationship cannot be removed on its own. |

With no enabled cell actions, the matrix is read only. The form offers suitable actions; the
model's validation also rejects impossible declarations. Enabled actions still require each
person's data permissions. If Create is missing despite a default on a required field, ask a
specialist to inspect the declaration: the visual form checks that required fields are selected.

Uniqueness and conditional activity come from the relationship's rules, not a second rule on
the view. They describe the relationship's target end. An incoming matrix does not apply those
target-end rules to its cells, so it has no inactive or uniqueness-conflict states from them.
To inspect those states, use a suitable outgoing matrix. The matrix shows at most five cell
records as a preview with the full count; open a cell to inspect the rest.

## Tree declarations

A tree starts with parentless records of its root types. Every root type must also be a node
type and allow top-level creation. All shown node types must be listed in the application and
reachable from a root through containment using types the tree shows. A missing intermediate
type prevents that branch from being a valid tree. Recursive containment can show several levels
of the same type.

The main label is the name or a non-JSON field attached to every node type. An optional second
field can show identifying information, type, path, timestamps or another non-JSON field shared
by the node types. Child ordering is declared per type; without an entry, children sort by name.
Descending order is supported. Timestamp ordering falls back to name in change sets and
publications, which do not keep those live-only timestamps. Branches read 1–100 records at a time.

The declaration can offer creating children, renaming, moving and changing a Yes/No availability
field. With no actions it is read only. Create and Move need a containment possibility among
shown types. Rename cannot target a read-only label field. Availability needs an editable Yes/No
field attached to every node type, and that field cannot be declared without the availability
action. These choices enable controls; they do not grant permissions.

At runtime a node's menu offers allowed actions; F2 renames where enabled. Creating a child
offers only shown types the parent can contain. Move lists possible parents with unsuitable
choices disabled and their reasons. Search and opening a record reveal its path by loading
the relevant branches. **Add a view…** and **Change…** offer roots, a label, a second line, one shared child-order
field and an availability field. The editor includes reachable contained types already listed
in the application. New trees read 50 records per branch page. The form does not offer
separate ordering for each type, descending order, page size or the create, rename and move
actions: a specialist maintains those in the JSON view. Applying Change rebuilds the tree’s
action choices from the availability selection, so review previously declared actions afterwards.
