---
title: Consumer APIs in the model
description: Define the types, fields and read operations that other systems can consume.
reader: model-admin
---

A consumer API gives other systems a deliberate view of workspace data. Its contract chooses
which types and fields they read and the operations available to them. It is not a second copy
of the records. You need **Model authoring** to edit the draft; activation needs release access.
Start with [Define a consumer API](/docs/guide/model/define-a-consumer-api/).

## Choose the content within a shared form

Every consumer API uses the same patterns for presenting business objects, reading lists,
looking up values, resolving several inputs and reporting changes. Within your API, all exposed
record types share one declared object shape. Selected fields, related records, system codes,
translations and parent information fit into that shape. A field without a value uses its declared
fallback or stays empty; it does not require a different form for that record type.

Your choices supply the content: which types are exposed, what fields mean, which relationships
are followed, how lookups match and which changes are reported. The engine supplies the common
forms for objects, pages, errors and events. Systems that read your API can reuse their reading
and change-handling processes across types and contracts.

You still choose public field names, related fields and whether a relationship returns one record
or several. You also choose which operations are offered. These choices define your particular
contract; another consumer API can make different choices. A consuming system that reads the
contract's declared structure can adopt new types through configuration, while one written for
fixed names may need changes. Review the generated documents with that system's team.

Keep the agreed output stable as the underlying model evolves. The consumer contract's version
is separate from the model release version; a breaking change needs a higher contract version.
See [the shared patterns and two example record types](/docs/integrate/consumer-apis/#learn-one-way-to-read-business-objects)
for the integrator's explanation.

## From an editor choice to a consumer's answer

A **business object** is one record presented in the shape you choose for other systems.
It can include fields from that record, its parent and related records. Get by ID, lists
and lookups all return this same shape. A lookup adds a match score; a list wraps objects
in a page. Changing the shape therefore affects more than one operation.

**Reference-data example:** Stops API exposes stops, municipalities, operators and modes. A stop’s business object includes its name, stop number, operator, modes and selected system codes. An operator uses the same declared fields, with stop-specific values empty. These are choices in this model, not built-in transport features.

## The business object consumers read

On **Fields**, **Role** says which field supplies the identity, code, name or validity dates.
The identity role always reads the record's stable ID. A business code such as a stop number
is a separate field; it does not replace that ID. **Output name** controls the name in the
answer, while **Served type** shows the value's type and whether it can be missing.

![Stops API fields with output names, roles, ordered sources, served types and defaults](/docs/screens/model-consumer-tab-fields.png)

Above: Stops API in the reference model. The code has three ordered sources; stopNumber is
an integer and validTo can be null.

**Reference-data example:** Chur’s stop is named Chur, has stop number 8509000 and abbreviation CH. Its operator is Schweizerische Bundesbahnen SBB and its mode is Train. The containment path names Graubünden, Plessur and Chur, excluding the stop itself.

A field does not inherit a parent’s or related record’s value automatically. Choose the parent’s fields in **Parent**, or publish related values through an explicit related block. A single-valued relationship gives one related object or an empty value; a many-valued relationship gives a list, which can be empty. This shape follows the relationship’s cardinality and is part of the contract. Decimal values retain precision; integers, booleans and dates keep their declared types.

### The parent can carry its own values

Serve the parent when consumers need the containing record's identity and values in the same
answer as the child. On **Fields**, choose **Parent, path and hierarchy…** and turn on
**Serve the parent (objectType, id, code, name)**. Below the object's fields, **Parent** then shows **Output name** and
**Fields**. The field picker offers the built-in type, identity, code and name choices, plus
attributes attached to the types that can directly contain an exposed type. Those parent types
do not have to be exposed as business objects themselves.

Each parent field has a public output name you choose and a source it reads. In
**Parent fields…**, review the rows pairing a name with its source. The editor proposes
camelCase words for the name; you can change it. The Parent table shows name=source when
they differ. For example, a category's approval flag can be published as isApproved.

A parent field keeps its declared type. Without a default, it answers null if this parent's
type does not bind its source or the record has no value. With no parent, the whole parent
output is null. An unexposed parent's public type is null. A specialist can also give a field
ordered sources and a default, as for the object's fields. Sources must share a value type.

An existing short list of parent sources remains valid. Built-in fields keep their role's
public output name; other sources use their words in camelCase. For example, a category-code
source is served as categoryCode. Editing the parent writes out the explicit names.

Under **Parent's related records**, use **Add related**, then choose **Output name**, **Via**
and **Fields**. The relationship starts from the parent, rather than the child. The block
appears beside the parent's selected fields, as an object or list according to cardinality.
There is one parent level: it has no nested parent, path or hierarchy. The main object's path
and hierarchy remain available for ancestor names. A specialist can also select a value from
the parent's own ancestors; the field picker does not offer new ancestor sources.

**Example:** a catalogue item can carry its category's identity, an approval flag and related
external codes. The consuming system can read them together without fetching the category
separately. On a list, the category's block repeats on every child row. Consider serving a
large or rarely used block only on request.

### Serve related records always or on request

In **Types and related**, each related block has a **Served** column. The same column appears
under **Parent's related records** on **Fields**. Choose **Always** for a block in every answer,
or **On request** when consumers should explicitly ask for it. Always is the default for an
existing block and for a new one.

An on-request block is absent from an ordinary answer. When requested, it has its usual object
or list shape, including null or an empty list when there is no related record. This keeps the
default answer small without losing its declared types. On **Operations**, **Include** lists
the accepted choices automatically; edit **Served** to change that list. Parent choices have
a parent prefix there, even when you choose a different output name for the parent itself.

A filter can still use an on-request block without returning it. On **Filters**, **On related**
offers both the object's blocks and the parent's. **Keep only matching records** removes a
child if its parent's selected block has no matching item. Without that option, the filter
only trims the block. **Crosswalk** applies to the object's own blocks, not the parent's.
The filter's Name belongs to the contract; the Include parameter's name is reserved.

Turning an always-served block into an on-request block removes it from existing consumers'
ordinary answers. Review the compatibility warning and raise the contract version. Adding
parent fields or blocks, or adding filters, does not by itself require a higher version.

![Consumer API Fields tab showing Parent fields and a related block served on request](/docs/screens/model-consumer-parent-fields.png)

The Parent section shows the selected parent attributes and **Parent's related records**,
including **Via**, **Fields** and **Served**.

### Sources and defaults

Sources are tried in the displayed order, skipping missing values and empty text. Zero and
false are values, not missing data. If none supplies a value, the declared **Default** is
used; without one, the answer contains null. A default affects the output only and never
writes a value into a record. It must have the field's served type.

**Reference-data example:** the reference API has no field defaults. If you set a default abbreviation of “—”, records without an abbreviation receive that fallback in the consumer answer. Chur still shows CH. Neither record’s stored abbreviation changes.

### Values belonging to a relationship

A related block can publish values of the connection as well as values of the related record.
In its **Fields** picker, **Attributes of the relationship** lists the shared attributes carried
by the allowed pair in the selected direction. Choose a public output name for each one.
The answer uses its declared type: Yes or no stays boolean, for example. A connection without
a held value returns null for that field. If no related record exists, the whole block still
uses its usual empty object-or-list form.

These choices belong inside the related block, not the main object's **Fields**. The main object
has no single connection from which to read such a value. If a carried field is missing from
the picker, review **Via**, the exposed types and the allowed pair's **Carries** before editing
the contract. The same values appear in object reads, lists, lookups and resolved objects.
Publications retain their saved values; a business date filters validity rather than rewinding
later edits. See the [integrator's reference example](/docs/integrate/consumer-apis/#publish-values-of-the-connection)
for the resulting contract and answers.

![Consumer related-field picker showing Attributes of the relationship beside record sources](/docs/screens/model-consumer-relationship-field-picker.png)

*Above: Stops API’s Add related dialog in a reference-model draft. The proposed output
operatorLinks follows Operated by (forward) from Stop to Operator and has fields name,
localName and isPrimary. The isPrimary source list is open: Attributes of the relationship
offers Local name (text), Primary contact (boolean) and Inspected on (date), with Primary
contact selected. Built in and Attributes of the exposed types are separate groups. Nothing
has been applied.*

An **On related** filter can select one of these carried attributes in **Matches on**. It
matches that particular connection, not every object connected to the same related record.
A lookup's **Also match through** rule can also use a carried text value in **First of**.
A scored match needs text; a filter can compare other declared types, including Yes or no.
These matching choices do not require the attribute to be searchable or unique.

## Lists, filters and the requests they enable

A list selects the type to return and its order. **Within the filter** gives a list a
containment scope. A filter's **Name** becomes a parameter name; **Matches on** chooses
which values a consumer can supply. These are public choices: changing a filter name or
its accepted values can break a consuming system even if the output fields stay the same.

![Stops API filters and the records and related blocks they read](/docs/screens/model-consumer-tab-filters.png)

Above: the reference API's municipality filter matches an ancestor by ID, name or FSO
number on ordinary reads. A list's Within parameter with the same name takes parent IDs
only. Its mode filter reads related modes and keeps only matching records.

**Reference-data example:** the reference API has a list of stops within a municipality, sorted by stop number. A consumer selects the municipality by its stable identity. On a list without that special parent scope, the ordinary municipality filter can match a municipality’s name or FSO number instead. Omitting the parent selection returns the whole listed type. A page size controls one response, not the entire collection.

A related mode filter can keep only stops linked to Train and show only matching modes in their related block. Another related filter can trim the block without removing the object. A filter does not create another output field. Agree both effects with the consuming team.

## Lookups and batch answers

**XREF** finds records by the values another system knows. **Exact** and **Contains** are
numeric weights. Exact comparison ignores letter case for text; Contains matches part of
text and applies only to terms of at least three characters. A higher match score ranks
first; it is not a percentage or a guarantee that the record is the intended one.

**Reference-data example:** the stop number rule has an Exact weight of 900. Looking up 8509000 identifies Chur with that score. Looking up its Wikidata code Q663869 instead reaches Chur through a related system-code record, with the configured weight of 90. These weights rank candidates; they are not confidence percentages.

Use **Preferred types…** on an **Also match through** row to select **Prefer records of
these types**. The choices are exposed types; clear them for no preference. Review its effect
with the consuming team, especially when the same related value reaches several types.

A request for one answer succeeds only with an untied best candidate. No match and a tied best score are distinct outcomes. **Also match through** lets related records identify their owners. **First of** uses the first matching related rule; **Prefers** can choose which exposed owner types receive its score.

**Resolve** applies Get by ID or lookup rules to many inputs. Each gets its own found, missing, ambiguous or refused outcome, in input order. Shared request filters can be overridden for an individual item; those defaults narrow the question, whereas a field’s Default fills a missing output value. **Crosswalk** enables asking for a selected related representation, such as a system code. It does not resolve a tied source match by guessing which source has a target.

## Events describe changes to the output

An event's **Types** selects the records, **Changes** selects creation, update or deletion,
and **Watches** limits which output changes trigger an update event. Leaving Watches empty
watches any change to the business object, including related blocks. **Events per type**
adds a standard event for each exposed type. The reference API leaves that option off
and declares only its custom `stops-changed` event.

**Reference-data example:** Stops API watches code, name and validity dates. Renaming Chur to Chur Bahnhof produces an update notification naming the name output. Changing latitude alone does not trigger that event. This is an example change, not a record of a change in the reference snapshot.

A related record’s edit or a relationship joining or leaving a watched block can also trigger an update.
Changes to a parent's selected attributes, values read from its ancestors or items in its
related blocks can report an update for each child showing that parent. Watch the parent
output, or leave Watches empty, to cover those changes. Events and webhook deliveries have
no Include choice: their full objects leave on-request blocks out.
If a block exposes connection values, an update of that relationship can report the block as
changed too. Add the block to **Watches**, or leave Watches empty to include all output changes.
A notification watching only unrelated main fields does not report that edit. Watched source changes can be reported even if a fallback leaves the displayed answer equal. A validity date passing without a write produces no notification. Moving a record into an event’s types counts as creation, moving it out as deletion, and moving between included types as an update to its type.

Full notifications carry current business objects when delivered, rather than a saved historical copy. Deleted records have no object body. Declaring an event does not register a receiver or grant access. Administrators manage delivery separately; see [Webhooks](/docs/administer/webhooks/).

## What the editor shows

Select **Consumer APIs** in the model pane, then an API. Its facts show **Contract version** and
**Compatible with what consumers read**, **Needs contract version …**, or **Checked once the
draft is valid**. Fix model errors before relying on the compatibility result.

| Tab | What you decide or inspect |
| --- | --- |
| Types and related | Exposed record types, their public names, related blocks and optional parent, path and hierarchy. |
| Fields | Output names, value sources and roles. Ordered sources use the first non-empty value. |
| Operations | Get by ID, cross-reference and resolve choices, lists and custom events. |
| Filters | Named ways to narrow or match records, including through related blocks. |
| Schema | The generated description of the data shape. |
| Message example | A generated example of the declared shape, rather than a live record sample. |

![Consumer API definition on the Types and related tab](/docs/screens/model-consumer-tab-types.png)

A field's **Output name** is the word consumers receive. **Sources…** chooses the fields it
reads, in order; **Role** identifies a purpose used by the contract. **Add related…** follows
an allowed relationship and selects the related fields to expose. The declaration can also
serve parent, path and hierarchy information.

## Operations and matching

**Get by ID**, **XREF** and **Resolve** are offered for the API’s exposed types. **Resolve**
requires both Get by ID and XREF; **Events per type** enables the standard type events. Lists specify **Of**,
an optional **Within the filter** and **Sorted by**. Cross-reference rules choose how values
identify related records. Matching can use **Exact** and **Contains** weights and **Also match
through** a related block. Check **Matches on…**, **Fields…**, **First of** and **Prefers** where
shown rather than assuming the display name is the unique identifier.

Filters have a **Name** and **Verb**: **By type**, **Under**, **Linked to** or **On related**.
Their further choices depend on what they read. **Through** can use the record itself, a related
block or records sharing that block. **On related** can keep only matching records, score only
matching items or expose a crosswalk. These choices change what a consumer can ask and receive.
Custom events select **Types**, **Changes** and **Watches**; leaving Watches empty watches any
change to what consumers read. An event declaration does not create a delivery subscription.

## Contracts, access and limits

A contract version is separate from the model release version, draft version and model language
version. Removing or changing something consumers read can require a higher contract version.
Renaming a public field or changing relationship cardinality can affect the output too. Review
the differences with the consuming teams, then
[raise the contract version](/docs/guide/model/raise-a-contract-version/). Raising it keeps the previous definition served beside the new version by default. The editor preserves the definition from the draft’s base release, including when the draft already contains breaking edits. An API or version not served by that base release has no previous definition to retain. An invalid model still needs repair.

A consuming system needs a client granted this particular API in each workspace it reads.
Defining the API, granting a role or giving a person Model authoring does not grant consumer
access. A security administrator manages these grants. Without the API grant, a data read
is refused with Forbidden; the consumer does not receive a reduced version of the object.
Agree the exposed fields with that administrator: a grant opens this API's declared output,
not a field-by-field selection.
**Rename…** changes its display name; **Describe…** supplies its generated description.
A released key identifies consumers' existing access point: keep it stable. A released API's
key can still be changed, but consumers of the old key then get 404, as with removal. Removing an API
stops its consumers reading it once active. Review that warning even where removal is allowed.

A specialist can edit the definition or an item as one saved step.
No visual form covers every detail of the model language. Use the
[specialist view](/docs/model/json-view/) with a specialist for unsupported combinations, then inspect
Issues and the generated documents. Do not infer support solely from a field being accepted as text.

See [the generated documents](/docs/guide/model/see-a-consumer-apis-documents/) for review and handover;
integrators use [Integrate](/docs/integrate/overview/) for requests and authentication.

## Review edits that remove behavior

Turning **XREF** off asks **Stop offering XREF?**. It removes the match rules and also stops
**Resolve**, which depends on XREF. **Undo** restores the step; switching XREF on again starts
without those rules. Inspect the contract changes before activating. An operation not declared
in the contract is unavailable to consumers and absent from its generated operation document.

A field's editable **Default** supplies its declared fallback when sources do not yield a value;
it differs from a default on a record attribute. An identity-role output reads the record's
stable ID; publish other identifiers as separate fields. Output roles must not conflict, related
blocks must name valid relationships, and a filter must choose one kind of read. The Issues
list points to invalid references or combinations.

The model language also supports per-type events, watched fields and related blocks, scoped
lists and parameters based on types, ancestors or related records. Use the specialist document
view for declarations the current form does not expose. Reducing event coverage, changing
crosswalk availability or removing an operation can require a higher contract version just as
removing a field does. Adding more output is usually compatible; lowering a contract version
is refused.

*Source for the reference examples: opentransportdata.swiss, Service Points (Didok), Federal Office of Transport / SBB, snapshot 2026-11-02. Wikidata, CC0.*

## Keep an earlier version available

Use this when consuming systems need time to move to a changed contract. In the model
editor, select the consumer API and open **Types and related**. You need **Model authoring** to edit;
the release must then be installed and activated in each workspace that serves it.

1. Raise **Contract version** when changing what existing consumers read. **Raise contract
   version to …** advances it by one. The editor keeps the definition from the draft’s base
   release, rather than copying any breaking edits already made in the draft. An API or
   version not served by that base release leaves no earlier version to keep.
2. Make the breaking edits to the new current version. In **Earlier versions**, check the
   retained **Version**, **Superseded** day and **Sunset day**. Earlier versions keep their
   output shape but read current data; they are not historical copies of records.
3. To announce an end date, select the row's **Sunset day** value or its pencil. In
   **Sunset day (YYYY-MM-DD)**, enter the calendar date and choose **Save**. Emptying it and
   saving withdraws the announcement; the table then shows a dash. A refused date stays in
   the form with **Not saved** and its reason; the saved date is unchanged. Correct it and
   save again, or **Cancel**. The day is announced to consumers in the response's Sunset
   header after activation. It is an announcement: refiroo serves the version until you
   explicitly stop it, whatever the date.
4. Review Issues and the generated documents, then install and activate the release. Installing
   alone does not change a workspace. Existing consumers and webhooks on a retained version
   continue using that version's shape.

The model administrator chooses the notice period with the consuming teams. The software's
own compatibility period does not impose a deadline on your organisation's consumer APIs.

If you already made breaking edits, **Needs contract version …** offers **Raise to version …**
and **Raise and stop serving version …**. **Raise to version …** keeps the base release’s
definition while your edited definition becomes the new version. Choosing
**Raise and stop serving version …** instead leaves no copy of the
version being replaced. Use that choice only when its consumers are ready to lose access.

![Earlier versions table with a retained version, superseded day, sunset day and Stop serving](/docs/screens/model-consumer-earlier-versions.png)

### Stop serving and undo

In **Earlier versions**, choose **Stop serving** for the intended version. Read the confirmation:
consumers lose access once the draft is active. Cancel to keep serving it, or confirm the removal.
**Undo** restores that draft step before activation. Review compatibility, install and activate
the release only after the receiving teams have moved. Stopping an earlier version preserves
records and other versions. It stops that version's reads and suspends subscriptions bound to it;
ask the integration administrator to check the receiver before resuming on the current version.

Follow [Stop serving an earlier contract version](/docs/guide/model/stop-serving-an-earlier-contract-version/) for the sunset announcement, removal and undo steps.

After activation, restoring service needs a release that retains the original definition again;
an old installed release does not keep a route running by itself. Do not recreate an earlier
version with a changed shape under the same number.

### When the retained version prevents activation

Every retained version must still refer to types, fields and relationships present in the new
model. Keep those sources while consumers need them. An issue names the version and the missing
source; restore the source or coordinate stopping that version.

A retained number must be lower than the current version and appear only once. Invalid dates,
duplicate numbers and invalid references must be corrected before release. If a kept contract
would change, the finding says **a kept version is served as it was: restore it, or stop serving
it**. Raising the current version again does not repair the retained copy. The install review
shows this finding rather than offering a version-raise fix for it. A warning that a version
stops serving is expected only when removal is deliberate; inspect it before activation.

## Edit version and remove a contract

The API’s **Settings** table has an editable **Contract version**. Enter a positive whole
number and Save, or Cancel to leave it unchanged. The menu’s **Raise contract version to …**
advances it by one without typing. Lowering a version is refused; increasing it does not
repair an invalid definition. When the draft’s base release served the version being raised, its definition appears in **Earlier versions** and remains available after activation.

Use **Remove consumer API** only after coordinating with its consumers. The confirmation
warns that they receive 404 once this draft is active. Cancel keeps it; Undo restores a saved
removal in the draft. Existing releases remain immutable, but do not keep the old contract
running in a workspace that activates the new model.

**Edit as JSON…** on the API edits its complete definition as one step; on a row, it edits
that item. These are specialist controls, not a prerequisite for the named forms. Ask a
specialist to handle combinations the forms do not expose, then review Issues, compatibility
and the generated documents again.

guide/src/content/docs/model/issues-and-:
---
title: Issues and dry runs
description: Distinguish model validity, compatibility with stored records and predicted data changes.
reader: model-admin
---

Check a model before applying it. refiroo answers three different questions: are the definitions
valid, does the selected workspace's data fit, and what happens to incoming or moved records?
A green result for one question does not answer the others.

## Issues in a draft

Expand **Issues and history**, then choose **Issues**. Each issue gives its severity, message and,
where available, a link to the affected element. The header also reports the validation state.
A draft can be saved while invalid so you can repair it in several steps. It cannot be installed
until its blocking model errors are resolved.

![Issues tab naming an unavailable field and linking to its view](/docs/screens/model-issues-error.png)

*Above: a deliberate error in Guide draft makes the Municipalities view refer to a field that
is not available. The issue links to the view, and the header says 1 error.*

Read the whole message. A missing field in a view may need removing from the view, or attaching
the intended field to its record type. Creating another field simply to silence the message can
leave the wrong design in place. Recheck after the correction.

**No issues** means the draft is valid. With a workbook, the list also includes import-profile
warnings and errors. Warnings need review even when they do not block model installation; a
valid model can still have refused source rows.

![Issues tab showing no issues and a Valid header](/docs/screens/model-issues-none.png)

*Above: Guide draft is valid again after the faulty view setting was corrected.*

Follow [Fix issues before installing](/docs/guide/model/fix-issues-before-installing/).

## Does stored data fit?

**Install and activate…**, **Apply to this workspace…** and an installed release's
**Activate in a workspace…** check the selected workspace's data. Compatibility means its records,
values and relationships fit without migration. It does not copy data from another workspace.

A removed type still holding records, a newly required field with missing values, duplicate values
under a uniqueness rule, or too many relationships under a tighter cardinality can prevent a
switch. Read the named data and reason. Correct the data under the current model, revise the draft,
or use the offered migration preview where records must move. Ordinary activation does not silently
convert or discard incompatible records.

Consumer APIs are checked separately. A change that breaks what other systems read needs a higher
contract version before activation. Review the listed differences with the people responsible for
those systems before using **Raise to v…**. This is separate from the model release version.

A check reflects the data and versions it read. Another edit or activation can invalidate it;
refiroo checks again at the write boundary and can refuse the confirmation.

## A workbook's dry run

With an attached workbook, **Dry run** checks the whole mapped file against the draft and the
comparison workspace without writing records. It identifies the draft version and check time.
Figures include records created or updated, values, relationships, related records created and
refused rows. Open a figure to inspect the rows and reasons behind it. A **was** figure compares
with the previous result.

Wait for **Checked** after an edit. **Checked** means the file was checked, not that every row
was accepted. **Failed** or **Stopped** is not a completed result. Read the failure and retry;
do not rely on a result from an older draft version. A draft without a workbook has no file rows
to check. See [Workbook onboarding](/docs/model/workbook-onboarding/) for this flow and its screenshots.

## A copy or move dry run

Between workspaces with different models, a dry run checks every selected item through a mapping.
Its five summary figures count different things:

| Figure | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Create | Records to add in the target. |
| Update (copied before or found) | Target records found again and updated instead of duplicated. |
| Cannot be copied / Cannot move | Records refused or left out. |
| Relationships carried | Relationships that can be represented in the target. |
| Relationships dropped | Relationships refused or left out by the mapping or selection. |

**What cannot be copied** or **What cannot move** groups the reasons and lists affected items.
A **Value not carried** can leave a record copied without that field; a refused record is left out
entirely. Do not read an item total as a count of records: the report also concerns relationships
and values.

![Copy dry run report grouping refused records, dropped relationships and values not carried](/docs/screens/model-mapping-dry-run.png)

*Above: the Graubünden-to-Default dry run predicts 79 records created. Its report includes invalid
parents, missing required values and unmapped relationships. Nothing has been copied.*

Use **Open the mapping** on an item to repair the relevant choice. Review a fresh dry run after
changing the mapping or selection. See [Model mappings](/docs/model/model-mappings/) for the rules
and [Move records to another model](/docs/guide/model/move-records-to-another-model/) for the task.

Some issues offer a direct fix, such as **Use as the profile's key** or removing a panel naming
a removed field. Read what the action changes before choosing it, then recheck the issues.
A workbook's Dry run has separate source tabs; inspect each, including the dialog listing
refused sheet rows for its type. The figures' **was** values compare with the last check, not
with a completed import.
guide/src/content/docs/model/json-view.m:
---
title: The JSON view
description: Use the specialist document workbench for definitions beyond the visual editor.
reader: model-admin
---

Most modelling tasks use the visual editor. The **JSON** view is the specialist workbench for
the complete model document, including settings without visual forms. Ask a specialist model
author to maintain those settings if you do not work with model documents. Both views edit the
same draft; neither directly changes the active workspace.

Open **JSON** in the editor header, or **Open as JSON** in its menu. The workbench has **Draft
name**, **JSON model**, **Authoritative validation**, a summary and **Compile and compare**.
You need **Model authoring** to save. See [Edit a draft as JSON](/docs/guide/model/edit-a-draft-as-json/)
for the workbench controls, without needing to learn document syntax here.

![Document workbench with draft name, validation and compile actions](/docs/screens/model-draft-json.png)

## Saving and checking

A syntax error prevents saving the text. Valid syntax does not prove that referenced definitions
exist or that the model is usable. **Authoritative validation** checks those rules and lets you
select a diagnostic to reach the affected text. Saving keeps the draft, including work still
needing model corrections. **Compile and compare** uses the saved version and shows **Canonical
model**, **Ready for review** or **Invalid**, a model hash and the semantic differences.

**Export JSON** downloads the current document. It does not install or activate it. **Install
immutable release…** separately confirms creation of an inactive release; activation still
requires a workspace compatibility check. The visual editor's **Install and activate…** combines
those stages. See [Releases](/docs/model/releases/).

## Other editors and unsupported visual settings

Unsaved text is local to this workbench until **Save draft**. If another author saves first,
**A newer draft version exists** preserves your text. **Copy local JSON** keeps it for review;
**Reload saved version** reads the saved draft without merging. Saved document edits appear
as **JSON edit** in History.

The document covers application descriptions and presentation settings; type display, placement
and effective periods; shared and relationship attributes; validation and uniqueness rules;
full view and panel declarations; consumer contracts; and import-profile instructions where
applicable. Visual controls cover only the options described on their pages. Do not infer that
an absent form means the model cannot declare a feature. Integrators use
[Integrate](/docs/integrate/overview/) for the model contract details rather than browser steps.

## Settings that still need a specialist

Use the named controls first. The type’s **Settings** now sets its display attribute,
effective period, grouped field requirement and parent relationships; attribute Settings
sets numeric limits, Hidden and Help text. Relationship **Carries**, application **Default
view**, **Add a view…**, **Header and breadcrumbs…** and panel **Settings…** also have forms.
See [Types](/docs/model/types-attributes-relations/), [Views](/docs/model/applications-and-views/)
and [Record pages](/docs/model/record-pages-and-tables/) for those tasks.

These supported choices still require the complete document workbench:

| Choice | What to review with the specialist |
| --- | --- |
| Model title and description | The product wording used by the top bar comes from the default workspace’s model. A draft title alone does not change it. |
| Application or type icon | Choose an icon supported by refiroo; the visual editor displays it but has no icon picker. |
| Existing application, type or shared-field description | The new-application form takes a description; the element tables do not provide a general description editor. |
| Released field’s value type | A specialist can save the changed definition here when the visual editor refuses it. Compile and compare, install the release, then review the workspace migration before changing stored values. |
| Attribute default | A typed starting value used on creation, not a rule that refills cleared values. |
| Relationship uniqueness within an ancestor and its condition | Review the allowed type pair, ancestor and target field; these rules govern writes, not just one view. |
| Tree actions and detailed ordering | Create, Rename and Move, different ordering per child type, descending order and reading size. The visual tree form controls availability and one common child-order field. |
| Mapping-grid reading size | The visual form chooses endpoints, columns and candidate search, and new grids read 20 rows at a time. |
| Relation-matrix search and reading size | The matrix form sets structure, displayed fields and cell actions; additional row search fields and reading size need the workbench. |
| Full panel declarations | Creating a Table or Hierarchy panel directly, changing a table panel’s record type or a contained panel’s type list after creation. Existing hierarchy and table panels have Settings controls. |
| Detailed consumer declarations | The consumer editor has named forms for ordinary choices; a specialist can edit an entire API or item with **Edit as JSON…** when a combination has no form. |

Every saved change still needs validation. A free-form setting accepted in a document is not
proof that refiroo uses it. Ask the specialist to confirm the behavior and inspect the preview
and release checks before activation. Export preserves model definitions; it does not back up
workspace records, files, access settings or history. Use the operator’s
[backup and restore procedure](/docs/run/backup-and-restore/) for the installation.

## Relationships table configuration

Start with the [visual relationships-table form](/docs/guide/model/add-a-relationships-table/).
A specialist maintaining its configuration uses `fromColumns` and `toColumns` as ordered,
non-empty lists of `name` or scalar attribute keys attached to the respective endpoint type.
Each list must contain unique fields. `attributeColumns` is an ordered list of attribute keys
declared by that specific relationship binding; it may be empty but cannot repeat a key.
A JSON relationship attribute may be a column, but cannot be a filter or sort.

`groupBy` is `from`, `to` or null (no grouping). It heads the rows by the chosen record.
`layout` is `rows` by default, or `grid`: each from record once, with a column group per to
record, headed by the first `toColumns` field. The grid ignores `groupBy`; `from:` sorts
order its rows.

`filterFields` and `sortFields` identify the field's location as `from:<field>`, `to:<field>`
or `relation:<attribute>`. Endpoint fields must be `name` or attached scalar attributes;
relationship fields must be declared on the binding. Attribute filters require Filterable.
The visual form derives these lists from selected columns, excluding JSON; it starts
`defaultSort` at `from:name` and `pageSize` at 20. A specialist may declare other valid fields.
`sortFields` must be non-empty, `defaultSort` must name an entry (optionally prefixed with
`-` for descending), and `pageSize` must be 1–100.

Validation identifies the offending location. The following quoted diagnostic fragments are
from the validator; words in braces stand for the names in the affected declaration:

| Diagnostic wording | Correction |
| --- | --- |
| “references unknown object type '{key}'” / “references unknown relation type '{key}'” | Use existing definitions for both ends and the relationship. |
| “cannot use containment relation type '{key}'” | Choose a non-containment relationship. |
| “references a relation binding ({relation}, {from} → {to}) that is not declared in objectTypeRelations” | Declare the directed pair or choose a permitted one. |
| “View {list} must contain unique fields” | Remove repeats from the named column, filter or sort list. |
| “{list} references '{field}', which is not 'name' or a scalar attribute attached to '{type}'” | Use a field of the correct endpoint type. |
| “attributeColumns references '{field}', which binding ({relation}, {from} → {to}) does not declare in attributeTypeKeys” | Use an attribute carried by that pair. |
| “{purpose} field '{ref}' must be from:<field>, to:<field> or relation:<attribute>” | Qualify the filter or sort with its location. |
| “{purpose} field '{ref}': the binding does not declare attribute '{field}' in attributeTypeKeys” | Correct the relationship attribute reference. |
| “{purpose} field '{ref}': '{field}' is not 'name' or a scalar attribute attached to '{type}'” | Correct the endpoint reference. |
| “filter field '{ref}': attribute '{field}' is not filterable” | Remove the filter or enable filtering on that attribute. |
| “{purpose} field '{ref}' holds JSON and cannot be used” | Keep JSON as a relationship column only. |
| “defaultSort must name one of its sortFields” | Choose a declared sort field. |

guide/src/content/docs/model/managing-wo:
---
title: Managing workspaces
description: Create and manage independent datasets and choose which model each runs.
reader: model-admin
---

Manage datasets under **Settings › Workspaces**. You need **Workspace administration** for
workspace changes; reading data, changing models and granting access need their own permissions.
For everyday navigation, see [Workspaces](/docs/use/workspaces/).

## Find a workspace


Where your access permits it, **Manage workspaces** or **Settings**, **Workspaces** opens the
workspace list. It shows the model and release of each workspace and marks the default.

![Workspace management listing each workspace and its model release](/docs/screens/use-workspaces-manage.png)

*Above: Graubünden and Default run different models. This capture only views the list.*

Open a workspace row to inspect **Overview**, **Access**, **Approval** and **Activity**.
**Open workspace** returns to its data; **Activity** shows [history across records](/docs/use/history/).
The other actions require administrative permissions: **New workspace**, **Edit model**,
**Copy or move data…**, **Rename…** and **Retire…** change the workspace or its configuration.
Opening the page does not perform them.

![A workspace detail with its actions and Overview, Access, Approval and Activity tabs](/docs/screens/use-workspaces-detail.png)

*Above: Graubünden's Overview shows its key, model, applications and default status.*

A retired workspace remains readable but refuses changes. Open it through workspace management,
rather than the active workspace selector. The default workspace cannot be retired or deleted;
an administrator must make another workspace the default first.

## Create or rename a workspace

1. Open **Settings › Workspaces**. Search the list before creating another dataset. Active
   workspaces appear first, then retired ones.
2. Choose **New workspace**. Complete its name and key. The key forms its address; choose it
   carefully. Use the default workspace's model, or choose another usable installed release.
3. Confirm creation and check the new workspace's **Overview**, model and applications. It has
   its own data; creation copies no records from the default workspace. Read any refusal before
   retrying. Cancel leaves the list unchanged.
4. To change its displayed name later, choose **Rename…**, enter the new name and save.
   Renaming does not change its key or create a new dataset.

## Retire, reactivate, make default or delete

- **Retire…** asks for confirmation. It removes the workspace from the active selector and
  refuses writes, keeping data, change sets, publications and history readable. Open it from
  this list later. **Reactivate** makes it available for work again.
- **Set as default** chooses the default destination. It neither copies data nor changes the
  models of other workspaces. Check the Default mark after the action.
- **Delete…** is only for an empty, never-published workspace with no change sets or webhook
  subscriptions. A workspace ever published can only be retired, even after its data is removed.
  The screen explains what prevents deletion. Confirm only after checking the name and key.

The default workspace cannot be retired or deleted. Make another active workspace the default
first. If another administrator changed the workspace or default while the page was open, review
the refreshed state and repeat only the action still needed.

## Tabs and model changes

**Overview** shows the workspace's facts and its model's applications; each application opens
in this workspace. **Access** lists grants for people, groups and clients. **Approval** holds
[publication policies](/docs/administer/approval-policies/). **Activity** lists changes newest
first, grouped by day, with filters; see [History](/docs/use/history/). Only tabs your access allows
are shown.

**Edit model** opens the saved draft for the workspace, reopening it on later visits. It needs
Model authoring, Model release and Browse, and an active workspace. Check **Applies to**, then
use **Apply to this workspace…** after editing. The confirmation lists model changes, data
compatibility, open change sets left behind and other workspaces left unchanged. If records must
move, review the separate preview before confirming. Follow
[Install and activate a release](/docs/guide/model/install-and-activate-a-release/).
**Copy or move data…** starts [a copy or move](/docs/guide/model/move-records-to-another-model/).

Workspace administration can also be switched off by the deployment. The page then stays read
only and names the setting; ask the operator to enable it if administration is needed.

## Workspace tasks

[Create a workspace](/docs/guide/model/create-a-workspace/),
[Edit its model](/docs/guide/model/edit-a-workspaces-model/),
[Make it the default](/docs/guide/model/make-a-workspace-the-default/) and
[Retire or delete it](/docs/guide/model/retire-or-delete-a-workspace/) give the steps.
To choose an installed release, use [Change a workspace's model](/docs/guide/model/change-a-workspaces-model/).

**Cannot be opened** on a workspace whose model language is unsupported needs the offered
model-language repair or operator help; see [Model language versions](/docs/model/model-language-versions/). A missing application
bookmark can instead mean **Not in this model**: open a collection declared by this workspace.
**Rename…** changes the displayed name, with the permanent key retained. A stale save asks you
to review newer state; it does not silently overwrite another administrator's edit.

## Permanent keys and changes made at the same time

A workspace key has at most 160 characters, using lowercase letters and digits separated by
single hyphens. Leading and trailing spaces are removed. Its key cannot be changed after
creation, and a retired workspace still reserves its key. Change **Name** to rename the dataset.

Retirement waits for a write already in progress to finish. Once retirement succeeds, later
live and change-set writes are refused. If two administrators change the default from the same
starting state, one succeeds and the other must refresh and review the new default.

Retiring also suspends active webhook subscriptions for this workspace. Reactivation makes the
workspace writable again but does not resume those subscriptions automatically. Ask their
administrator to review and resume them; undelivered events are kept only for their retention
period. See [Webhooks](/docs/administer/webhooks/) for delivery recovery.

---
title: Migrations
description: Review conversions, renamed definitions and removals before switching a workspace’s model.
reader: model-admin
---

Use a migration when a workspace's records do not fit a selected model release unchanged.
The preview checks every record and lists conversions, type changes, created items, removals and
items that must be fixed. Workspace data stays unchanged until you confirm. You need **Model release** in the workspace;
background jobs and model administration must be available. Publication also needs the normal
data permissions and any required approval.

Start from the editor when a draft changes stored data, or from
[Change a workspace’s model](/docs/guide/model/change-a-workspaces-model/) for an installed release.
Follow [Migrate a workspace](/docs/guide/model/migrate-a-workspace/) to review and confirm.

## From an editor step to a migration

The editor applies changes to released elements, including key changes, moves, splits, merges,
removals and tighter rules. **History** marks steps that affect stored data **Needs a migration**;
a released key change needs one even with no records. Undo takes that step's part out of the
proposed migration; redo restores it. Saving a draft does not convert live data.

In **Install and activate…** or **Apply to this workspace…**, **Activation needs a migration**
states what the draft proposes. Review the steps, where records go, counts of records moving,
records and relationships created, and refused items. Each released key change warns that
integrations naming it must change and names the consumer APIs of the base release that use it.

**Install … and preview the migration…** installs the release and opens the migration page.
From Apply, use **Preview what happens to the records…**. The release is installed but the
workspace keeps its current release until you confirm the migration.

**What the draft proposes** opens filled in from the draft's remaining steps and the two models.
Its rows show **Records of**, **Become**, **In**, **Under** and **Records**, with a **Proposed** mark
for the draft's choice. Split, list-conversion and relationship-key changes appear beneath the rows.
Change **Become** to review another destination type, or **Not kept**; each choice previews again
without editing the draft. Check the new outcome before continuing.

![Migration preview with a Proposed destination row and outcome counts](/docs/screens/model-migration-proposed.png)

*Above: the draft proposes moving 12 Stop code records from Network to the top level of Systems. The row is marked Proposed, and Type changed counts 12 records; nothing has changed yet.*

## What the preview means

| Outcome | What to review |
| --- | --- |
| Converted | Values changed to the target definition's value type. Inspect before and after. |
| Type changed | Records kept under a new type, with their IDs and history. |
| Created | Records and relationships a split or list conversion creates. Shown when the migration creates them. |
| Removed | Records, values or relationships lost if you explicitly accept removal. |
| Must be fixed | Items blocking confirmation, such as missing required values or relationships, duplicate unique values or invalid parents. |

For each missing type or field, **Became …** says which target definition replaces it.
**Not kept** removes that type's records and relationships, or that field's values. Choices are
not merely labels: each starts a new preview. The page explains what is kept and what is removed.
Do not accept removal until you have inspected its individual items. While any item
**Must be fixed**, confirmation stays disabled and the loss-acceptance checkbox is hidden.
After those blockers are resolved, a preview with removals offers the acceptance checkbox.

![Migration review with missing-element choices and outcome counts](/docs/screens/model-migration-review.png)

The data conversion and workspace release switch succeed together. A failed execution does not
leave half a migration. A model release installed before this flow can remain installed even
when migration fails. Record history keeps what was removed; that is an audit trail, not an undo button.
Open change sets stay on their previous release until moved or discarded. Publications remain fixed.

## Cancellation, waiting and stale results

**Cancel the preview** stops a running preview; **Cancel** leaves a reviewed one unapplied.
The preview may briefly make writes to the live records it checks wait. Let it finish or cancel
before retrying a waiting edit. Leaving the page alone does not stop its background job.

Confirmation is bound to the reviewed workspace and data versions. After an intervening edit,
publication or model change, a stale-review notice asks for **Preview again**. Nothing was
migrated by the refused confirmation. Review every refreshed outcome before confirming again.
**Not migrated** and **Something went wrong** require reading the failure and correcting its
cause; they are not successful migration results.

## Change sets on another release

A change set can move to **the release its workspace currently runs**. **Move this change set
to …** opens the same review for its content. The page says nothing live changes. Confirmation
converts its content and updates its base and release together against current live records.
Conflicting authored records, relationships or mapping sets block the move. Open the resulting
change set, review it and validate before publishing normally.

Alternatively, **Move … to … and publish…** migrates the workspace to the change set's release
and publishes that change set in one step. The review explicitly says **Then publishes …** and
the confirmation says **Migrate and publish**. Required approval and publication conflicts still
apply; neither migration nor publication succeeds alone. Review the named publication afterwards.

Jobs retain the actual counts and item outcomes, with refused items prominent. Open only links
your permissions allow and compare the actual result with the preview. For moving data between
two workspaces instead, see [Model mappings](/docs/model/model-mappings/).

Value conversion uses supported source and target value-type pairs. A value that has no valid
conversion is listed as a loss; the preview does not invent a conversion for every pair of types.
Inspect those items before accepting removal. Activation can also suspend the selected workspace's
consumer subscriptions that its new contract no longer serves; other workspaces' subscriptions
are unaffected. Coordinate changed contracts with their owners before confirming.

## What the migration carries

- A renamed type or a merged type keeps its records under the resulting type. Renamed attributes
  carry their values to the new definitions. A relation type's new key carries its relationships.
- A type moved to another application takes its records to the application named by the draft,
  including when several applications list the type. A type the target release still has never
  loses its records: with no named application they go to the one application that lists the type,
  or the one that lists it newly; when several qualify the preview refuses them under **Must be
  fixed** and a mapping's application chooses. Moving from containment to the top level
  removes the old parent and its containment relationship. Under different parent types, records
  whose existing parent is no longer allowed appear under **Must be fixed**.
- A split creates a related record of the new type for each source record holding at least one
  moved value. It carries the selected values there. With **Many to one**, source records with
  identical moved values share one new record. The first moved value supplies its name, falling
  back to the source record's name. A source record holding none of those values gets no new record.
- A list conversion creates one list record per distinct value, named by that value, and connects
  each source record to its list record. The values leave the source records.
- Moving an attribute attachment to a different type removes its values from the original type's
  records. The preview lists this as loss: the destination type has different records, so moving
  the definition cannot transfer those values to them.
- Tighter requirements, number limits, value types and bounds are checked against stored data.
  Records breaking the target rules appear under **Must be fixed**; values that cannot convert
  appear as loss. Removing definitions also lists the lost content for explicit acceptance.

**Example:** a stop-code type that stood under stops in Network can move to the top level of
Systems. Its records keep their identities and values in Systems and lose their old stop parents.
This is one configuration of the same move available to any model.

To return to an earlier release, select that release and review its compatibility or migration.
This does not automatically recover content removed by an earlier migration.

## A move proposed by the assistant

A [model change from words](/docs/model/ai-model-changes/) can prepare whole-type mappings
for this preview. You still inspect and confirm the migration yourself; no change set is
created for a whole-type move. For an AI-written account, ask in the activation or Apply
dialog before coming here: [Explain a model change](/docs/guide/model/explain-a-model-change/).
The migration page itself lists conversions, removals and refusals without an AI account.
guide/src/content/docs/model/model-chang:
---
title: Accounts of model changes
description: Understand the explanation of a proposed activation, its source facts and its limits.
reader: model-admin
---

Before activating a release or applying a workspace's draft, you can ask for a plain-language
account of what the change does. **What this change does** appears in the activation dialog and
in **Apply to this workspace** when an AI provider is available and you hold **Model release**
and **Use AI proposals** in that workspace. Follow
[Explain a model change](/docs/guide/model/explain-a-model-change/) to use it.

The account helps you read the change. It does not approve it, activate anything or remove a
blocking rule. Keep reading the data and consumer API checks alongside it.

## What is sent, charged and kept

Opening the dialog sends nothing to the AI provider. Only **Explain this change** asks it to
write an account. The request contains model changes and record counts, without record names
or values. The account is available at every configured send level. It needs the separate AI
provider; enabling the Claude Code assistant alone does not offer it.

A request can incur provider charges. refiroo records the call and its usage; request and answer
content is not kept in the call log unless the operator enables it. A successful account can
be reused for the same inputs within an hour without another provider call. It is a reading
aid, not part of the release or a permanent history entry. The provider's own retention is
separate. See [About AI in refiroo](/docs/run/ai/) for full access, costs and retention details.

## Facts first, wording second

refiroo supplies the facts that the provider puts into sentences:

- Differences between the model definitions.
- Rules the workspace's records would break, with counts.
- Changes that affect consumer APIs.
- Reasons activation is blocked, including a required migration or a consumer contract version change.
- Record counts for each affected type in the workspace.

The counts cover the whole relevant set of records. A release's differences are against the
workspace's running release. A draft's differences are against its base release; the data check
still uses the selected workspace. Check the workspace and baseline shown in the surrounding
dialog rather than assuming every comparison has the same starting point.

Each AI-written statement has numbers that lead to the facts it cites. **The facts** lists all
facts, initially showing ten; **Show the other …** reveals the rest. For a large change, the
provider receives at most 40 facts of each kind and the true totals. A **+** citation refers to
other facts of a kind. You still have the complete fact list in the dialog.

The note below the statements says the account was written by AI and can be wrong. A citation
shows the source; it does not prove the sentence interprets it correctly. Statements without
a valid source are removed, and the page reports how many were removed. If none remain, the
facts themselves are the account.

## Failure and limits

**The account could not be written** means the provider failed or returned an unusable answer.
The facts remain available because they do not depend on it. **Try again** makes another
attempt. A failure to request the account instead shows **The account could not be asked for**;
read its reason before retrying.

An invalid draft cannot be explained: fix its issues first. If a newer draft version exists,
reload and review it before asking again. A fresh compatibility check clears the old account.
Changed facts, including record counts, need a fresh request; failures and accounts with no
usable statements are not cached for reuse.

The browser account is in English. There is no follow-up conversation, and the account is not
shown in the install dialog or on the migration page. The [migration preview](/docs/model/migrations/)
lists its own conversions, removals and refusals; read those before confirming. An account saying
why activation is blocked is an explanation of the block, not permission to bypass it.
guide/src/content/docs/model/model-langu:
---
title: Model language versions
description: Understand unsupported model definitions and when to ask an operator for help.
reader: model-admin
---

A model language version says which definition format refiroo can read. It is separate from
the model's release version, the draft's editing version and each consumer API's contract version.
The current supported model language is **0.10**. The release and workspace screens show it as
**schema**. See [Releases](/docs/model/releases/) for selecting usable releases.

New drafts, including imported documents, accept only the current model language. The
recovery flow below applies to older releases already stored before an engine upgrade;
it is not a way to import an old document as a new draft.

Installation, activation and workspace creation refuse releases outside the supported window.
A historical release can still have readable metadata and an export even when semantic comparison
is unavailable. A workspace whose language cannot be served reports **Cannot be opened**;
this does not mean its records have been deleted.

Use the browser repair below where offered, or ask the operator to inspect the reported model
language and the version of refiroo running the instance. Older stored definitions have an offline procedure that first reports whether they
can be raised to the supported language. It leaves definitions that cannot be converted validly
or would duplicate another release and reports them. This is a deployment operation, not the
browser's **Raise contract version** action. See
[Model releases and rollback](/docs/run/model-releases-and-rollback/) for the operator's procedure.

A definition from a newer language needs a refiroo version that supports it. Changing its displayed
version or editing the language number alone does not convert it. If no workspace can be served,
or the configured startup model is outside the window, the operator must recover the deployment
before browser work can continue. Ordinary data [migrations](/docs/model/migrations/) and updating
the model document's language solve different problems.

## Reopen an older-language workspace in the browser

Where conversion is available, **Bring it up to date** offers **Review the change…** to someone
with instance-level model installation permission. Follow
[Raise a model language version](/docs/guide/model/raise-a-model-language-version/) to preview
and **Raise and reopen**. It lists every workspace using the release and leaves records, history,
change sets and publications unchanged. This recovery is a special in-place definition update;
ordinary model editing continues to create immutable releases. If the browser cannot offer the
repair, use the operator path above.
