---
title: How workbook proposals are made
description: Understand the patterns behind proposed types, lists, keys and relationships, and check their limits.
reader: model-admin
---

With **Model authoring**, use the evidence behind a workbook proposal to decide whether it describes
your data correctly. The rules look at column values, repetition, headings and shared identifiers. They do not know
what a stop, municipality or operator means. Choosing to propose from a workbook applies the
suggestions as draft steps; it does not install a model or load records.

Select a **Proposed** element, read **Proposed because**, then open **Evidence**. Use
[Map a column](/docs/guide/model/map-a-column/) to change its interpretation, or
[Propose again](/docs/guide/model/propose-again-with-a-newer-workbook/) to reconsider the file.
Your manual edits are retained. The percentages below are recognition rules, not confidence
scores, and cannot be tuned in the mapping form.

## Keys and names

The first suitable fully filled, distinct column is proposed as the key. Text without spaces
and whole numbers take precedence over a GUID. A GUID is the fallback when every row has a
different one. The proposed name is another text column filled on at least 95% of rows, excluding
code-like columns and lookups; a heading containing “name” takes precedence. If a text key would
leave no name beside a GUID, the GUID becomes the key and the text becomes the name.

Check that the proposed key stays stable between files. A different value on every row is not
proof that a column identifies the same real record next month.

## Lists, parents and connections

| Shape in the workbook | What refiroo proposes and what to check |
| --- | --- |
| A code and its name | A list with code and name, or the row's own identifying fields. The rule allows at most 1.5 names per code on average and expects each name to belong to one code in at least 98% of groups. |
| Different names for one code | A value map from less frequent names to the most frequent one. Check the correct spelling before accepting a majority choice. |
| A repeated text column | A parent when there are at most a third as many distinct values as rows and other columns stay constant in at least 98% of its groups. A constant code or GUID can identify the parent. |
| More than one repeated parent candidate | The first becomes the parent; further ones become related lists. A record has one parent. Empty parent cells allow records at the top level. |
| Numbered level headings, or references to the same sheet's keys | A hierarchy. A parent-code column needs at least 90% of its values to match the sheet's keys; empty parent codes identify roots. |
| A few repeated text values | A lookup list when there are at most 50 distinct values and no more than 20% as many values as filled cells. An ordinary text field remains an alternative. |
| Values matching another sheet | A relationship when at least 90% of distinct values match the other sheet's keys or names. One referenced record per row can still be shared by many rows. |
| Several values in one cell | A many-valued relationship when a delimiter occurs in at least 10% of cells and at least 80% of its parts also occur as whole values. Check the delimiter before splitting. |
| Several Yes/No columns | One relationship to a list whose members come from the headings. Recognised sets are Y/N, yes/no, X/empty, true/false and 1/0. The columns need not be adjacent. A nearby multi-valued column can join the set. A lone Yes/No column becomes a field with a value map. |
| A GUID column left over | An external identifier. Check which related record and system it describes rather than relying on its shape alone. |

Text averaging more than 60 characters is treated as description text, not a parent, lookup or
code's name. Remaining columns become typed attributes; a candidate key can make one unique.
Placeholder suggestions map values such as N/A, ?, TBC and a dash to empty. Read the affected
counts: an intentional value must not disappear because it resembles a placeholder.

Matching headers and value types across sheets can share an attribute definition. It is proposed
as unique only when the sheets do not share its values. Two or more lists proposed from a sheet
can be gathered into a navigation group. Generated labels come from headings and sheet names,
with underscores and joined capitals separated; you can rename them all. When table headings repeat,
the proposal leaves a later same-named column out and reports a warning. Review those columns
manually; the mapping and loading facilities can distinguish repeated headings by numbered names.

## Names in several languages

A sheet with no key can describe names for another sheet's records when it has at least two
ISO 639-1 language codes or English language names and at least 90% of the reference column's
distinct values match that sheet's keys, once per language. Columns such as Name (de) and Name FR
can also be recognised as language variants of a name column.

Repeated base values can reveal translated columns even without useful headings. The translation
must have 80%–125% as many distinct values as the base, at least 80% correspondence in each
direction, and at most half its rows identical to the base. A recognised language in the heading
names it; otherwise the proposal uses **Language 1**, **Language 2**, and so on. Rename these
before loading. A translation of a type's name becomes a related name record; translations of
other base fields remain attributes. Similar-looking columns alone do not establish their language.

## Sheets that describe fields

A workbook can describe a model rather than contain its records. refiroo checks this shape first,
then excludes the description and the referenced list sheets from ordinary table interpretation.
It looks for a filled, distinct text column naming fields, a column with at least 80% recognised
field-type words and a target column with at least half its cells naming other sheets. The
recognition uses values, rather than requiring particular headings. Automatic description detection
checks sheets with up to 1,000 data rows; type-word and target columns must each have at most
200 distinct values to be considered. Outside these bounds, map the file deliberately rather
than expecting this proposal.

| Field-type words | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| lookup, list, reference, select | Choose one record from the target list. |
| multi, multiple, multi-select, multi-lookup | Choose several records. |
| flag, yes/no, boolean, checkbox | A member of a target flag set; a Yes/No field without a target. |
| text, string | Text field. |
| long text, description | Long text field. |
| number, integer | Whole number field. |
| decimal | Decimal field. |
| date | Date field. |

An unrecognised word produces a text field and a warning. The described type takes the sheet's
name. Target sheets supply lists using their IDs and names. Placeholder IDs are skipped; a sheet
holding only placeholders produces a list to define, with no loaded records and a warning. A target
without a sheet produces an empty list too. Placeholder recognition here also includes “to be
defined”, “to be decided” and “to be confirmed”.

Review the resulting type and empty lists before installing. A description does not create
instances of the type it describes.

## Extend a model using another file

Files meet through the stored model and records. Install and load the first file before using
**Additions to the model** for a second file that refers to its records. Choose the comparison
workspace deliberately; without an explicit workspace the comparison uses the default workspace.

A sheet can match a type by its name, by at least 50% overlap between its keys and stored unique
values or names, or by headings matching at least half of the type's field and relationship names
(at least two). Name comparison ignores case, accents, punctuation and ordinary plural endings.
A same-named attribute is reused when at least 95% of cells fit its value type; a shared global
attribute is preferred to a new one. Existing allowed relationships are reused.

A code column matching at least half of a stored unique field's values takes precedence over name
matching. Missing IDs are reported with their rows; creating missing records is an alternative,
not an assumed repair. If an ID has a different name in the file, the stored name stands by default;
loading the new name is an alternative. Resolve drift explicitly before loading.

## Sheets laid out as lists

When a sheet has several blocks, a block with at least three columns and 60% of the sheet's
cells is treated as its main table. Other blocks are named in warnings. Without a main table,
a sheet laid out for reading can be interpreted list by list when no more than 2,000 rows hold
cells. This also covers several lists stacked in a block of at most two columns. Colour, bold
text and merged-cell formatting do not determine the structure.

Empty columns and rows separate ranges. A row above a range can be its header; a single cell
above several neighbouring lists can be their shared title. Text averaging over 60 characters
is treated as prose rather than list data. Inspect **Under**, **Cells** and **Note** to confirm
the inferred titles and boundaries. **Proposed**, **Loaded** and **Not loaded** distinguish
interpretations in the source pane; Loaded here means a source reads the list, not that its
records have already been published.

The first column supplies names and identifies list items. Within the range, a Yes/No column
becomes a field; several such columns form a flag set. A text column filled on at least 80%
of the rows with names can be proposed as translated names. A language word in its heading
names that language; otherwise you must rename the proposed language. Columns containing only
a heading are reported and not read; remaining columns become fields.

English note words such as “multiple answers”, “multiple choice”, “multi-select” or “several”
indicate several choices. “Single answer”, “single choice” and “one answer” indicate one.
“Free field” or “free text” identifies free answers rather than a list. A header with no values
or a free-answer range proposes no list and raises a warning. Recognised note rows are skipped,
and their note becomes the type's description. An extra heading row in a flag list can also be
recognised and skipped; it does not become a record.

Two or more lists beneath one innermost title can form a navigation group. At least three with
the same column kinds under one title, or none, also offer **Read these N lists as one list under
their headers**. The initial proposal keeps them separate because shape alone cannot tell
whether their headings are categories or independent lists.

Follow [Read lists in a sheet](/docs/guide/model/read-lists-in-a-sheet/) to adjust a range or
choose that alternative. Adjusting a range keeps column bindings by their column letters.
**Don't load this list** removes its source and can remove its proposed type when nothing else
loads, relates to or contains it. Review History and Issues after that choice. Always finish
with the [current dry run](/docs/guide/model/check-a-workbook-with-a-dry-run/).
guide/src/content/docs/run/ai.md:
---
title: About AI in refiroo
description: Choose which AI features to enable, control what leaves the instance, and understand access, costs and retention.
reader: operator
---

AI is optional. You choose which features to enable in the engine's environment, then restart it.
People review the proposals before using them. To enable it, follow [Set up AI](/docs/run/set-up-ai/).

## Choose what to switch on

Three settings control separate capabilities. None requires the other two.

| Setting | What it enables | When left unset |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AI_AGENT_COMMAND` | The built-in assistant: a Claude Code session that reads a workbook or instructions, works with the workspace's model and records, and prepares changes for review. | No built-in assistant is offered. |
| `AI_PROVIDER` | Requests for mapping targets, questions in words, and accounts of model changes or what changed over a period. | No provider features are offered. |
| `MCP_ENABLED=true` | Access for external assistants through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). | The MCP endpoint, metadata and registration are absent. |

The built-in assistant uses Claude Code's own credentials. Setting `AI_PROVIDER` does not configure
it. Conversely, you can run the assistant without a provider. With both AI settings empty, refiroo
sends no AI requests; separately enabled MCP access still lets an external assistant read what its
permissions allow.

The provider can be `claude`, `openai-compatible` for an endpoint using the chat-completions
protocol, or an operator-supplied factory named `package.module:function`. A locally hosted provider
is an option when reference data must stay within your organisation.

## Control what leaves the instance

`AI_SEND_LEVEL` sets the most data an AI feature may send. The default is `values`.
A feature that needs more than you allow is unavailable.

| Level | What may be sent |
| --- | --- |
| `structure` | Model keys, labels, headers and types, with the question or facts needed by the feature; no record values. Summaries can include counts. |
| `samples` | Also sample values, normally up to `AI_SAMPLE_VALUES` per column or attribute. The default is 20. |
| `values` | The values the feature needs. `AI_SAMPLE_VALUES` does not cap this level. |

A question in words is available at every level. At `samples` and `values`, it can also send all
record names for a relationship's type when its list in the current context has at most 50 records.
That list is not capped by `AI_SAMPLE_VALUES`. At `structure`, it sends none of those names.

The assistant requires `values`: it receives your words, the workspace's model and the whole workbook
if supplied, and can read workspace records as needed. Mapping targets also require `values`:
requests include the source and candidate target names and the fields displayed in the view.
Sources are sent in groups of 25; candidates are all eligible targets up to 100, or each source's
20 closest targets by name for larger sets.

An account of a model change sends the changes and record counts, without record values. An account
of what changed sends counts and model labels; names of records, people, change sets and files are
included only at `values`.

These settings govern refiroo's AI features. They do not impose a send policy on an external MCP
assistant after it reads permitted data. Check that assistant's settings and your organisation's
agreement with its provider too. Even `structure` sends information outside the instance when the
provider is external.

## Who can use it

The **Use AI proposals** action group allows a person to request AI help. The predefined **Data
steward**, **Data owner**, **Model administrator**, **Workspace administrator** and **Integration
administrator** roles include it. Grants determine where those rights apply.

Other permissions still matter: AI access alone does not grant permission to import, edit a model
or work in a change set. People without the action group are not offered AI actions. Operators need
**Operations** to inspect **Settings › This instance › AI** and send a provider test request.

External MCP assistants act within their person's or client's permissions, restricted to browsing
and work in change sets. They cannot approve, publish or write directly to live data. Security
administrators manage them on **Settings › Connections › Agent access**.

## The assistant's session

In the shipped engine container, sessions run as users from a pool, `assistant-1` to
`assistant-N`. Each turn takes a free user until it ends. An engine process runs one session at a time,
so sessions running at the same time use different users. They cannot read each other's process
environment. The image's `ASSISTANT_USERS` build argument sets the pool size, default 8; it must
cover the engine processes in the container (`WEB_CONCURRENCY`). If no user is free, the task
fails with a note naming `ASSISTANT_USERS`; rebuild with a larger pool before trying again.

Each task has a randomly named folder under `/opt/refiroo/rdm-engine/data/assistant`. Session
users can enter that parent folder but cannot list it to discover another task. Inside the task's
folder, `work` holds working files and `claude` holds its own Claude Code configuration and
transcripts. The engine sets `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` for each session. Turn logs are kept inside the
same task folder and are readable only by the engine.

Unix permissions separate the tasks. Between turns, only the engine can enter a task's folder.
For a turn, the engine opens it only to the session user running that turn, then closes it
again afterwards. At engine startup it also closes folders left open by stopped turns; a folder
held by another running turn stays open for that turn. Knowing a folder's name gives another
session no access.

Before each turn, while the task folder is closed, the engine runs
`/usr/local/bin/refiroo-session-reset` as the selected session user, never as root. The reset
repeatedly ends that user's processes until none remain, then empties its home and its files in
`/tmp`, `/var/tmp` and `/dev/shm`. Only a successful reset allows the task folder to open and the
turn to start. After the turn, the reset runs again while the folder is still open. It also makes
that user's files in `work` and `claude` readable and writable by the group, so another session
user can continue the task, and ends the user's processes once more. The engine then closes the
folder. A failed reset before a turn fails the turn; a failure afterwards is logged, and the next
turn under that user must pass its own reset.

Compose runs the engine with `init: true` to collect ended processes. If you run the image directly,
use `docker run --init`.

Each task has a separate client, workspace scope and jobs; concurrent tasks do not share them.
A task is visible only to its requester and the workspace's administrators. The session receives a dedicated refiroo client and temporary grants drawn from the requesting
person's permissions. It cannot publish a change set or activate a model release, even if that
person can. A person reviews the result and takes those steps. Grants end with the session's turn.

The engine does not pass its database address, encryption key or other server secrets to the
session. It passes only named variables: the temporary API token, `LANG`, `LC_*`,
`TMPDIR`, `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`,
`CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`, `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`, `ANTHROPIC_MODEL`,
`ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL`, `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL`,
`ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL` and `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS`. The switch
`CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK` is passed when set; only when it is on are `AWS_REGION`,
`AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, `AWS_SESSION_TOKEN` and `AWS_PROFILE`
passed too. Other variables, including `HTTPS_PROXY`, are not passed. The session user cannot
read the engine's job-file directory or its process environment.

**The provider's key or token still reaches the session.** Claude Code calls the provider itself.
A session steered by text in a workbook could use or send that credential. Use a dedicated
credential with a spending limit and no unrelated access.

With `AI_AGENT_SANDBOX=container`, Claude Code's own operating-system sandbox is off because it
cannot run there. The session runs with Claude Code's permission prompts off so it can execute
shell commands. The separate session user, which cannot read the engine's secrets or job files,
is its boundary inside the container. **The container does not restrict the session's network
access.** Apply any required outbound network restrictions in your deployment. Outside a container,
refiroo requires the operating-system sandbox; an unavailable sandbox refuses the session.

**Isolation between tasks inside one container rests on Unix permissions and the reset around
each turn.** This has been reviewed twice, with defects found and fixed each time; those reviews
are not proof of isolation. A separate container for each session is a stronger boundary and is
not built into refiroo. Together with the provider credential and unrestricted network access
above, this is a limit to consider before enabling the assistant.

A turn running longer than `AI_AGENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (30 minutes) is stopped like a person's Stop. The task returns to where it can be continued or tried again. Text in records is treated as data, but AI output can still be wrong; review
proposals before accepting them.

## Calls and costs

Open **Settings › This instance › AI** to see which switches are on, the send level and, when a
provider is configured, its model, endpoint, whether a key is set, and the features available.
The key itself is never shown. This page displays settings; change them in the environment.

**Calls** lists provider requests and assistant turns, newest first: who asked, what for, the model,
outcome, tokens, cost when reported, and duration. A failed call includes a failure message.
**Load more calls** reads older entries. With no entries, the page says **No call has been made yet.**
When content logging is on and has not expired, expand **Show what was sent and answered** on a row.
Treat that content as sensitive.

Totals cover the last 30 days. An assistant turn counts as one call, including cache reads and
writes in its token figures. A dash for cost means no cost was reported, not that the call was free.

Claude Code authentication and billing belong to Claude Code. An API key uses API billing; a
subscription token uses its Claude subscription. Provider requests use their separately configured
credentials. Check actual charges and usage limits with the provider; refiroo's call log is not a
billing statement.

**Send a test request** sends a fixed request containing none of your reference data. It tests the
provider, appears in the call log and may incur usage. It does not test the assistant.

## What is kept

| Information | Retention in refiroo |
| --- | --- |
| Call metadata, outcome, tokens and reported cost | Kept after request content expires. There is no configured expiry for the call records themselves; the 30-day totals are a reporting window. |
| A call's request and answer | Not kept in the call log by default. `AI_LOG_CONTENT=true` keeps them for `AI_LOG_CONTENT_DAYS`, default 7, after which content is cleared while the call record remains. For assistant turns this is the prompt and final answer, not the full stream. |
| Assistant task and workbook | `AI_TASK_RETENTION_DAYS`, default 90 days after completion or the last change. The worker's expiry sweep deletes the task and its files; cleanup needs a job-enabled instance. |
| Session folder, session logs and Claude Code transcript | Kept while the task can continue, including failed, stopped and loaded tasks. Once the change set is published or discarded, the migration confirmed, or the task discarded, the next task read removes them and deactivates its client. Expiry also triggers cleanup. |
| MCP tool-call records | `MCP_CALLS_DAYS`, default 90 days. Argument names are recorded, not their values. |

`AI_LOG_CONTENT=false` does not disable the assistant's working files or Claude Code transcripts.
Enable call-content logging only while needed: it can contain reference data. These settings do not
control the provider's own retention.

The shipped Compose file persists each task's working files, Claude Code configuration,
transcripts and turn logs in the `assistant` volume at `/opt/refiroo/rdm-engine/data/assistant`.
Container replacement keeps that volume. A backup may omit it: losing it loses open tasks'
folders and session logs, not records. Normal task cleanup still applies.

When upgrading from the earlier shared-transcript layout, the engine gives existing task folders
random names and keeps their workbooks and files. A task begun before the upgrade starts a new
Claude Code session on its next turn; the old shared transcripts are not moved. The obsolete
`assistant-claude` volume is no longer mounted. See [Upgrades](/docs/run/upgrades/#volumes-and-open-assistant-tasks)
before removing it.

## Provider and assistant settings

Set these in the engine's environment, then recreate the Compose container or restart the host
service. **Settings › This instance › AI** displays them; it does not edit them.

| Setting | Default | What to choose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AI_PROVIDER` | Empty | `claude`, `claude-code`, `openai-compatible`, or a factory `package.module:function`. Empty disables provider features, independently of the assistant. See [credential choices](/docs/run/set-up-ai/#choose-the-features-and-credentials). |
| `AI_MODEL` | Empty | Provider model. Claude defaults to `claude-opus-5-5`; a compatible endpoint requires a model. A factory defines its own default. This does not choose the assistant's model. |
| `AI_API_KEY` | Empty | Provider secret; required for `claude`, optional for compatible endpoints. Never displayed. |
| `AI_BASE_URL` | Empty | Required for a compatible endpoint, for example `http://models.internal:8080/v1`. Claude uses `https://api.anthropic.com` unless a gateway is specified. |
| `AI_SEND_LEVEL` | `values` | `structure`, `samples` or `values`; see the send policy above. A request can choose a lower level, never exceed this ceiling. |
| `AI_SAMPLE_VALUES` | `20` | Positive number of sample values per column or attribute at `samples`. Does not limit `values` or the short relationship lists described above. |
| `AI_MIN_CONFIDENCE` | `0.5` | Number from 0 to 1. Mapping proposals below this confidence are left unmapped. |
| `AI_LOG_CONTENT` | `false` | Keep requests and answers with call records for debugging. |
| `AI_LOG_CONTENT_DAYS` | `7` | Positive number of days to keep logged content; metadata remains. |
| `AI_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` | `60` | Positive number of seconds per provider call. The Claude API adapter makes up to three attempts for temporary failures, so total time can be longer. Does not change the assistant's 30-minute turn limit. |
| `AI_REASONING_EFFORT` | Empty | Compatible endpoints only: `none`, `low`, `medium`, `high`. Empty omits the option. For a local thinking model, `none` can avoid a long reasoning phase. |
| `AI_CONTEXT_TOKENS` | Empty | Actual context window of a small model, at least 256 tokens. Mapping requests are sized to half this window; too small a window can refuse even one source. Empty uses the feature's own batch limit. |
| `AI_TASK_RETENTION_DAYS` | `90` | Positive number of days to retain tasks after completion or last change; see retention above. |
| `AI_AGENT_COMMAND` | Empty | Claude Code command, for example `claude --model sonnet`. Empty disables the assistant. refiroo enforces its own tools and permission mode even if the command supplies another. |
| `AI_AGENT_SANDBOX` | Empty | `container` is set in both the shipped image and Compose; Compose overrides any .env value. Otherwise the operating-system sandbox is used. Do not use `container` on a host to bypass sandbox requirements. |
| `AI_AGENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` | `1800` | Longest one turn of the assistant's session may take; a turn over it is stopped like a person's Stop and the task goes back to its last point. |
| `AI_AGENT_API_URL` | `http://127.0.0.1:8000` in Compose; otherwise `PUBLIC_URL` | Address the session uses to reach this engine's API. Compose supplies the address inside the engine container unless overridden. Outside Compose, unset or empty uses `PUBLIC_URL`; override it if the engine's machine cannot reach that address. See [Set up AI](/docs/run/set-up-ai/). |

The Claude API needs outbound HTTPS to `api.anthropic.com`, or the configured gateway. Compatible
endpoints need JSON-schema answers. For Ollama, use its reachable `/v1` address and set
`AI_CONTEXT_TOKENS` to the window the server actually serves, rather than the model's advertised
maximum. `localhost` inside Docker means that container. Increase the provider timeout if the model
cannot answer within it; inspect failed calls before changing it.

## What people review

- **Mapping targets:** the person chooses **Propose targets**. Results are mappings in a change set,
  with confidence and a reason. The **Proposed** filter finds them. A person reviews and edits them,
  then uses the normal approval and publication flow. Editing a target removes its AI mark; history
  retains the origin of published proposals. Sources changed while the request ran are left alone.
  Stopping the job keeps proposals already written.
- **Questions in words:** **Ask** on a table list turns the question into editable filters. It
  changes no record. If only part can be expressed, nothing is applied until the person chooses
  **Use these filters**. It is absent from trees, mapping grids and the Changes page.
- **Model and history explanations:** **Explain this change** or **Explain this period** sends
  facts only when pressed. Counts cover the whole set; the provider receives at most 40 facts of
  each kind with the true totals. Statements link to the facts behind them. Unsupported statements
  are dropped. An empty history period makes no call. Matching facts are cached for an hour, so a
  repeated explanation can avoid another call. Current explanations are in English; they are not
  an assurance that a change is safe.
- **The built-in assistant:** the person reads the proposed model, the check of every workbook row,
  questions and warnings, and can edit the draft or tell the assistant what to change. **Accept the
  model** lets it install a release and load a change set. A person takes the activation, approval
  and publication steps. A saved import profile that still fits can load without an AI session or
  AI cost. Words alone can also prepare changes; a workbook is optional.

A whole type becoming another ends with **Preview the migration**: a person checks and confirms the
migration, which goes live at that confirmation. A partial move uses three steps: activate a release
with both types, review and publish the change set, then activate the final release to remove emptied
types. The proposal is checked against live records and consumer API contracts before this handoff.
An incompatible consumer contract needs its contract version raised; a proposal the data cannot
accept returns with the reason for correction. The assistant does not confirm these steps itself.
If the final model keeps the old type, only activation and publication are needed; no removal step
is shown. Unused session-installed releases are retired when the task ends; a final release needed after a
partial move survives. Do not prune releases in use by workspaces or change sets.

## Recover an assistant task

A task's page gives its reason and the next action. **Stop** ends the current turn, preserving the
task so the person can continue. A stopped correction returns to the last proposal, with a warning
if the draft was already changed. A stopped load discards the change set it was making and returns
to the accepted proposal. With no proposal yet, the task is stopped and takes words or discard.

After a failure or stop, give corrected instructions or choose **Try again as it was**. The same
session continues, or starts if it never ran. If the worker died during a turn, the next turn records
that earlier call as `interrupted` from the session log. Look for **Failed** and the failure sentence
in **Calls**, not only at the latest successful turn. In the container, turn logs sit inside the task folder beside `work` and `claude`; on a host they sit beside the task folder.

On a loaded task, **Discard and load again** discards the unpublished change set, including manual
edits, and asks the assistant to reload with the new words. **Discard this task** ends the task;
if it has an unpublished change set that set is discarded too. A published task cannot be corrected
this way: start a new task. A missing or expired task leads back to workspaces. A saved layout's
check offers **Back to the proposal**; if it no longer fits, **Read it with the assistant** starts a
session. A refused migration leaves the reason and the words box on the task.

## External agent access

`MCP_ENABLED` enables MCP Streamable HTTP, protocol `2025-11-25`, at `/mcp`. The shipped web proxy
passes `/mcp` and `/.well-known/`; forward both when supplying your own proxy, and keep `PUBLIC_URL`
consistent with the public HTTPS address. With the switch off the endpoints return 404 and no agent
token is issued. **Settings › Connections › Agent access** then says **Agent access is off**.

| Setting | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MCP_ENABLED` | `false` | Expose agent access after restart. Independent of both AI switches. |
| `MCP_RATE_PER_MINUTE` | `120` | Positive number of calls per person or client per minute, shared across processes. A refused excess call says how long to wait and is recorded as **Limit reached**. |
| `MCP_OPEN_REGISTRATION` | `true` | Allow assistants to register themselves. Turn off to require registration by a security administrator. |
| `MCP_REDIRECT_HOSTS` | Empty | Comma-separated HTTPS hosts a self-registered assistant may return to, besides loopback addresses. The assistant's displayed name is its own claim. |
| `MCP_CALLS_DAYS` | `90` | Positive number of days to keep tool-call records. Names of arguments are kept, never their values. |
| `MCP_ANSWER_BYTES` | `40000` | Positive maximum bytes for a tool answer. Large pages shrink and return a cursor; an oversized answer that cannot page is refused. Resources return whole. |

A person's assistant opens this instance's own sign-in page with OAuth and PKCE; signing in is
consent. A system's assistant uses an agent client and its grants, with an `agent` token. These
tokens reach only MCP; management and consumer tokens cannot call MCP. A consumer-only grant exposes
only that consumer API's lookup tool. Browse exposes model, record, mapping coverage, history and
change reads. Work in change sets permits adding or editing records and relationships, setting
values, checking and submitting the caller's own change sets. It cannot remove records or clear
values, discard or withdraw change sets, batch, restructure the model, approve or publish. Submitted
change sets stay frozen. Under a second-person rule the person who asked the assistant cannot also
decide its submission.

Security administrators manage clients, registrations and call records on **Agent access**. Blocking
an assistant or deactivating its client stops access on the next call. Restoring a blocked assistant
does not restore ended sessions. People can end their own assistant sessions in their session list.
Unused self-registrations with no open session are removed after 30 days; at most 1,000 unused
registrations can stand. A registration accepts at most 10 return addresses, each at most 2,000
characters. Repeated registrations from one address are slowed; self-registered return hosts are
checked again at sign-in. Tool and resource listings count against the rate limit too. Neither your provider send level nor provider content retention controls
what an external assistant keeps after reading permitted data.

## Read failures and restore service

| Code or outcome | Meaning and action |
| --- | --- |
| `AI_NOT_CONFIGURED` | The feature's own switch is missing: assistant command for tasks, provider for tests and suggestions. No provider means no test call is recorded. Configure the required switch and apply settings. |
| `AI_SEND_LEVEL_TOO_LOW` | The feature needs more data, or the request exceeds the instance ceiling. Agree a send policy before changing it. |
| `FORBIDDEN` | Check the missing action group and workspace grants. AI permission alone grants no other write rights. |
| `AI_TASK_NOT_FOUND` | The task expired, does not exist or belongs to someone else. Ask its requester or a workspace administrator; start a new task if expired. |
| `AI_TASK_VERSION_CONFLICT` | Another action changed the task. Reload it before trying again. |
| `AI_TASK_CHECK_STALE` | The draft changed after the check. Check it again before loading. |
| `AI_TASK_NOTHING_TO_LOAD` | The check has no work to load. Review the proposal and its counts. |
| `AI_TASK_STATE` | That action is unavailable at this stage. Reload and use the page's offered next action. |
| `AI_TASK_DRAFT_HELD` | Another task owns the draft; use a separate draft rather than changing that task's work. |
| `AI_TASK_NEEDS_WORDS` | Supply instructions or a supported workbook. |
| `IMPORT_TOO_LARGE`, `UNSUPPORTED_FILE_FORMAT` | Respect `IMPORT_MAX_BYTES`; supply XLSX or CSV instead of legacy XLS. |
| `unreachable`, `unauthorized`, `rateLimited` | Check endpoint/connectivity, replace the refused key, or wait before retrying, respectively. |
| `declined`, `malformed`, `failed` | The provider declined, returned the wrong shape or otherwise failed. Inspect the failure sentence, model and gateway. No partial malformed answer is used. |
| `timeout`, `cancelled`, `interrupted` | An assistant turn exceeded the session limit (`AI_AGENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`), was stopped or lost its worker. Read the task's notes and continue when the cause is resolved. |

A failing provider leaves the feature's ordinary work available. Explanations still show their
facts; a failed question applies no filters; a mapping request reports a warning and a failed
call. **Neither the assistant nor an AI provider is set up** is the AI page's notice when both are
unset. For command, credential, sandbox and startup failures, follow [Set up AI](/docs/run/set-up-ai/#if-startup-or-a-request-fails).

![AI settings showing the assistant and provider on and the permitted send level](/docs/screens/run-ai-settings.png)

![AI provider test result and recorded calls](/docs/screens/run-ai-provider-calls.png)


## Switch off a feature or change its credentials

Use each feature's own switch. Empty `AI_PROVIDER` removes provider features; empty
`AI_AGENT_COMMAND` removes the built-in assistant; `MCP_ENABLED=false` removes external agent
access. Apply the change by [recreating the engine](/docs/run/configure/#apply-a-change) on every
instance that serves the feature. Turning off one switch leaves the other two independent.

Before a planned assistant shutdown, ask requesters to stop running turns and review outstanding
loads. Removing a command is not a way to undo an accepted proposal or published data. Stored call
records, tasks, drafts and files are not erased by these switches; their normal lifetimes still
apply. Keep job workers enabled where expiry cleanup is needed. For external agents, use the
[registration and session controls](/docs/administer/agent-access/) when access must be revoked,
rather than assuming an endpoint switch deletes identities or stored grants.

To replace a provider credential, change `AI_API_KEY` in the private environment, recreate the
engine and send the fixed provider test. To replace the assistant credential, update its
`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` or `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`, recreate, then test an actual assistant turn.
These are separate checks. Revoke the previous credential at its issuer after checking the new
one, or immediately when responding to a leak. refiroo does not renew external credentials for you.
Changing the sealing key does not rotate a provider's API key.

A provider/model change affects later requests; it does not rewrite existing proposals or call
records. Keep the previous private configuration for a reversible setting change, apply it again
if needed, and repeat the relevant feature test. The provider's credential expiry and billing
limits are determined by that provider; inspect a refused call and its issuer's controls.
guide/src/content/docs/run/background-jo:
---
title: Background jobs
description: Operate workers, retained files, imports, exports and model-authoring jobs.
reader: operator
---

Background workers run inside each engine process. `INTEGRATION_JOBS_ENABLED=true`, the default,
enables creating and running jobs. Turning it off keeps job reads available but stops workers and
job mutations. Work also needs a healthy model. Check **Settings › This instance › Jobs** for job
state and outcomes, and **Operations** for worker health. Permissions determine which jobs a person
may inspect or cancel; see [Jobs](/docs/use/jobs/).

## Inspect results before retrying

A job may be queued, running, awaiting confirmation, completed, failed, cancelled or expired.
A completed job can still contain rejected rows. Read its applied, unchanged, rejected and
unprocessed counts, and open individual outcomes for the refusal code and reason.

The request's failure policy matters. An `atomic` batch applies all its items in one transaction
or none if an item is refused; an `independent` batch keeps successful items and reports refused
ones separately. Cancellation of independent work retains committed chunks. Do not promise an
all-or-nothing result merely because the work was submitted as one job.

Correct refused rows before retrying. For imports, preview the corrected file again: already-loaded
rows can be reported as unchanged. For a batch, submit the corrected items with current versions;
blindly sending every create again can return duplicate-ID refusals. An expired preview needs a
new preview, even if an old browser page still shows it waiting.

For an integration, the sequence is submit a batch or import, follow the returned job, inspect its
outcomes, then confirm a preview or correct its refusals. See the [batch, import and job operations
in the API reference](/docs/api). The requester needs write permissions in the chosen workspace
and any required change-set claim; jobs recheck the requester's rights as they run. Losing access,
retiring the workspace, or changing its selected release can stop remaining work.

If creation or cancellation routes are missing, check `INTEGRATION_JOBS_ENABLED` on Deployment.
With it off those routes are absent, not merely paused buttons. Existing job reads still work.
Enable it on the intended deployment and recreate the engine before retrying; enabling it grants
no additional permissions. Monitor the worker before submitting the same work again.

## Restart and cancellation

A graceful stop finishes the running chunk and releases the lease. After a crash, that chunk rolls
back. Another worker resumes at the first item without an outcome after the lease expires;
completed items are not applied twice. `JOB_LEASE_SECONDS` defaults to 120 and is renewed by a
heartbeat every third of that interval. A queued job may be waiting behind another batch or import.

Cancellation takes effect at the next chunk boundary. An atomic job rolls back completely.
An import that is still reading checks cancellation every 10,000 rows. Exports also check every
10,000 rows, with CSV checks between records and relationships. A database outage is retried every
two seconds and does not need a process restart when connectivity returns.

`JOB_CHUNK_ITEMS` defaults to 500; larger chunks keep a workspace's write lock longer.
`JOB_RETENTION_DAYS` defaults to 7 for finished outcomes and idempotency keys. Expiry runs hourly.
Check the [limits catalogue](/docs/run/configure/) before raising item counts or file sizes.

## Keep and back up the file directory

`JOB_FILE_DIR` defaults to `var/job-files` under the backend; the Compose image uses the persisted
`/opt/refiroo/rdm-engine/data/job-files` volume. Startup creates it and refuses an unwritable directory when job creation
is enabled. Share it across instances. Do not remove files manually to free space: extend storage
or adjust retention and let cleanup enforce the lifecycle.

| Work | File lifetime and recovery |
| --- | --- |
| Export | Writes a `{jobId}.{lease}.partial` belonging to that worker, then renames to JSON Lines, CSV or XLSX on completion. Output remains until job expiry; failed/cancelled and orphan files are cleaned at startup or the hourly sweep. `410 JOB_OUTPUT_MISSING` means rerun the export. |
| Import | Upload is `{jobId}.source`, retained while waiting or running, including preview confirmation. Removed on finish. `IMPORT_FILE_MISSING` means upload again. |
| Model draft or import-profile source | `{sourceFileId}.upload` remains with its draft/profile. Superseded files remain for `JOB_RETENTION_DAYS`; orphan cleanup waits at least ten minutes. `SOURCE_FILE_MISSING` means upload again. |

Back up source files with the database. Disk sizing is **not measured** for your workload: allow
for concurrent uploads, retained exports and current plus superseded source workbooks.

## Exports and previews

Exports have their own worker, so they do not wait behind imports or batches. Exports run one at
a time per worker. Each reads one repeatable-read snapshot; it does not block writes, but a long
export keeps PostgreSQL from reclaiming rows changed since that snapshot. A crashed export restarts
from the beginning after its lease, rather than appending to its old file. Each lease has its own partial file, so an old worker that
resumes after takeover cannot overwrite the current worker's partial output.

Imports read XLSX cached values, CSV and JSON Lines; legacy `.xls` must be converted to XLSX.
An import binds its file in one transaction, then applies items in chunks. A crash before binding
commits causes binding to start again.

A preview applies up to `JOB_PREVIEW_MAX_ITEMS` (default 10,000) in a transaction that rolls back.
Beyond that it is a sample. It holds the workspace's write lock or change-set claim during the
preview, then holds neither lock nor lease while waiting for confirmation. Its file remains until
confirmation, cancellation or expiry, normally seven days after preview completion. Confirmation
binds the file again against current data.

Profiling and model dry runs share the batch worker. Profiling stages filled workbook cells in the
database. A dry run previews every row in one rolled-back transaction and can delay writes for its
whole duration; the preview sample limit does not bound that work. A newer dry run cancels a running
one for the same draft. Keep the proxy's job event stream unbuffered; it sends keep-alive comments
every 15 seconds.

Source-workbook uploads also obey `IMPORT_MAX_BYTES`. Profiling copies every filled cell into the
database, so file-volume space alone does not cover this storage. For sizing, a
10,000-row, two-sheet workbook can produce about 330,000 staged cells, depending on its width. These rows are removed with
the source file. Size your database for the actual workbook widths as well as their row counts.

For spreadsheet safety, XLSX exports write text as text. CSV preserves strings beginning with
`=`, `+`, `-` or `@`; spreadsheet software may interpret them as formulas when opening the file.

With HTTP/1.1, a browser's roughly six connections per site can make additional job streams wait.
Use HTTP/2 at the public entry for many simultaneous streams; this is separate from whether the
workers themselves are progressing.

## Check worker storage and restart one reference instance

You need Docker access, Operations access, a workspace with a servable model and permission to
inspect the affected job. First inspect Deployment's `INTEGRATION_JOBS_ENABLED` and Operations'
worker state. In the reference image the engine user is UID 10001 and the persistent directory is
`/opt/refiroo/rdm-engine/data/job-files`. Confirm that existing storage is mounted and writable:

```bash
docker compose exec -T engine python -c \
  'import os; from pathlib import Path; p=Path("/opt/refiroo/rdm-engine/data/job-files"); print("exists:",p.is_dir(),"writable:",os.access(p,os.W_OK))'
docker compose exec -T engine df -h /opt/refiroo/rdm-engine/data/job-files
docker compose logs --tail=100 engine
```

Expect `exists: True writable: True` and enough free space for queued inputs and retained outputs.
The access check does not reserve space or prove a future write can succeed; startup also performs
an actual write/delete probe. For `JOB_FILE_DIR` followed by `cannot be created or written`, fix
the mount, disk space and user permissions, then recreate the engine if configuration changed.
Do not make the whole directory world-writable or delete source workbooks to silence that refusal.

Before an ordinary restart, record the job ID and its current applied/rejected counts. Run:

```bash
docker compose restart engine
curl -i https://refiroo.example.org/health
```

Check that readiness returns 200 and the worker is Running on Operations. Follow the **same** job,
not a duplicate submission. If a process was forcibly terminated rather than stopped cleanly,
allow the default 120-second lease to expire before expecting takeover. A changed `.env` requires
`docker compose up -d engine`, not just restart. Reopen the job to check its actual outcomes after
recovery; a completed job can still have refusals.

## Missing files and cancellation recovery

| Code | What remains and what to do |
| --- | --- |
| `JOB_OUTPUT_MISSING` | The completed job exists but its output file does not. Run another export; the old job cannot recreate its download merely by being reopened. |
| `IMPORT_FILE_MISSING` | The import cannot read its retained input. Re-upload through the import workflow and inspect already committed outcomes before confirming another load. |
| `SOURCE_FILE_MISSING` | A draft/profile's source file is absent. Upload the intended workbook again; a database row alone does not contain its original bytes. |

Use the [Jobs workflow](/docs/use/jobs/) for permission-aware cancellation. A cancel request is not
an immediate kill of the SQL statement in progress. Confirm the job reaches its terminal state
before deciding what needs correcting. Atomic work rolls back; independent work keeps earlier
committed chunks and has no automatic undo. Review corrective changes through the normal
record/change-set workflow. For a load that must be wholly undone outside those changes, use a
planned whole-instance restore and account for unrelated writes since the backup.

Do not extend retention to repair missing files. Changing `JOB_RETENTION_DAYS` helps preserve
future retained results; it cannot reconstruct content already deleted. An export's long snapshot
can delay PostgreSQL cleanup without blocking writers: if disk use rises while large exports run,
inspect those jobs and database activity before assuming a workspace lock is stuck.

## Change retention or move the file directory

`JOB_RETENTION_DAYS` sets the expiry recorded when a job finishes or a preview begins waiting.
Changing it does not reset the stored expiry of jobs already finished or awaiting confirmation.
It also cannot restore expired outcomes, removed input files or old idempotency keys. Before
lowering retention, agree the download and preview-confirmation window with users and integrators.
Source workbooks still attached to a draft/profile have their own lifetime, as listed above.

Only the batch worker performs the job/file expiry sweep. With `INTEGRATION_JOBS_ENABLED=false`,
that instance runs no job cleanup; another job-enabled instance sharing the database and files
can do it. Disabling jobs is not a disk-cleanup action. Expiry retains the job's summary but removes
its item outcomes, inputs and idempotency keys. A later request with an expired key is new work,
so the integration must not rely on that key forever to prevent duplicates.

To relocate storage, stop every engine that uses the directory, take the
[consistent database and file backup](/docs/run/backup-and-restore/), then copy the whole directory
with its ownership and permissions preserved. Mount the replacement at the configured container
path on every instance before starting any worker. In the reference image, changing
`JOB_FILE_DIR` alone does not move the Compose volume: its mount is fixed at
`/opt/refiroo/rdm-engine/data/job-files`. Adapt the mount too or keep that container path and move
the storage underneath it.

Start with the matching database and check writability, readiness and an existing source/download
file as well as a new export. Preserve the previous copy until these checks pass. If the storage
change fails, keep all workers stopped while restoring the previous mount and path; do not let
different instances process the same jobs against different file copies. Assistant folders and
session files require their separate mounts too, as [What you run](/docs/run/overview/#network-and-storage)
explains. No running instance automatically copies files to a new directory.

## Consumer-event derivation

The `eventDeriver` thread reads each workspace's change feed for consumer APIs whose model declares
events. It runs while a model is healthy, needs no separate setting and takes no workspace write
lock. Disabling webhook delivery does not stop this derivation. It looks for changes once a second.

Several processes share the work, deriving one workspace at a time. A crash rolls back the page in
progress and derives it again without losing or duplicating events. Database outages use the same
two-second retry and bounded outage logging as other workers. Hourly cleanup follows
`FEED_RETENTION_DAYS` and the change-feed floor.

If a receiver seems behind, compare the consumer events response's `headPosition` with the
workspace feed head. The first is how far events have been derived; the second is how far writes
have reached. A gap here is derivation lag rather than a receiver failure. Check `eventDeriver` on
Operations before resetting a subscription. See [Consumer events and webhooks](/docs/integrate/consumer-events-and-webhooks/)
and the [API reference](/docs/api) for the reads used by the integration.

## Assistant and mapping-proposal jobs

The built-in assistant uses a separate worker for its tasks; mapping proposals run as background
jobs too. The assistant needs `AI_AGENT_COMMAND`, `AI_SEND_LEVEL=values`, enabled job creation and
the requester's workspace permissions. A provider alone does not enable assistant tasks. See
[Set up AI](/docs/run/set-up-ai/) before enabling these jobs: workbook and record data can leave the
instance and each turn can consume paid usage.

For an assistant task or mapping job, the job page shows its summary and links to the task or view
when the reader may open it. Inspect the task's notes and check as well as the job's outcome. A turn
has a 30-minute limit, separate from the provider timeout. After a worker interruption, the next
turn records the earlier turn as interrupted. **Stop** during an assistant load discards the change
set being loaded and returns to the accepted proposal; stopping a mapping-proposal job keeps
proposals already written. Neither publishes to live data.

Tasks use `AI_TASK_RETENTION_DAYS` (90 by default), separately from ordinary job retention. Session
folders, logs and transcripts stay while a task can continue; the next read after publication,
discard or confirmed migration removes them, and expiry also cleans them. In the shipped image,
each task has a randomly named folder under `/opt/refiroo/rdm-engine/data/assistant`, with
working files in `work`, Claude Code configuration and transcripts in `claude`, and turn logs
inside the same task folder. Session users cannot list the parent folder to find other tasks.
Compose persists this in the single `assistant` volume across container replacement, until normal
cleanup. Backups may omit it; losing it loses open tasks’ folders and session logs, not records.
After upgrading from the earlier shared-transcript layout, existing files are kept but the next
turn starts a new session. See [Upgrades](/docs/run/upgrades/#volumes-and-open-assistant-tasks).
**Calls** on **Settings › This instance › AI** keeps turn outcomes and usage separately. See
[AI retention and recovery](/docs/run/ai/#what-is-kept) before maintenance or a retry.

![Jobs with queued, running and completed work](/docs/screens/run-jobs.png)
guide/src/content/docs/run/backup-and-re:
---
title: Back up and restore
description: Protect the database and source files, rehearse recovery, and restore a consistent installation.
reader: operator
---

Back up PostgreSQL, the job-file volume and the configuration needed to read them. The database holds
all workspaces, records, history, change sets, publications, installed models, jobs, subscriptions and
feeds. Model-authoring source files live in `JOB_FILE_DIR`, outside PostgreSQL. Protect backups as
sensitive data, with encryption keys stored securely outside the database.

Keep the application version, `DATABASE_URL`, `RDM_MODEL_PATH`, capability settings, worker count,
`RDM_CURSOR_SIGNING_KEY` and `SECRETS_ENCRYPTION_KEY` with each recovery record. Losing the sealing
key makes stored secrets unreadable. Backups made before a key change need the old key.

The Compose installation also has an `assistant` volume at
`/opt/refiroo/rdm-engine/data/assistant`. Each randomly named task folder holds its working files,
Claude Code configuration, transcripts and turn logs. A backup may omit this volume: losing it
loses open tasks’ folders and session logs, not records. The database and job-file backup below
does not copy it; after restoring without it, open tasks may lack the files they need to continue.

## Take a database backup

From the repository root of the reference installation:

```bash
docker compose exec -T database pg_dump -U rdm -d rdm -Fc \
  --exclude-table-data=engine_processes > refiroo-backup.dump
```

Check the command's exit status and retain only a successful dump as a backup. Use unique names
for successive backups. Omitting process heartbeat rows avoids showing old processes as silent
after a restore; dumps containing them still restore.
Arrange a consistent copy or snapshot of `job-files` alongside it, quiescing file-changing work
while taking that pair. Do not treat a database dump alone as a backup of source workbooks.

## Rehearse in a separate database

Use PostgreSQL client tools and an administrative account allowed to create and drop a scratch
database. The engine's runtime role should not need that privilege. The following is for a configured
backend environment with network access to the same database server; substitute its connection
options and your dump name. These host commands do not read Compose's `.env` automatically.
Set the live instance's `DATABASE_URL` and original key securely before running the check.

```bash
createdb -T template0 --locale-provider=icu --icu-locale=und --locale=C rdm_restore_check
pg_restore --no-owner --exit-on-error -d rdm_restore_check refiroo-backup.dump
cd backend
.venv/bin/python -m app.cli.restore_check \
  --restored postgresql+psycopg://rdm@db/rdm_restore_check \
  --backup refiroo-backup.dump
```

Use a restored URL that actually reaches that scratch database. Supply passwords securely, never
as literal secrets in shell history. Stop if restoration fails. The check must target the copy,
while `DATABASE_URL` continues naming the live instance where its result is recorded.
It refuses the live database as the restored target.

The check prepares and may migrate the copy, clears old process rows, and tries each active
workspace's model. It compares workspace counts with the live instance. It does not validate every
record again or require counts to match a live instance that has changed since the backup.

| Exit | Meaning and action |
| --- | --- |
| `0` | Copy prepared and every active workspace served. Record the result and remove the scratch database. |
| `1` | Check failed. Follow its collation, extension, revision, migration, connectivity or workspace reason; preserve needed diagnostics before removing the copy. |
| `2` | Nothing checked: wrong target, non-PostgreSQL URL or unreachable live instance. Correct the configuration and repeat. |

After inspection, remove only the scratch database, using the same server connection options:

```bash
dropdb rdm_restore_check
```

Open **Settings › This instance › Operations › Last backup rehearsal**. Before the first check,
**No backup has been rehearsed** means no result has been recorded. After a check it shows **Passed**
or **Failed**, the backup name when supplied, the copy's revision and the workspace results.
**Records**, **Relationships**, **Open change sets** and **Publications** count the restored copy;
**Live now** compares the current instance. Different counts alone do not fail the check.
The same results are readable as JSON through the [backup rehearsal operation](/docs/run/monitoring/#backup-rehearsals), with its [API reference](/docs/api/?api=management#tag/system).

Use **Show earlier rehearsals (N)** to expand older results, **Load more rehearsals** when offered,
and **Hide earlier rehearsals** to collapse them. **How to rehearse a restore** gives the command
sequence; it does not execute it. Nothing on Operations runs a restore.

| Failure code | Safe next step |
| --- | --- |
| `DATABASE_COLLATION` | Recreate the scratch database with ICU root `und`, restore and check again. |
| `DATABASE_EXTENSIONS` | Install the required extensions in the copy or allow the preparation role to do so. |
| `DATABASE_REVISION_UNKNOWN` | Use the engine version that understands the backup's revision. |
| `DATABASE_MIGRATION_FAILED` | Preserve the diagnostic, resolve the reported migration cause, then repeat on a fresh copy. |
| `DATABASE_UNREACHABLE` | Correct the copy's server address, credentials or network access. |
| `DATABASE_URL_INVALID` | Correct the restored database URL before retrying. |
| `WORKSPACES_NOT_SERVED` | Inspect each failed workspace's release. Use a compatible engine or resolve its model before relying on that backup for recovery. |

Keep the failure result as evidence and repeat the rehearsal after correcting its cause. For local development, `scripts/postgres.sh backup` and
`scripts/postgres.sh rehearse` automate the private server's backup, restore check and scratch cleanup.

![Operations before the first backup rehearsal, showing No backup has been rehearsed](/docs/screens/run-backup-rehearsal.png)

## Recover the installation

1. Stop every engine process and prevent traffic and integrations from writing.
2. Create a replacement database with ICU root `und`, or empty the recovery target deliberately.
   Restore the dump there with `pg_restore --no-owner` using PostgreSQL client tools.
3. Restore the matching source-file volume and configuration, including the backup's encryption key.
   Point `DATABASE_URL` to the recovery database; do not change a database password merely by editing `.env`.
4. Start the application version kept with the backup, or a compatible newer one that migrates it.
5. Check readiness, every active workspace, sign-in and needed files before reopening traffic.

For a host or custom installation, `DATABASE_URL` selects the recovery database. In the reference
Compose file it is constructed from the database service and `POSTGRES_PASSWORD`: a
`DATABASE_URL` line in `.env` does not override it. Recover the service's `rdm` database and its
matching volumes, or explicitly adapt your deployment configuration to the replacement database
before starting engines. Preserve the old volume until the recovery has been checked.

A restore replaces the whole database. Activating an older model, withdrawing a publication or
starting a change set from an earlier publication does not restore data. For partial recovery, read
the desired records from a restored copy and write reviewed changes through the API or a change set.
Recovery time and production backup sizing for your installation are **not measured**; rehearse your
own data and record the result.

## Make a consistent database and file backup with Compose

For the reference installation, you need Docker access, free space outside the named volumes and
a maintenance window. The database image supplies PostgreSQL 17 client tools; the engine image
supplies Python for archiving its mounted job files. The commands below use the standard Compose
file and a new host directory. Choose a unique directory for every backup. Keep traffic and all
external writers closed until the engine is started again.

1. Create a private backup directory and stop all file-changing engine work. The database stays up:

   ```bash
   umask 077
   mkdir -p backups/before-maintenance
   docker compose stop engine
   ```

   In a multi-instance installation, stop every engine using this database and file directory.
   Verify the stop completed. Background work stops too; an interrupted chunk is rolled back or
   recovered under its lease. No browser or integration should write directly to the database.
2. Dump the database, then archive the unchanged file volume:

   ```bash
   docker compose exec -T database pg_dump -U rdm -d rdm -Fc    \
     --exclude-table-data=engine_processes      > backups/before-maintenance/database.dump
   docker compose run --rm --no-deps -T engine python -c    \
     'import sys,tarfile; t=tarfile.open(fileobj=sys.stdout.buffer,mode="w|"); t.add("/opt/refiroo/rdm-engine/data/job-files",arcname="."); t.close()'      > backups/before-maintenance/job-files.tar
   ```

   Both commands are silent on success and must exit 0. Check each status before proceeding.
   Redirection can leave a partial file after failure; do not label that file a successful backup.
   A database dump and file archive made while every engine is stopped represent one unchanged
   application state. No running file cleanup can remove inputs between the two copies.
3. Keep the matching private environment securely, and write the source/application version into
   your recovery record. For the default settings file:

   ```bash
   cp .env backups/before-maintenance/installation.env
   chmod 600 backups/before-maintenance/installation.env
   tar -tf backups/before-maintenance/job-files.tar
   ```

   Expect relative file paths, or only `.` for an empty job directory. Put encryption keys in
   separately controlled storage, outside the database backup, and associate their version with
   this recovery record. Preserve any custom bootstrap files and valid TLS materials too. With
   automatic HTTPS, preserve the `caddy-data` volume using your storage platform's backup process.
4. Resume normal operation with `docker compose up -d engine`, check readiness and sign-in, then
   reopen writers. Copy the backup off the application host into your protected backup storage.
   Rehearse before relying on it. Backup schedule, disk minimums, offsite retention and recovery
   duration are **not measured** for your organisation.

## Rehearse the reference dump inside Compose

These commands create only `rdm_restore_check`. Confirm that name is unused before starting;
do not substitute `rdm`, the live database. The reference PostgreSQL account initializes the server
and can create the scratch database; a custom runtime role should not be given that privilege
merely for this task.

```bash
docker compose exec -T database createdb -U rdm -T template0 \
  --locale-provider=icu --icu-locale=und --locale=C rdm_restore_check
docker compose exec -T database pg_restore -U rdm --no-owner --exit-on-error \
  -d rdm_restore_check < backups/before-maintenance/database.dump
```

Stop on either failure. A successful restore finishes with exit 0. Then run the checker in the
engine image, deriving the scratch URL from its configured connection without writing the password
in a command argument:

```bash
docker compose run --rm -T engine python -c \
  'from app.db import configured_url; from app.cli.restore_check import main; raise SystemExit(main(["--restored",configured_url().set(database="rdm_restore_check").render_as_string(hide_password=False),"--backup","before-maintenance/database.dump"]))'
```

Expect `Backup rehearsal passed.`, each workspace's model and counts, and
`Recorded in the instance (Settings › Operations). Delete the copy when done.`
The recorded result belongs to the live instance. The checker changes/prepares only the restored
copy's schema and records the result in live; it does not activate the copy as the live database.
Its database/model check does **not** verify the file archive: inspect the archive and separately
exercise needed source/download files during your isolated recovery trial.

After reading the result, remove the scratch database:

```bash
docker compose exec -T database dropdb -U rdm rdm_restore_check
```

A failed rehearsal is evidence that recovery needs work. Keep its recorded failure and diagnostics,
correct the cause and retry from a fresh scratch restore; do not switch production to a failed copy.

## Restore on a replacement host

The safest whole-instance recovery keeps the old host and volumes untouched, isolated from
writers, while a replacement is checked. On that host, obtain the matching source version,
Compose files, private configuration and backup pair. Use the same project and environment-file
selection as the original; then:

:::caution[Automatic HTTPS needs both Compose files]
If the original used [automatic HTTPS](/docs/run/install-with-compose/#5-start-with-automatic-https),
set `COMPOSE_FILE=compose.yml:compose.acme.yml` in the replacement host's shell before these steps,
and restore the `caddy-data` volume too if you have it. Without `compose.acme.yml`, web starts
without Caddy in front and the site does not answer.
:::

1. Restore the protected configuration to `.env`, restore certificate files if using file mode,
   and make sure DNS/traffic still cannot send production users to the replacement.
2. Start only PostgreSQL: `docker compose up -d database`. Wait for its health check.
   An empty reference volume creates an empty `rdm` database with the required collation.
3. Restore into that **empty replacement** database:

   ```bash
   docker compose exec -T database pg_restore -U rdm --no-owner --exit-on-error    \
     -d rdm < backups/before-maintenance/database.dump
   ```

4. Build the matching engine image with `docker compose build engine` before restoring files.
   On a fresh host this downloads dependencies and prints build progress; wait for success.
   Restore the matching file archive with the engine stopped:

   ```bash
   docker compose run --rm --no-deps -T engine python -c    \
     'import sys,tarfile; t=tarfile.open(fileobj=sys.stdin.buffer,mode="r|*"); t.extractall("/opt/refiroo/rdm-engine/data/job-files",filter="data"); t.close()'      < backups/before-maintenance/job-files.tar
   ```

   Use only your trusted backup archive. The command runs as the engine user and must exit 0.
   The archive is extracted into a new job-file volume; do not overlay it on unrelated newer files.
5. Start the matching images with `docker compose up -d --build` (with automatic HTTPS, with both
   Compose files, as in [Upgrades](/docs/run/upgrades/#upgrade-the-compose-installation)), inspect bounded engine logs,
   readiness, every workspace, sign-in and important files. Review integrations before reconnecting
   them: external receivers can already hold events sent after the backup, so reconcile them rather
   than assuming their state rolled back too.
6. Only after those checks move traffic and reopen writers. Keep the old host isolated and retained
   until recovery is accepted. Switching back after new writes requires another reconciliation or
   recovery decision; it is not a lossless automatic undo.

Restoring into a populated database causes conflicts; stop and prepare a deliberate empty recovery
target instead of ignoring errors. A wrong encryption key may allow database restore yet prevent
sign-in or stored-secret use: supply the key associated with that backup. Never generate a new key
as a recovery shortcut. Whole-instance recovery reverts data written after the backup.


## Move the installation and retire the old host

Use the replacement-host procedure for a planned move too. Keep one authoritative writer:
stop every old engine before making the final database/file pair, restore that pair on the new
host and leave the old host isolated while validating. Preserve `PUBLIC_URL` if the public name
stays the same; changing the name also needs the
[sign-in cutover](/docs/run/sign-in-and-mail-setup/#change-the-public-address-or-move-the-host).

Keep the old environment, source version, keys and volumes until the replacement and its first
new backup have been checked. Forward new backups and monitoring to protected storage independent
of the replacement host. A working restored database alone does not check DNS, TLS, mail,
provider callbacks, webhook receivers or the availability of retained source files.

After acceptance, stop/remove the old containers and arrange deliberate retirement of their volumes,
private configuration, certificate keys and backup copies according to your retention policy.
`docker compose down` keeps volumes; `down -v` destroys them. Do not run either against the wrong
project or while relying on its only recovery copy. Credentials shared with the replacement must
remain valid there; retire obsolete host access and rotate compromised credentials separately.
The application supplies no host decommissioning or offsite-backup scheduler.
