Keep this source address with the version and configuration in your upgrade and backup records.
Changing it provides the link; it does not publish the source for you.

## Set and verify the source offer

You need the corresponding source for the running build, permission to publish that source, a
reachable HTTP/HTTPS address and access to the installation's private environment. Determine the
exact source revision before changing the link. The default project tag is suitable only when it
corresponds to the code you actually serve.

1. Make the source, including your modifications and needed build scripts, available at the
   intended address. Review its contents for secrets; publish safe templates in place of private
   installation values.
2. For a modified installation, put its source address in `.env`, for example:

   ```dotenv
   SOURCE_CODE_URL=https://source.example.org/refiroo/installed-version
   ```

   This setting is not secret. It is read at startup and requires engine recreation, not a browser
   refresh alone. Leave it unset for the unmodified version's default project tag.
3. Apply and check:

   ```bash
   docker compose up -d engine
   curl -i https://refiroo.example.org/health
   ```

   Expect readiness 200. Sign in, open About and follow **Source code**. Verify the published
   source matches the reported engine/build version and is accessible to the people receiving
   the offer. Merely returning an HTTP success page does not prove it is the correct source.
4. Keep the source/version association with the backup and upgrade record. If the link is wrong,
   correct the private setting and recreate again. The source publication itself is managed by
   your source-hosting service, not by refiroo.

A malformed value is refused with the exact prefix
`SOURCE_CODE_URL must be an absolute http or https address, not`, followed by the supplied value.
Correct its scheme/address; do not repair it by publishing a filled `.env` or a credential-bearing
source URL. This procedure provides the product's source link; evaluate your organisation's licence
obligations against the licence text accompanying the source.
guide/src/content/docs/run/model-release:
---
title: Model releases and rollback
description: Separate model selection from bootstrap files and application recovery.
reader: operator
---

A workspace runs an installed model release selected in the database. `RDM_MODEL_PATH` is only
bootstrap input: its default is `model/rdm-starter.json`, or `/opt/refiroo/rdm-engine/model/rdm-starter.json` in the image.
Startup validates the file and installs its release if missing, assigning it to a workspace without
one. Existing workspaces keep their selections. Editing that file never activates a new model.

For browser tasks, use [Releases](/docs/model/releases/). Model mutations require
`MODEL_ADMIN_MUTATIONS_ENABLED=true` (default false), plus the person's model permissions.
A draft is validated and compiled, installed as an inactive immutable release, then activated with
concurrency checks. Activation refuses a model incompatible with existing data.

## Roll back model content

Activate a previously installed compatible release through the model administration workflow.
The same data checks apply in either direction: if current data no longer fits the older model,
rollback is refused. Resolve the incompatibility in a reviewed model/data change instead of editing
release JSON or pointing the bootstrap file at an older version.

An unsupported model schema makes affected workspaces unavailable. Check Operations to distinguish
that from a database outage. Follow [Upgrades](/docs/run/upgrades/) to raise older stored models;
use an appropriate later engine for newer schemas.

## Retire and remove releases

Retiring a release removes it from pickers without stopping workspaces already using it. A release
used by the default workspace cannot be retired; first select a usable release for that workspace.
Retirement is not deletion. Deletion
requires that nothing refers to it: workspaces, records, change sets, publications, jobs, import
profiles and mappings can keep a release in use.

For many releases, inspect candidates first:

```bash
docker compose run --rm engine python -m app.cli.model_release_prune --dry-run
```

Then remove retired releases with no references:

```bash
docker compose run --rm engine python -m app.cli.model_release_prune
```

`--unused` also considers active releases with no references. Preview that wider selection before
using it:

```bash
docker compose run --rm engine python -m app.cli.model_release_prune --unused --dry-run
```

Pruning uses one transaction under the installation lock and can run while the service runs.
Drafts based on a removed release remain, without their link to it. Check the command's report;
exit 0 is success, 1 a database startup failure.

## Roll back the application

Restoring an older application requires its pre-upgrade database backup and matching configuration.
This restores all database state, unlike model activation. See [Back up and restore](/docs/run/backup-and-restore/).
Database downgrades and manual edits to release rows are unsupported.

## Check model selection before maintenance

You need Operations access to inspect readiness and model permissions for any browser activation.
Pruning on the server requires access to the private configured environment. Back up before any
irreversible deletion, and verify the engine version is intended for this database: even a prune
dry run first prepares its schema.

1. Open Operations and record each active workspace's release and schema. Check unavailable
   rows before pruning or changing bootstrap files.
2. For an intended model rollback, ask the model administrator to preview activation of the
   previously installed release in the workspace. Review incompatibilities and current runtime
   versions in the activation workflow; do not restart engines as a substitute for activation.
3. After successful activation, open the workspace, read a representative record and inspect its
   readiness in Operations. Other processes pick up the selection on their next request.
4. To reverse that selection, activate the prior release again, subject to the same current-data
   checks. If data changed meanwhile, that reverse operation can be refused too.

For pruning, a dry run prints each candidate as public release ID, `key@version`, lifecycle status
and schema, then a total. With no eligible candidates, the exact default message is:

```text
No retired and unused release; nothing to do.
```

A successful deletion reports `Deleted N retired and unused release(s).` With `--unused`, the
wording is `unused` and active unreferenced releases are included. Counts vary with your database.
Exit 1 means database preparation failed; use its diagnostic, then retry after correcting the
cause. A release still referenced is excluded rather than forcibly detached. Re-run the dry run
if references changed after your earlier inspection.

Pruning cannot be undone by restarting or changing `RDM_MODEL_PATH`. If a required release was
removed, review reinstalling its original source through model administration or restore the whole
matching backup in an isolated recovery process. Do not reconstruct immutable release rows using
SQL. Retire a release rather than delete it when you want it hidden from future choice while
preserving its identity and existing references.

## Releases prepared by the assistant

The assistant installs releases for review; a person activates or confirms a migration. A whole-type
move uses the migration preview and goes live on confirmation. A partial move can need a release
with both types, publication of the change set, then activation of the final release; if the old
type remains in the final model, the last activation step is unnecessary. The task shows the steps
for its result. Unused session-installed releases are retired when the task ends; the final release
needed by that result is kept. Do not mistake an installed release for an activated one.

An optional provider can explain a model change after **Explain this change** is pressed. It receives
model differences and record counts, not record values. Its statements cite the engine's facts and
never replace activation checks. See [AI policy and review](/docs/run/ai/) for who may ask, what is
sent, usage costs and retention, and [model changes with AI](/docs/model/ai-model-changes/) for the
browser task.
guide/src/content/docs/run/monitoring.md:
---
title: Monitor refiroo
description: Read process and workspace health, collect metrics, and trace a reported failure.
reader: operator
---

Start with **Settings › This instance › Operations**, available with Operations access. It shows
workspaces served or unavailable, live and silent processes, jobs, and webhook subscription states.
Below the totals are workspace failures, process threads and pool use, the latest backup rehearsal,
and probe addresses. It refreshes every 15 seconds while visible; **Refresh** reads again immediately.
A failed refresh preserves the previous figures and says when they were read.

![Operations showing workspace readiness and process health](/docs/screens/run-operations.png)

## Read the Operations page

1. Read the summary figures for workspaces, processes, jobs and webhook subscriptions. Check
   **As of** before acting on the figures. **Refresh** reads immediately; automatic refresh runs
   every 15 seconds while the page is visible. **Could not refresh** means the previous figures
   remain on screen and may be stale.
2. In **Workspaces**, read **Workspace**, **Release**, **Schema**, **State** and **Not served by**.
   **Served** means every live process can serve that workspace's release. **Unavailable** identifies
   a missing release or the processes and reasons preventing service. Overall `/health` can still
   pass while a workspace row is unavailable. Follow [startup recovery](/docs/run/health-and-startup-checks/).
3. Expand a row under **Engine processes**. It shows the engine version, start and last report,
   **Live** or **Silent**, and **Ready**, **Ready at last report** or **Not ready**. A silent process's
   former readiness is historical. **Background threads** distinguishes **Running**, **Failing**
   (with reason and time) and **Off**. Off can be expected for a disabled capability or while no
   workspace is servable; failing calls for investigation.
4. Read **Database connections** as connections in use against pool size plus overflow, with counts
   of connection failures. **Requests since start** counts answers and server errors for that
   process. **Releases it cannot serve** names blocked releases and their reason. These counters
   restart with a new process; they are not a durable audit log.
5. Use **Last backup rehearsal** to inspect recovery evidence, as explained in
   [Back up and restore](/docs/run/backup-and-restore/).
6. Under **For monitoring**, use the Copy control beside **Liveness**, **Readiness** or **Metrics**.
   Probe addresses reflect the browser's API address. The public Compose entry blocks Metrics;
   configure the scraper with an internal engine address instead.

The page is read only. It cannot stop a process, change settings, run a backup or restore data.
Use the operator commands for those tasks. Operations access covers monitoring, not editing people,
mail or subscriptions; those tasks need their own grants.

## Collect logs

```bash
docker compose logs --tail=100 engine
```

| Setting | Default | When to change it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `LOG_FORMAT` | `text` | Set `json` for one object per line in a log collector. Other values refuse startup. |
| `LOG_LEVEL` | `INFO` | Choose `DEBUG`, `INFO`, `WARNING` or `ERROR`. Temporarily use DEBUG for detailed causes; protect those logs. |
| `PROCESS_HEARTBEAT_SECONDS` | `15` | Interval between process reports; change with failure-detection latency in mind. |

Logs go to standard error. JSON records include UTC time, level, logger, message, process and thread;
requests also include `requestId`, method and route. Access lines add status and `durationMs`.
Probe and metrics access lines are DEBUG to keep normal logs small.

Use the response's `X-Request-Id` or an error's `correlationId` to locate its log records. A supplied
request ID is accepted only when it is 1–64 letters, digits, dots, underscores or hyphens; otherwise
the engine creates one. Expected operational failures have concise normal logs; DEBUG retains
underlying tracebacks. Avoid putting secrets into support reports.

## Scrape metrics privately

`GET /metrics` on the internal engine address returns Prometheus text for the whole instance, including all live processes.
Scrape once through an engine address reachable on the private network; scraping each process
repeats the same instance series. The public Compose web service returns 404 HTML from nginx for `/metrics`, even with a valid management token. This is the expected response at the public address; keep `/metrics` as the path and use the private engine address for scraping.

Create a monitoring client with the Operator role in your configured environment:

```bash
docker compose run --rm engine python -m app.cli.create_client \
  --name "Monitoring" --role operator
```

Store the printed secret once in the monitoring system's secret store. Configure Prometheus OAuth2
client credentials against `/oauth/token`, using the default management scope, or a bearer
credentials file that your token-refresh mechanism maintains. Tokens last 60 minutes by default;
a static expired token stops scrapes. See [Clients](/docs/administer/clients/) and the
[API reference](/docs/api) for authentication operations.

For a first scrape test, obtain a management `ACCESS_TOKEN` with this client using
[the token commands](/docs/run/sign-in-and-mail-setup/#api-authentication). From the
Compose checkout, pipe it to a probe inside the running engine container:

```bash
printf '%s' "$ACCESS_TOKEN" | docker compose exec -T engine python -c \
  'import sys,urllib.request; token=sys.stdin.read(); request=urllib.request.Request("http://engine:8000/metrics",headers={"Authorization":"Bearer "+token}); print(urllib.request.urlopen(request,timeout=10).read().decode())'
```

Expect Prometheus text including `rdm_process_ready{...} 1` for a ready process. The token
is read from stdin and is not printed. A 401 needs a fresh valid management token; a 403
needs the Operator grant. A public `/metrics` 404 is expected, even with a token. Keep the
engine port private. Clear the temporary token with `unset ACCESS_TOKEN` after testing.

The metrics response uses Prometheus text exposition format version `0.0.4`.

## Read the same figures as JSON

Use these read-only operations to investigate an incident or collect structured monitoring results.
Send a management bearer token with the instance Operator grant, as for the scraper above.
All four require **Operations** access (`operations.read`) at the instance; sign-in alone is
not enough. See the [system field reference](/docs/api/?api=management#tag/system).
They do not start jobs or restore backups. For paged results, follow the page's links until
all items have been read before calculating totals.

### Engine processes

`GET /api/v1/system/processes` returns every engine process on this database in ID order.
`pageSize` defaults to 100 and accepts at most 500. The answering process reports itself first,
so its figures are current; other processes' figures date from their last heartbeat.
Each item corresponds to a row under **Engine processes**:

| JSON fields | What to read |
| --- | --- |
| `id`, `host`, `pid` | Identity: `host:pid:random`, host and operating-system process ID. A restart creates a new identity. |
| `engineVersion`, `startedAt`, `heartbeatAt` | Engine version, start time and last report. |
| `state`, `ready` | `live` or `silent`, and whether it serves at least one workspace's model. Silent readiness is historical. |
| `threads` | **Background threads**: each has `name`, `state` (`running`, `failing`, `off`), optional failure `reason` and `since` time. |
| `pool` | **Database connections**: `size`, `maxOverflow`, `inUse` (connections checked out when reported). |
| `unavailableReleases` | **Releases it cannot serve**: each has `releaseId`, `schemaVersion` and `reason`. |
| `counters` | **Requests since start**: `requests`, `serverErrors` (5xx answers), and `databaseUnavailable`, counts by reason. Counters reset with a new process. |

Thread names are `jobWorker`, `exportWorker`, `assistantWorker`, `jobListener`, `eventDeriver`,
`webhookDispatcher`, `mailSender` and `heartbeat`. Failure reasons are `poolExhausted`,
`tooManyConnections`, `transactionEnded`, `unreachable` or `error`. An `off` thread has not
started in this process: its capability may be disabled or no workspace may be servable.

A process is `silent` after three `PROCESS_HEARTBEAT_SECONDS` intervals without a report.
A clean stop removes it; a process that died remains listed silent for a day.
Check the host and logs before relying on a silent process's old figures.

### Workspace readiness

`GET /api/v1/system/readiness` lists active workspaces in key order. `pageSize` defaults
to 100, at most 500. Each item has `workspaceKey`, its `release` (`id`, `key`, `version`,
`schemaVersion`, or `null` for none), `state` (`served` or `unavailable`) and `unavailableIn`.
This is the **Workspaces** table; **Not served by** comes from `unavailableIn`, which lists
live processes unable to serve the release, each with `processId`, `schemaVersion` and `reason`.

`unsupportedSchema` means the schema is outside that engine's supported window; `invalid`
means model validation failed; `notLoaded` means an activated release has not loaded in
that process and needs a restart. No release also makes a workspace unavailable.
Follow [startup recovery](/docs/run/health-and-startup-checks/) for the next action.

### Instance totals

`GET /api/v1/system/summary` is not paged. It counts the same instance figures as the
instance gauges of `/metrics`, now: `processes` (`live`, `silent`), `workspaces` (`served`,
`unavailable`), `jobs`, and `webhookSubscriptions` (`active`, `failing`, `suspended`).
Each jobs entry has `kind`, `state` and `count`, for `queued`, `running` or
`awaiting_confirmation`. Kind/state combinations with no jobs are omitted. Treat an omitted
combination as zero in a dashboard rather than carrying forward an earlier count.

### Backup rehearsals

`GET /api/v1/system/backup-rehearsals` lists checks made with
`python -m app.cli.restore_check` against backups restored into separate databases,
newest first. `pageSize` defaults to 20, at most 200. These are the results in
**Last backup rehearsal**, not a list of backup files on disk.

Each gives `id`, `checkedAt`, `result` (`passed` or `failed`), supplied `backup` name,
`dataAsOf` (the copy's newest audit change), `revisionBefore`, `revisionAfter`,
`engineVersion` and `host`. Backup name and data time may be null; `revisionAfter`
is null if the copy was not prepared. A failure includes `failure.code` and
`failure.message`, explaining what recovery would meet and what to do.

Each item in `workspaces` gives the copy's `workspaceKey`, `release`, `state` (`served`
or `unavailable`), and `reason` (`unsupportedSchema`, `invalid`, `noRelease`, or null).
`records`, `relations`, `openChangeSets` and `publications` count the restored copy;
`liveRecords` counts that workspace's records in the live instance when checked.
Relationships are counted by their source workspace. Different counts alone do not fail
the rehearsal. Follow the [rehearsal procedure and failure-code actions](/docs/run/backup-and-restore/#rehearse-in-a-separate-database)
for a failed or outdated check; reading this operation never performs one.

## Choose alerts

| Signal | What to investigate |
| --- | --- |
| `rdm_workspaces_unavailable > 0` | Release schema, model validity and processes failing to load a workspace. |
| `rdm_process_ready = 0` | Readiness and startup messages. |
| `rdm_processes{state="silent"} > 0` | Missing heartbeats; a process may have crashed or lost database access. |
| Rising `rdm_database_unavailable_total` | Its reason: pool exhaustion, server connection ceiling, ended transaction or unreachable database. |
| `rdm_background_thread_failing = 1` for minutes | The named thread's reason and logs. |
| Growing `rdm_jobs{state="queued"}` | Worker state, capability switch, leases and sustained demand. |
| `rdm_webhook_subscriptions{state="suspended"} > 0` | Subscription reason, receiver health and retained event positions. |

Request counts and duration histograms are `rdm_http_requests_total` and
`rdm_http_request_duration_seconds`. Pool size, overflow and checked-out connections are exposed
under `rdm_database_pool_*`. Process counters restart with a new process label. Labels do not
include individual records or workspaces. Tune alert thresholds to your own measured workload;
production capacity and latency targets are **not measured** for your installation.

A process becomes silent after three heartbeat intervals, normally 45 seconds. Clean stops remove
the row; crashed rows expire after a day. Other processes' figures can be one heartbeat old.
Use [liveness and readiness probes](/docs/run/health-and-startup-checks/) alongside these metrics.

## Metrics reference

Every process metric below includes the `process` label. Its value identifies a host, PID and
random suffix; restarting makes a new series. Other processes' samples can be one heartbeat old.
Instance gauges have only the labels listed in the table and are counted when scraped. Missing
series for work that has never happened are not necessarily zero-valued samples.

| Metric | Kind | Labels in addition to `process` | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `rdm_process_ready` | Gauge | `version` | 1 when the process is ready, 0 otherwise. |
| `rdm_process_start_time_seconds` | Gauge | None | Start time as Unix seconds. |
| `rdm_http_requests_total` | Counter | `method`, `route`, `status` | Completed answers, using the route template or `unmatched`, never a record-specific path. |
| `rdm_http_request_duration_seconds` | Histogram | `route`; buckets also have `le` | Time until response handling finishes, including a streamed response's duration. |
| `rdm_database_unavailable_total` | Counter | `reason` | Request connection refusals and background outages begun; reasons are `poolExhausted`, `tooManyConnections`, `transactionEnded`, `unreachable`. |
| `rdm_database_pool_size` | Gauge | None | Configured persistent pool size. |
| `rdm_database_pool_max_overflow` | Gauge | None | Configured extra busy-period connections. |
| `rdm_database_pool_connections_in_use` | Gauge | None | Connections checked out at the process's report. |
| `rdm_background_thread_failing` | Gauge | `thread` | 1 when a started thread is failing, 0 otherwise; off threads have no sample. |
| `rdm_releases_unavailable` | Gauge | None | Releases used by workspaces that this process cannot serve. |

| Instance metric | Kind | All labels | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `rdm_processes` | Gauge | `state` | Number of `live` and `silent` processes. |
| `rdm_jobs` | Gauge | `kind`, `state` | Jobs `queued`, `running` or `awaiting_confirmation`, by kind. |
| `rdm_webhook_subscriptions` | Gauge | `state` | Subscriptions `active`, `failing` (retrying) or `suspended`. |
| `rdm_workspaces_unavailable` | Gauge | None | Active workspaces missing a release or unavailable in some live process. |

The histogram exports `_bucket`, `_sum` and `_count` series. Bucket bounds, in seconds, are
`0.005`, `0.01`, `0.025`, `0.05`, `0.1`, `0.25`, `0.5`, `1`, `2.5`, `5`, `10` and `+Inf`.
Buckets are cumulative; `le` is the upper bound. An illustrative excerpt from an instance with one
process is:

```text
# TYPE rdm_process_ready gauge
rdm_process_ready{process="host:123:example",version="0.16.0"} 1
# TYPE rdm_http_requests_total counter
rdm_http_requests_total{process="host:123:example",method="GET",route="/api/v1/workspaces",status="200"} 4
# TYPE rdm_workspaces_unavailable gauge
rdm_workspaces_unavailable 0
```

Configure a scraper attached to the private Compose network. Its `engine:8000` name resolves there,
not from an arbitrary external monitoring host. For example, a Prometheus scrape job can use:

```yaml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: refiroo
    metrics_path: /metrics
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["engine:8000"]
    oauth2:
      client_id: "REPLACE_WITH_MONITORING_CLIENT_ID"
      client_secret_file: /etc/prometheus/secrets/refiroo-client-secret
      token_url: http://engine:8000/oauth/token
```

Put only the client's secret in that protected file; grant the client the instance Operator role.
The HTTP hop above stays on the private network. Use protected HTTPS connectivity for a scraper
outside that trust boundary. Expect `rdm_process_ready` and a successful scrape. A 401 requires
checking client credentials or token expiry; 403 requires the Operator grant; public 404 means the
scraper hit web instead of the internal engine. Do not expose port 8000 to repair a scrape.

## Log field reference and examples

With JSON format, all lines have the first six fields. Request context and access fields appear
only where applicable. Other log messages may add fields relevant to that event.

| Field | Example | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `time` | `2026-11-03T10:00:00.123+00:00` | UTC timestamp with millisecond precision. |
| `level` | `INFO` | Log severity. |
| `logger` | `app.access` | Source logger; access lines replace uvicorn access logging. |
| `message` | `GET /api/v1/workspaces 200 12.3 ms` | Human-readable event. |
| `process` | `123` | OS process ID; differs from the metrics process identity. |
| `thread` | `MainThread` | Thread that wrote the event. |
| `requestId` | `operator-check` | Request correlation reference, when in a request. |
| `method` | `GET` | Request method. |
| `route` | `/api/v1/workspaces` | Matched route template when available; context can use the path before routing. |
| `path` | `/api/v1/workspaces` | Access record's actual request path. |
| `status` | `200` | Access record's HTTP status. |
| `durationMs` | `12.3` | Access record's elapsed time, in milliseconds. |
| `exception` | Traceback text | Present only when logged with exception details; expected operational failure traces are DEBUG. |

Illustrative lines for the same request in the two formats:

```text
2026-11-03 10:00:00,123 INFO app.access: GET /api/v1/workspaces 200 12.3 ms [request operator-check]
```

```json
{"time": "2026-11-03T10:00:00.123+00:00", "level": "INFO", "logger": "app.access", "message": "GET /api/v1/workspaces 200 12.3 ms", "process": 123, "thread": "MainThread", "requestId": "operator-check", "method": "GET", "route": "/api/v1/workspaces", "path": "/api/v1/workspaces", "status": 200, "durationMs": 12.3}
```

To trace a harmless probe, temporarily enable DEBUG, recreate the engine and send:

```bash
curl -i -H 'X-Request-Id: operator-check' https://refiroo.example.org/health
docker compose logs --tail=200 engine
```

Expect `X-Request-Id: operator-check` in the response and the same reference in the access line.
Restore INFO and recreate after diagnosis. The text timestamp uses the process's local logging
clock; JSON explicitly writes UTC. Retain logs using the container platform or your collector;
refiroo supplies no deployment-wide log rotation or archive policy. Do not leave unbounded debug
capture running. All three logging/reporting settings above are non-secret and need recreation.

## Watch AI and agent calls

**Settings › This instance › AI** needs Operations access and lists each provider call and
assistant turn with its purpose, requester, outcome, tokens, reported cost and duration. Totals
cover 30 days. This is usage evidence, not a billing statement. **Send a test request** checks only
the provider and sends no reference data; test a real assistant task separately. Read the failure
sentence before retrying; a provider failure leaves ordinary work available.

For external assistants, a security administrator uses **Settings › Connections › Agent access**.
Its separate call list shows answered, refused, limited and failed calls, including argument names
but never values. Use its request identifier when tracing a failure. See [AI and agent settings](/docs/run/ai/)
for send policy, cost, retention and revocation. Logging provider content is optional and can retain
sensitive reference data; do not enable it merely to collect call counts.


## Keep monitoring history and retire a scraper

refiroo exposes current metrics; it does not store a Prometheus time series archive. The Operations
page's process reports and counters are not a replacement for your monitoring history. Set metric
retention, storage capacity and backups in Prometheus or your monitoring platform. A rebuilt engine
cannot restore the old process's in-memory counters from a database backup.

Keep log retention separate from `JOB_RETENTION_DAYS`, feed retention and webhook delivery-log
retention. Those settings do not rotate container logs or shorten a metrics archive. The reference
Compose files do not set a Docker logging rotation policy. Configure bounded retention in the
container platform or collector for engine, web, database and Caddy, and watch the host disk too.
Avoid leaving DEBUG enabled after diagnosis.

When replacing the monitoring client secret, update the scraper's protected secret file and verify
fresh token acquisition and successful scrapes before retiring the old secret where overlap is
available. Use the [client administration workflow](/docs/administer/clients/). To remove a scraper,
remove its scrape job and deactivate its dedicated client. This stops new collection; retained
metrics and logs remain under the collector's own retention policy. Removing monitoring grants
does not stop the engine or erase application records.
guide/src/content/docs/run/overview.md:
---
title: What you run
description: Understand the reference installation and choose your next operator task.
reader: operator
---

Run refiroo with the repository's Docker Compose installation. It builds the application from
source and runs three containers:

| Container | Responsibility | Persistent storage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `web` | Serves the browser application and forwards requests to the engine. Ends HTTPS when using your certificates. | Certificate files supplied by you. |
| `engine` | Serves the API and documentation, checks the database at startup, and runs background work. | `job-files` and `assistant` volumes. |
| `database` | PostgreSQL 17, the only supported database. | `database` volume. |

Only the web service publishes host ports. The engine runs as an unprivileged user. Jobs run in
threads inside the engine process; there is no separate worker service to install. The optional
[automatic HTTPS overlay](/docs/run/https/#get-and-renew-public-certificates-automatically)
adds Caddy and makes it the only public container. For a public DNS name, it obtains a Let's Encrypt
or ZeroSSL certificate and renews it automatically. Set `PUBLIC_URL` to that name's HTTPS origin
and start with `compose.acme.yml` alongside the base Compose file. You can instead supply your
organisation's certificates or use its existing HTTPS proxy; [Serve over HTTPS](/docs/run/https/)
explains all three choices.

## Start here

1. [Install with Compose](/docs/run/install-with-compose/) and [choose HTTPS](/docs/run/https/).
2. [Configure the installation](/docs/run/configure/), preserving its [secrets and keys](/docs/run/secrets-and-keys/).
3. [Set up sign-in and mail](/docs/run/sign-in-and-mail-setup/), if needed.
4. Check [readiness](/docs/run/health-and-startup-checks/), set up [monitoring](/docs/run/monitoring/), and [rehearse a restore](/docs/run/backup-and-restore/).
5. Complete the [production checklist](/docs/run/production-checklist/).

For local code work, use the [developer instance](/docs/run/developer-instance/). It is a development
setup, separate from the tested Compose reference installation. Several processes can share a
database, but arranging several nodes and their shared storage is outside that reference installation.

AI is optional. Read [About AI](/docs/run/ai/) before [setting it up](/docs/run/set-up-ai/).
Production CPU, memory and disk sizing for your workload is **not measured**. Set capacity from
observations of your own records, files, traffic and retention; defaults are limits, not sizing guarantees.

For supplier-file synchronisation, the operator keeps workers, shared file storage and database
connectivity available; a restarted independent job resumes after its last committed chunk.
The integrator reviews rejected rows and maintains its change-feed position. Use
[File exchange](/docs/integrate/files-imports-and-exports/), [Following changes](/docs/integrate/following-changes/)
and [Background jobs](/docs/run/background-jobs/) together when recovering an interrupted load.

## Network and storage

The reference Compose file builds two local images and downloads the database image. The engine
image uses Python 3.14 slim and builds the guide using Node 22 Alpine. The web image builds the
browser client with Node 22 Alpine and serves it with
`nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:1.28-alpine`. PostgreSQL uses `postgres:17-alpine`; the optional
certificate overlay uses `caddy:2`. Building needs access to image and package registries. These are
source builds, so keep the exact source version with your deployment record. Base images are
pinned by digest, Claude Code by a named build version, Python dependencies by
`backend/constraints.txt`, and frontend and guide packages by their npm lock files. See
[Maintain build versions](/docs/run/upgrades/#maintain-build-versions) when moving those pins.

| Connection | Port and direction | Exposure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Browser → web | Host TCP 443 → container 8443 with certificate files | Public HTTPS entry. TCP 80 → 8080 redirects to the fixed public address. |
| Browser → Caddy, with the overlay | Host TCP 443; optional 80 for HTTP redirects | Caddy is public and forwards to private `web:8080`. |
| HTTPS balancer → web, in proxy mode | Container 8080, through your selected host port | Restrict to the balancer. This hop is HTTP on a trusted network. |
| web → engine | `engine:8000`, HTTP on the Compose network | Private. Never publish engine port 8000 with the reference trust settings. |
| engine → database | `database:5432`, PostgreSQL | Private. No host port is published. |
| Monitoring → engine | Internal 8000, authenticated `/metrics` | Private; public web returns 404 for this path. |
| engine → sign-in provider / webhook receiver | HTTPS to the configured host and port | Outbound only, when configured. |
| engine → SMTP | Configured port; commonly 587 STARTTLS or 465 TLS | Outbound only, when configured. |

The public proxy forwards `/api/`, `/oauth/`, `/mcp`, `/.well-known/`, `/docs`, `/openapi.json` and
`/health` paths. Other paths serve the browser application. `/mcp` is available only when agent
access is enabled; see [AI and agent settings](/docs/run/ai/).

| Storage or file | Location | Protect or recreate? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Database volume | `database` service, `/var/lib/postgresql/data` | Back up as PostgreSQL state. It holds records, models, identities, jobs, feeds and delivery logs. |
| Job-file volume | Engine, `/opt/refiroo/rdm-engine/data/job-files` | Back up with the database. Some files are temporary; draft/profile source workbooks are long lived. |
| Assistant task folders (`assistant`) | Engine, `/opt/refiroo/rdm-engine/data/assistant` | Each randomly named task folder holds working files, Claude Code configuration, transcripts and turn logs. Keeps them across container replacement; optional in backups. Losing it loses open tasks’ folders and logs, not records. |
| Private environment | Host `.env`, or your selected file | Keep securely outside database backups, associated with each backup. Losing its sealing key loses access to stored secrets. |
| Certificate directory | Host `./certs`, mounted read only at `/opt/refiroo/rdm-engine/frontend/certs` | Protect private keys; preserve or replace through your certificate issuer. Not needed with automatic HTTPS. |
| Certificate account and certificates | Overlay `caddy-data`, mounted at `/data` | Preserve and back up to avoid unnecessary reissuance and authority limits. |
| Built application and guide | Images, under `/opt/refiroo/rdm-engine` | Rebuild from the matching source and dependencies; not mutable business data. |
| Container logs | Docker's configured logging storage | Export/rotate according to your retention policy; replacing a container is not log archiving. |

The reference file persists the assistant’s folders and Claude Code configuration and session logs
in the `assistant` volume. Review their [storage and security requirements](/docs/run/ai/) before enabling
the assistant. Temporary exports may be regenerated, but deleting the entire job-file volume also loses input files. A database backup alone
cannot reconstruct those workbooks. See [Background jobs](/docs/run/background-jobs/) for each
file's lifetime and [Back up and restore](/docs/run/backup-and-restore/) for a consistent pair.

`docker compose down` keeps named volumes. `docker compose down -v` removes `database`,
`job-files` and `assistant`, and `caddy-data` when using the HTTPS overlay.
This loses the database records, job files, assistant task folders and session logs, and any
certificates and account held by Caddy. Do not use it to repair a startup problem.

## Know the boundary of support

The installation procedure covers the checked-in Compose services and HTTPS overlay. It supplies
no Kubernetes, managed-database, high-availability or automatic failover procedure. Multiple engine
processes have shared-database coordination, but assembling a multi-node deployment and its shared
storage requires your own operational validation. Hardware minimums, production service targets
and recovery times are **not measured** for your workload.
guide/src/content/docs/run/production-ch:
---
title: Production checklist
description: Check installation, access, monitoring and recovery before accepting production traffic.
reader: operator
---

Complete this checklist on the actual installation before accepting production writes. The commands
and setup steps are in the linked pages; record your outcomes and recovery contacts locally.

1. **Use the reference installation.** Build the intended source version with
   [Docker Compose](/docs/run/install-with-compose/). Keep only the entry web service public.
   PostgreSQL 17 must use ICU root `und` and the required extensions.
2. **Fix the public address and choose HTTPS.** Set the permanent HTTPS `PUBLIC_URL`, matching
   browser origins and provider callbacks. For a public name, choose [automatic HTTPS](/docs/run/https/)
   with `compose.acme.yml`: Caddy obtains and renews the certificate. Confirm DNS points here,
   TCP 443 is reachable from the internet and the `caddy-data` volume is preserved. Port 80 is
   optional for HTTP redirects; TLS-ALPN issuance and renewal work on 443 alone.
   Alternatively, supply your organisation's certificates or use its HTTPS balancer. Check
   certificate trust and renewal, plus HTTP redirection if port 80 is open. If behind a balancer, check its trusted address
   range and forwarded headers.
3. **Protect secrets.** Store the database password, sealing key and stable cursor key outside
   version control and images. Keep the same keys across processes. Associate each backup with
   its sealing key: [Secrets and keys](/docs/run/secrets-and-keys/).
4. **Confirm effective settings.** Read **Settings › This instance › Deployment**. Verify capability
   switches, limits, retention and migration revision. Recreate containers after environment
   changes; restarting alone does not apply them.
5. **Check access.** Test the first administrator, provider sign-in if used, appropriate grants,
   second-factor policy and a local recovery account. Reduce broad setup grants. Follow the
   [security checklist](/docs/run/security-checklist/).
6. **Test mail if needed.** Confirm the public link address, SMTP TLS and credentials, SPF/DKIM,
   a test message and actual receipt: [Sign-in and mail](/docs/run/sign-in-and-mail-setup/).
7. **Check readiness per workspace.** Require `/health` 200 and inspect every active workspace and
   process on **Operations**. Use `/health/live` for liveness so a database outage does not cause
   restart loops.
8. **Set monitoring.** Collect bounded/rotated logs, authenticate private metrics scrapes and alert
   on unavailable workspaces, silent processes, failed workers and growing queues. Verify that a
   reported request ID leads to its log: [Monitoring](/docs/run/monitoring/).
9. **Protect files and capacity.** Persist job files, share them if several instances run, and
   budget connections across all processes. Exercise a representative import/export and check
   disk retention. Use the [database growth checks](/docs/run/database/#watch-database-growth) and
   set external log/metric retention; job retention does not bound all storage. Production CPU, memory, throughput and recovery sizing are **not measured**
   for your workload; collect your own evidence.
10. **Check integrations.** Confirm receiver trust, signature verification, event deduplication,
    retry recovery and re-sync procedures if using [webhooks](/docs/run/webhook-delivery/).
    Review [AI send policy](/docs/run/ai/) separately before enabling AI or agents.
11. **Prove recovery.** Back up the database and source files, restore into a separate database,
    and inspect the recorded rehearsal on Operations. Keep the matching application and private
    configuration: [Back up and restore](/docs/run/backup-and-restore/).
12. **Prepare upgrades and support.** Record the cutover and restore plan, the expected model schema,
    support diagnostics and corresponding source URL for a modified build. See
    [Upgrades](/docs/run/upgrades/) and [Licence and source](/docs/run/licence-and-source/).

A container marked healthy alone is insufficient evidence for these steps. Record what you actually
checked, including any custom proxy or provider behavior that remains unverified.

## Run the checks and keep the results

You need the installed source version, private configuration, Docker access, the public DNS name,
an administrator for access/sign-in tests and an operator for Deployment and Operations. Arrange
an approved maintenance window before recovery or restart trials. This list assumes the reference
Compose installation; repeat the checks through the actual balancer if you use one. The standard
commands below use the base Compose file. Keep both `-f` arguments for automatic HTTPS and the
same alternate environment-file selection, if any.

### 1. Confirm service state and public transport

```bash
docker compose config --quiet
docker compose ps
curl -I http://refiroo.example.org/
curl -I https://refiroo.example.org/
curl -i https://refiroo.example.org/health/live
curl -i https://refiroo.example.org/health
curl -i https://refiroo.example.org/metrics
```

Use your real host. If port 80 is closed, skip the HTTP command; a failed connection there is
expected. Otherwise expect HTTP redirected to the fixed HTTPS origin. Expect valid Compose input,
running services, trusted TLS, health 200 with `{"status":"ok"}`, and **404** for public metrics.
Check container port mappings: only web (or Caddy) publishes. If an engine/database port is public,
correct that exposure before accepting users. Follow [HTTPS](/docs/run/https/#verify-from-the-callers-network)
for the response-header checks. Do not suppress certificate verification.

### 2. Confirm database, configuration and workspaces

Run the [database inspection commands](/docs/run/database/#inspect-the-reference-database).
Record PostgreSQL 17, ICU root collation, all three extensions and the current migration revision.
On Deployment confirm the intended capability groups, durable job path, stable cursor key,
permanent public origin and acceptable limits. No secret should be copied into the checklist.

On Operations inspect every active workspace and every live process. Overall readiness 200 is not
a substitute for this list: each expected workspace must be served. Confirm the expected worker
threads are running, off only for understood reasons, and none are silently failing. Record the
engine version from About and the source version you built.

### 3. Confirm a person can work and recover access

Sign in through the public origin using the recovery administrator. Sign in with the organisation's
provider as a test person if used. Check intended Browse access and refusal outside that person's
grants. Open an application and read a record; the home page should show only workspaces that
person may browse. Verify second-factor setup and the recovery procedure without taking away
the last working administrator. Deactivate the test person when no longer needed.

If mail is required, send a test and check actual receipt, then test a reset link for the test
person. Record sender, TLS mode and result without copying credentials or the link. Check
notifications/digest expectations with their recipient's saved time zone. See
[Sign-in and mail](/docs/run/sign-in-and-mail-setup/) for exact failure recovery.

### 4. Confirm retained files and background work

Run the [worker storage checks](/docs/run/background-jobs/#check-worker-storage-and-restart-one-reference-instance).
Preview a small intended reference-data workbook or use a test workspace through the normal
import workflow, then verify outcomes before committing. Run an export and confirm its download.
After a planned engine restart, check the completed export still downloads and every workspace
is ready. This checks persistence, not load capacity; use a noncritical job if checking takeover.

For webhooks, coordinate one reviewed change and confirm delivery and receiver deduplication.
Record the subscription state, receiver response and retention/re-sync owner. Do not confuse a
manual resend with recovery of the normal position. Review AI separately using its linked pages;
this checklist does not enable or validate it.

### 5. Confirm monitoring and recovery evidence

Check the private authenticated scraper, an actual log correlation reference and log retention.
Use [Monitoring](/docs/run/monitoring/) for metric/field names. Confirm an operator receives alerts
for unavailable workspaces and sustained failed background work. Store bounded diagnostic output;
never leave an unrestricted log-following process running for a checklist.

Run the [consistent backup and separate-database rehearsal](/docs/run/backup-and-restore/).
Record the backup identifier, source/configuration version, recorded **Passed** rehearsal and
file-archive inspection. A database-only rehearsal does not validate file recovery or public sign-in
on a replacement host. Rehearse those too before relying on an end-to-end recovery time.

## Decide whether to open traffic

Keep these local records with the installation, rather than secrets in the guide:

| Evidence | Record |
| --- | --- |
| Deployment | Public origin, application/source version, database revision, model releases, configuration version. |
| Security | Certificate expiry/renewal owner, recovery account custodian, access and provider test results. |
| Operations | Workspace/process readiness, file persistence and relevant integration outcomes, alert recipient. |
| Recovery | Backup identifier, key-version reference, file archive, rehearsal result, measured duration if rehearsed. |
| Capacity | Observed storage/connection use and any workload limits still unmeasured. |

If a check fails, keep writers closed, use the owning page's recovery procedure and repeat only the
failed check plus what its fix affects. A failed backup needs a fresh successful backup/rehearsal;
a proxy correction needs new public TLS and sign-in checks. Do not erase the old evidence or mark
an unexercised path as passed. A production capacity or recovery-time promise requires your own
measurements; neither follows from passing this checklist.
guide/src/content/docs/run/secrets-and-k:
---
title: Secrets and keys
description: Keep sealing keys recoverable and change them without losing stored secrets.
reader: operator
---

Keep secrets in the installation's private environment or secret store. Never commit filled `.env`
files, credential-bearing database URLs, encryption or cursor keys, provider or SMTP credentials,
client secrets, webhook keys, AI credentials or TLS private keys. Backups contain sensitive data too.
Keep their keys securely outside the database and associate each backup with the key it needs.

## Which key does what

| Key | Default | Purpose and change rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `SECRETS_ENCRYPTION_KEY` | Required | 32 URL-safe-base64-encoded bytes. Opens stored token/webhook keys, provider secrets and session ID tokens, authenticator secrets, SMTP passwords and queued message text. Reseal before replacing it. |
| `RDM_CURSOR_SIGNING_KEY` | Ephemeral per process | Signs pagination cursors. Set one stable secret across processes; replacing it invalidates existing cursors. |
| Token signing keys | Engine-generated | Sign access tokens; stored sealed in PostgreSQL. Automatically rotate after `TOKEN_SIGNING_KEY_DAYS`, default 30, when another token is issued. |
| Webhook signing keys | Generated for subscriptions | Let receivers verify deliveries. Rotate independently of the sealing key. |

Generate a sealing key with `python -m app.cli.generate_key` in the configured backend environment,
or use the OpenSSL command from [installation](/docs/run/install-with-compose/). Never generate a
replacement merely because an existing installation cannot open a stored secret: find its original key.

## Change the sealing key

Arrange downtime and take a [backup](/docs/run/backup-and-restore/) first. Tell people with recovery
codes that they must create new ones afterwards: those codes are keyed directly with the old key
and cannot be resealed. Their authenticator app continues working after resealing.

For Compose, from the repository root:

1. Stop every engine process. In the single-instance reference:

   ```bash
   docker compose stop engine
   docker compose run --rm engine python -m app.cli.reseal_secrets --check
   ```

   The check opens every sealed value with the current key without changing it, and reports how
   many people have unused recovery codes. Stop if any value cannot be opened.
2. Generate a new key and supply it as `NEW_SECRETS_ENCRYPTION_KEY` through a secure environment
   injection. Keep the old key in `SECRETS_ENCRYPTION_KEY`. Do not put either value in command
   arguments or shell history. With the new variable exported in your shell, run:

   ```bash
   docker compose run --rm -e NEW_SECRETS_ENCRYPTION_KEY engine \
     python -m app.cli.reseal_secrets
   ```

3. The command reseals all values in one transaction. If a value fails, it names its kind and
   identity without printing its contents and changes nothing. An absent, malformed or identical
   new key is refused. Fix the cause before retrying.
4. On success, replace `SECRETS_ENCRYPTION_KEY` in every instance's private environment with the
   new value, remove the temporary variable, and recreate the engine:

   ```bash
   unset NEW_SECRETS_ENCRYPTION_KEY
   docker compose up -d engine
   ```

5. Check readiness and sign-in. Ask affected people to make new recovery codes on
   **Account › Second factor**. An administrator must help anyone who also lost their authenticator.

Keep the old key for backups made before resealing, and the new key for later backups. Resealing
preserves the underlying signing secrets, so it does not itself invalidate access tokens or require
receiver reconfiguration. To respond to a signing-key leak, also rotate the affected key:
[Signing keys](/docs/administer/signing-keys/) and [Webhook delivery](/docs/run/webhook-delivery/).

## Supply the temporary new key without a literal secret in history

Before starting, have the old key available in the installation's private settings, a rehearsed
backup, downtime for every engine and a protected place to keep both key versions. The reference
image can generate key material without starting the database or engine server. One shell sequence
for the **new** key is:

```bash
NEW_SECRETS_ENCRYPTION_KEY="$(docker compose run --rm --no-deps -T engine python -m app.cli.generate_key)"
export NEW_SECRETS_ENCRYPTION_KEY
```

Check that generation succeeded before resealing; store the generated value securely without
printing it into logs. The command text in shell history contains no literal key. The shell's
export makes `docker compose run -e NEW_SECRETS_ENCRYPTION_KEY` pass the variable through. An
environment export alone does not replace Compose's configured `SECRETS_ENCRYPTION_KEY`.
Do not close that shell or discard the new key until you have stored it and changed the private
configuration after successful resealing.

A successful check begins `Every sealed value opens with the current key` and reports counts by
kind. A successful write begins `Re-sealed` and prints
`Set SECRETS_ENCRYPTION_KEY to the new key before starting the engine.` It also reports either how
many people lose unused recovery codes or
`No one has an unused recovery code, so no recovery code is lost with a new key.`
The detailed command status reference is [Command-line tools](/docs/run/command-line/).

## If checking or resealing fails

| Message fragment | State and action |
| --- | --- |
| `Not re-sealed: SECRETS_ENCRYPTION_KEY is not set.` | No resealing occurred. Restore the current installation key. |
| `Not re-sealed: NEW_SECRETS_ENCRYPTION_KEY is not set; generate one with` | No resealing occurred. Export the new key and explicitly pass it into the one-shot container. |
| `Not re-sealed: NEW_SECRETS_ENCRYPTION_KEY is the current key.` | No change. Supply a different generated key if rotation is intended. |
| `Not re-sealed:` followed by sealed-item identities | Some values could not be opened; none were replaced. Recover the correct old key or investigate damaged/mixed-key data before retrying. |

Before a successful reseal, the old key remains correct. After success, start engines only with the
new key. A safe undo of the whole operation is restoring the matching pre-change database and
file backup with the old configuration. Do not merely switch the environment back to the old key
after resealing: the database now contains ciphertext sealed under the new one.

After recreation, require readiness 200, sign in, and exercise the configured services that open
stored secrets: a mail test and provider sign-in where used, and webhook delivery with its receiver.
Existing TOTP apps should still work. Ask people with recovery codes to regenerate them; do not
invalidate an authenticator app just because its recovery codes need replacing. Keep both key
versions under separate backup-version labels until no retained backup needs the old one.

## Cursor keys and signing-key rotations

Changing `RDM_CURSOR_SIGNING_KEY` does not require resealing database values. It makes existing
pagination cursors invalid; arrange for clients to restart lists and deploy the same new value to
all processes together. To undo, restore the previous shared value and recreate the processes;
cursors issued under the temporary value then fail. This setting is unrelated to token signatures.

Token signing-key rotation and client/webhook secret rotation are administrator operations, with
their own overlap and retirement rules. Use [Signing keys](/docs/administer/signing-keys/),
[Clients](/docs/administer/clients/) and [Webhook delivery](/docs/run/webhook-delivery/).
Resealing is storage-key maintenance and does not rotate those underlying credentials.


## Change the database password

`POSTGRES_PASSWORD` initializes a new PostgreSQL volume. Editing `.env` alone does not change the
stored role password. For the reference installation, arrange a maintenance window and keep the
old private settings until you have checked the new connection:

1. Stop every engine using the database. For the single reference engine, run
   `docker compose stop engine`. Keep the database running.
2. Open an interactive PostgreSQL session through the database container:

   ```bash
   docker compose exec database psql -U rdm -d rdm
   ```

   At its prompt, enter `\password rdm`. Type the new password twice when prompted; do not put
   it in a SQL statement or shell command. Leave with `\q`. Use a URL-safe generated password
   for this deployment: Compose embeds it in the engine URL without encoding it.
3. Save the same password as `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` in the private environment file. Recreate the
   services with `docker compose up -d`, preserving the same project and volumes. This updates
   the engine connection; it does not reinitialize PostgreSQL.
4. Require readiness 200 and a successful sign-in. Inspect engine logs for connection failures.
   Update the protected configuration copy associated with your next backup.

If the new connection fails, check that the role and environment contain the same password and
that the URL is valid. To undo during the maintenance window, use the database session to set the
previous password, restore the previous private settings and recreate again. Do not delete the
database volume to make initialization run again. For an externally managed database, coordinate
the role change with its administrator and update every engine's connection secret together.

Provider, SMTP and AI credentials are changed at their issuing service and in their respective
[sign-in and mail](/docs/run/sign-in-and-mail-setup/) or [AI](/docs/run/set-up-ai/) configuration.
Test the replacement before revoking the old credential where the issuer permits overlap.
Resealing does not replace those external credentials. Certificate private keys follow the
[HTTPS renewal procedure](/docs/run/https/#renew-or-undo-a-proxy-change).
guide/src/content/docs/run/security-chec:
---
title: Security checklist
description: Check transport, secrets, access and recovery boundaries before opening an installation.
reader: operator
---

Use this list before opening traffic and after a proxy, sign-in or key change. The Docker Compose
reference is the tested installation. A custom balancer or network boundary needs checks of its
own; historical security tests do not certify your deployment.

- **HTTPS and one origin:** use a valid certificate and the permanent HTTPS `PUBLIC_URL`.
  Check certificate renewal and HTTP redirection if port 80 is open. Public TCP 443 alone is
  sufficient for automatic certificates; port 80 may remain closed. See [HTTPS](/docs/run/https/).
- **Private services:** publish only `web`, or Caddy with the automatic overlay. Keep PostgreSQL,
  engine and metrics ports private. Compose trusts forwarded caller addresses only from the private
  ranges in `FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS`, not every address. For another proxy, set that list in `.env`
  to the addresses that connect to the engine and recreate it.
- **Trusted balancers:** with `WEB_TLS=proxy`, restrict access to the balancer, replace untrusted
  forwarded headers there and set `WEB_TRUSTED_PROXIES` to its actual connecting range.
  Empty trusts nobody and combines users under the balancer's address for throttling.
- **Browser origins:** keep `CORS_ORIGINS` to the exact intended origins. The session refresh cookie is
  HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict, scoped to `/oauth`, and Secure when `PUBLIC_URL` uses HTTPS.
  Provider redirect cookies use SameSite=Lax so the external sign-in return can work.
- **Framing and scripts:** verify the application's Content Security Policy restricts scripts and
  requests to its own origin and includes `frame-ancestors 'none'`; check `X-Frame-Options: DENY`
  too. The engine's sign-in pages, guide and API reference supply their own policies. Preserve
  them through your proxy; see [content security policies](/docs/run/https/#preserve-the-content-security-policies).
- **Secrets:** never commit environment files, keys or credentials, and never bake them into
  images. Keep backup keys outside PostgreSQL. Rehearse [resealing](/docs/run/secrets-and-keys/)
  as a planned operation; changing the key voids unused recovery codes.
- **Access:** replace broad setup grants with appropriate [roles](/docs/administer/roles-and-grants/).
  Capability switches restrict deployments but do not grant permissions. Authentication cannot
  be disabled by a setting. Keep and test a local recovery administrator.
- **Passwords and sign-in:** leave `PASSWORD_MIN_LENGTH=15` in production. Choose session lifetimes
  to match policy and use the organisation's provider or second-factor requirements. Disable
  leavers in refiroo as well as at the provider.
- **Throttling:** sign-in has per-name and per-address delays; after the first five failures for
  a name or 20 for an address, delays grow up to 15 minutes. A known e-mail address can be slowed by
  another caller. Preserve real caller addresses and investigate repeated failures.
- **Outbound connections:** permit only needed providers, SMTP, webhook receivers and optional AI.
  Preserve TLS verification and supply internal CAs where needed. Check the optional assistant's
  [network and data boundaries](/docs/run/ai/) before enabling it. Webhooks refuse private and
  loopback destinations by default. Enable `WEBHOOK_PRIVATE_ADDRESSES_ALLOWED` only for intended
  internal receivers; link-local destinations remain refused. Check private receivers after an
  upgrade, as existing subscriptions are subject to the same rule.
- **Assistant sessions:** keep `AI_AGENT_SANDBOX=container` as supplied by the image and Compose.
  Size the `ASSISTANT_USERS` build argument for the engine processes (default 8). Each task keeps
  its transcript in its own folder. Permissions open that folder only to the user running the
  turn and close it between turns. Each turn takes a free session user and resets that user's
  processes, home and temporary files before and after running. Keep Compose's `init: true`, or
  use `docker run --init` with the image.
  The provider credential still reaches the session, and outbound connections are unrestricted.
  Use a dedicated credential with a spending limit and your deployment's network restrictions.
  Task isolation inside the container depends on Unix permissions and the reset; reviews are
  not proof of isolation. A separate container per session is stronger and is not built in.
  See [the assistant's session](/docs/run/ai/#the-assistants-session) for all three limits.
- **Files and logs:** protect job files, delivery payloads, database backups and debug logs as
  sensitive data. CSV exports prefix formula-like text with a single quote; keep that protection
  when opening or returning a file. Other CSV sources may lack it. XLSX exports are unaffected.
  See [CSV text rules](/docs/use/importing-and-exporting/#text-in-csv-files).
- **Recovery and updates:** test a [restore](/docs/run/backup-and-restore/) and watch
  [readiness and failures](/docs/run/monitoring/). Use a release receiving security fixes;
  before 1.0 that is the latest minor release. Keep image digests, the Claude Code build version,
  Python constraints and npm lock files with your source; move them using the
  [build-version procedure](/docs/run/upgrades/#maintain-build-versions).

## Repeat checks after a change

Check the real installation after changing a proxy, public address, identity provider, key or
permission. A sign-in test at the old address does not verify the new one. Use a narrowly granted
test person and a working recovery administrator; preserve previous configuration and a matching
backup before maintenance. Follow the linked procedures for credential rotation and recovery.

## Check the installed boundary

You need an operator shell, access administration support and a browser on the caller's network.
Perform these checks before public access and after a proxy change. They read the current
installation; they do not prove every possible attack is prevented.

```bash
docker compose ps
curl -I https://refiroo.example.org/
curl -i https://refiroo.example.org/metrics
curl -i https://refiroo.example.org/api/v1/workspaces
```

Replace the public name. Confirm no engine or PostgreSQL port mapping; framing and content-type
headers from [HTTPS](/docs/run/https/#verify-from-the-callers-network); public metrics 404; and an
unauthenticated workspace request refused with `401 AUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED` after startup.
A readiness failure or startup maintenance mode can prevent ordinary authentication handling;
resolve it before judging permissions. A 200 application page returned by a misrouted proxy is
not a successful API-authentication test: check status, content type and response content.

With a fresh browser session, sign in as a test person with narrow grants, verify only their
workspaces are offered, then sign out and confirm a protected page requires sign-in again. An
access administrator should confirm the local recovery account and second-factor recovery route.
Do not intentionally lock out the last administrator to test recovery.

## Review trust and secrets after a change

For a proxy-mode deployment, record the actual address range the balancer connects from and the
private route to web. `WEB_TRUSTED_PROXIES` must describe that route; a caller must not be able to
bypass the balancer to supply trusted forwarding headers. The base file publishes web ports, so
proxy mode also requires a host firewall/network rule restricting who can reach them. Setting a
trust variable alone does not install that firewall rule.

Keep `SECRETS_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, the database password, cursor key and TLS private key in protected
storage and test that recovery staff can retrieve the right versions. Check that backup storage
is protected as well as the live host. The application does not supply a secret store, host firewall,
SPF/DKIM, backup scheduler or deployment-wide log retention; configure these in your environment.
No hardware minimum or complete production threat assessment has been measured by this guide.

If a credential leaked, determine which one before acting. Resealing protects stored ciphertext;
it does not revoke a leaked client or webhook credential. Rotate that credential through its
administrator workflow and distribute the replacement securely. For a sealing-key change, follow
[the offline reseal procedure](/docs/run/secrets-and-keys/) and replace affected recovery codes.

A failed check should leave public writes closed until corrected. Restore the prior known-safe
proxy/configuration and recreate affected services where possible, then recheck TLS, authentication,
caller-address handling and readiness. Do not reopen a database/engine port as a temporary repair
for a proxy error. Preserve concise diagnostics and a request ID for escalation, with no secrets.
guide/src/content/docs/run/set-up-ai.md:
---
title: Set up AI
description: Enable the assistant and AI provider in Docker Compose, supply credentials, and check that each works.
reader: operator
---

Use these steps for an existing Docker Compose installation. Claude Code is already installed in
the engine image. You do not need `docker exec`, an installation command inside the container, or
an interactive sign-in there.

First decide what data may leave the instance and which features you need. [About AI in
refiroo](/docs/run/ai/) explains the separate switches, permissions, session guards and retention.

## Choose the features and credentials

Both switches are needed for all AI features. Set `AI_SEND_LEVEL=values` for the assistant and
mapping targets. The two switches can use different credentials.

| Features | Switch | With a Claude subscription | With an Anthropic API key |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Load a workbook or change records with the assistant; **Change this model…** | `AI_AGENT_COMMAND="claude --model sonnet --permission-mode bypassPermissions"` | `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` from `claude setup-token` | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` |
| Proposed mapping targets, asking a list in words, explanations of model changes and what changed | `AI_PROVIDER` | Development and trying features: `AI_PROVIDER=claude-code`, `AI_MODEL=sonnet`; built into the engine image, uses Claude Code's sign-in or `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` | `AI_PROVIDER=claude`, `AI_API_KEY`; optional `AI_MODEL` |

For a production provider, use the Claude API with an API key, or `openai-compatible` with a
chat-completions endpoint, including a model hosted inside your organisation. `AI_PROVIDER=claude`
cannot use a Claude subscription token. The development subscription option is explained below.

## 1. Open the installation's environment file

Run the commands below from the repository root, where `compose.yml` lives.

- For the normal Compose installation, edit `.env`. If you use a different environment file,
  edit that file and use your existing Compose invocation; `RDM_ENV_FILE` must name the file
  passed to the engine.
- For the documentation's reference instance, edit `guide/reference/.env`. It is generated on the
  first `guide/reference/reference.sh up`. If the instance has not been created, run that command
  first. Do not replace the generated database, encryption or sign-in settings.

Compose passes this file's settings to the engine, including Claude Code's credential variables.
Editing an example file does not configure a running instance.

**`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` and `AI_API_KEY` are secrets. Never commit them or a
filled environment file.** The examples below contain placeholders: replace them only in your
private environment file. Do not paste credentials into the assistant's instructions or a support
report.

## 2. Enable the assistant

Add or update these lines in that environment file:

```dotenv
AI_AGENT_COMMAND="claude --model sonnet --permission-mode bypassPermissions"
AI_AGENT_SANDBOX=container
AI_SEND_LEVEL=values
```

The command selects Claude Code and its model. refiroo adds its own session restrictions and
replaces the command's permission-mode option with the mode it enforces. The example does not
remove those guards. `AI_AGENT_SANDBOX=container` runs the session without Claude Code's permission
prompts so it can execute the shell commands needed for a task. The image and Compose already
set it to `container`; Compose overrides a different value in `.env`. Each turn takes
one of the image's separate session users, which cannot read the engine's secrets or job files.
Permissions open the task's folder only to that user for the turn and close it afterwards.
The engine resets that user's processes, home and temporary files before and after the turn;
a failed reset before a turn prevents it from starting. Compose supplies `init: true` to collect
ended processes; a deployment using `docker run` needs `--init`.
The pool has 8 users by default; see [session isolation](/docs/run/ai/#the-assistants-session).
**The provider's key or token reaches the session, and the container does not restrict outbound
network access.** Use a dedicated credential with a spending limit and apply any required network
restrictions in your deployment. **Task isolation inside one container depends on Unix permissions
and the reset around each turn.** Reviews found and fixed defects; they do not prove isolation.
A separate container per session is stronger and is not built in. `values` allows the assistant to read the
workbook and records needed by the task. Lower levels make the assistant unavailable.

`AI_AGENT_API_URL` is the address the assistant's session uses to reach this engine's API.
Compose sets it to `http://127.0.0.1:8000` unless you override it in the environment file, so no
extra setting is needed for the shipped installation. The session runs inside the engine container:
`localhost` there names that container, so a public address such as `http://localhost:8480` would
send it to the wrong port. Keep `PUBLIC_URL` as the address people open in their browsers.

Choose **one** of the following credential methods for Claude Code.

### Use an Anthropic API key

Put your API key in the same environment file:

```dotenv
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=replace-with-your-anthropic-api-key
```

This is Claude Code's variable. `AI_API_KEY` alone does not authenticate the assistant. Leave
`CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` unset for this method.

### Use a Claude subscription token

On a computer with Claude Code installed and access to your Claude subscription, run:

```bash
claude setup-token
```

Follow Claude Code's browser authorisation and copy the token it prints. Put it in the engine's
environment file:

```dotenv
CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN=replace-with-the-token-from-claude-setup-token
```

Leave `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` unset in that file when using the subscription token. Claude Code reads
these variables itself; refiroo passes only the [named session variables](/docs/run/ai/#the-assistants-session),
not every variable with an `ANTHROPIC_` or `CLAUDE_` prefix. Creating the token on your computer
does not automatically transfer it to the engine.
See [Claude Code's authentication documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/authentication#generate-a-long-lived-token)
for its token requirements and lifecycle.

The engine sets `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` separately for each task, inside its randomly named folder
in the `assistant` volume. No shared Claude Code configuration folder needs mounting.

## 3. Enable the provider if needed

For mapping targets, questions in words and summaries through the Claude API, add:

```dotenv
AI_PROVIDER=claude
AI_API_KEY=replace-with-your-anthropic-api-key
```

This key is separate from the assistant's credential setting. A subscription token is not a
replacement for `AI_API_KEY`. If you use API-key authentication for both, put the API key in both
`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and `AI_API_KEY`. If you only need the assistant, leave `AI_PROVIDER` unset.

You can set `AI_MODEL` to choose the provider's model and `AI_BASE_URL` to use a gateway. Leaving
both empty uses refiroo's default Claude model and Anthropic's API. The assistant's `--model sonnet`
does not select the provider model.

For an endpoint using the chat-completions protocol, set `AI_PROVIDER=openai-compatible`,
`AI_BASE_URL` and `AI_MODEL`; set `AI_API_KEY` if that endpoint requires one. A provider on another
container or host needs an address reachable from the engine container: `localhost` inside the
container refers to that container.

Keep `AI_SEND_LEVEL=values` for mapping targets. If you enable only features that need less data,
choose `structure` or `samples` instead. `AI_SAMPLE_VALUES=20` controls sampling at `samples`,
not the amount read by the assistant at `values`.

### Use the subscription for provider features in development

The built-in `claude-code` provider answers through Claude Code using the token's or the
developer's sign-in and limits. It is part of the engine image, so it works on a
[developer instance](/docs/run/developer-instance/), on the guide's reference instance and in a
container without extra files.

For a developer instance, put these settings in `.dev/settings.env`; install and authenticate
Claude Code on the host. For the reference instance, put them in `guide/reference/.env` beside the
assistant settings and subscription token from step 2:

```dotenv
AI_PROVIDER=claude-code
AI_MODEL=sonnet
```

Leave `AI_API_KEY` unset for this provider; it authenticates as Claude Code does (`CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`, or `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` for API billing). Each request runs a separate Claude Code call with no
tools, MCP servers or saved session. It still sends the feature's context to Claude. Usage and
cost are recorded in **Calls**; reported dollar amounts are usage at API prices, not a
subscription invoice. With a subscription token this option is for development and trying the
features. A production installation normally uses `claude` with `AI_API_KEY` or `openai-compatible`.

A custom provider can also be named as `AI_PROVIDER=package.module:function`. The module must be
installed in the engine's Python environment; the factory takes no arguments and returns an object
with `propose(request)`. A missing module or unsuitable result refuses startup.

## 4. Enable external agent access if needed

To let external MCP assistants connect, add:

```dotenv
MCP_ENABLED=true
```

This is optional and does not enable or authenticate the built-in assistant. The shipped web image
already forwards `/mcp` and `/.well-known/`; another reverse proxy must forward them too. After
restart, a security administrator can open **Settings › Connections › Agent access** to register and
manage assistants and agent clients. Their grants determine the data they can reach.

## 5. Apply the settings

:::caution[Automatic HTTPS needs both Compose files]
With [automatic HTTPS](/docs/run/install-with-compose/#5-start-with-automatic-https), run `docker compose up -d` with
`compose.acme.yml` too: keep `COMPOSE_FILE=compose.yml:compose.acme.yml` set in the shell, or add
`-f compose.yml -f compose.acme.yml` to each command. Without it, web is recreated without Caddy
in front and the site stops answering until you run the command again with both files.
:::

For the normal Compose installation, run:

```bash
docker compose up -d
docker compose ps
```

For the documentation's reference instance, use its own command instead:

```bash
guide/reference/reference.sh start
guide/reference/reference.sh status
```

The reference `start` command starts or recreates its dedicated Compose project's containers without
rebuilding the images or rerunning the data loader. Use `up` for the initial build and data load. It uses `guide/reference/.env`, rather than the repository-root `.env`. Open
`http://localhost:8480` and sign in with the reference administrator's credentials from that file.

Changing the environment requires the engine container to be recreated; `up -d` applies those
changes without rebuilding the image. A plain `docker compose restart` does not load an edited environment file.
The shipped Compose file keeps task folders, Claude Code configuration and session logs in the
single `assistant` volume. Recreating the container keeps it. After upgrading from the earlier
shared-transcript layout, existing tasks keep their files but start a new session on their next
turn; see [Upgrades](/docs/run/upgrades/#volumes-and-open-assistant-tasks).

## 6. Check the provider and assistant separately

1. With **Operations** access, open **Settings › This instance › AI**. Under **What is switched on**,
   check **Assistant** and **Provider** against what you enabled. **Assistant: On** means the command
   is set; it does not prove a session can authenticate. Check **What may be sent** too.
2. If a provider is configured, select **Send a test request**. Success shows **The AI provider
   answered** and a new **Calls** entry. The request contains none of your reference data. With
   only the assistant enabled, this button is absent.
3. To test the assistant independently, use an active workspace and a person with **Use AI proposals**,
   **Work in change sets**, **Bulk and import**, and permission to create jobs there. The model-change
